p. 14
Continued development of 
sustainability work
We continue to support our customers in their 
transition, with actions including broadened 
partnerships and the launch of new ­services. 
We have also updated the Swedbank Sus-
tainable Funding Framework, a framework 
that makes it possible to issue both green 
and social bonds. For more information, 
see pages 14–15.
p. 26
Increased availability and  
shorter queuing times
Common to all four Business Areas 
are several new services that make it 
easier for customers to manage their 
banking affairs. This development 
contributes to more efficient service 
and a better customer experience. 
Swedbank is increasing accessibility 
for our customers by allowing more 
banking matters to be performed 
directly in the app and the internet 
bank, while also improving our service 
over the phone. For more information 
about our ­Business Areas, see pages 
26–33.
p. 18
Updated 15/27 business plan
At the Investor Day in June, we presented Swedbank’s 
updated 15/27 business plan. The plan describes how 
we aim to maintain a return of at least 15 per cent 
through 2027 by strengthening customer focus, increasing 
volumes and improved efficiency. For more information, 
see page 18.

2 Swedbank Annual Report 2025

Stronger customer 
offering through 
partnerships
Swedbank continues to develop 
strategic collaborations that 
drive innovation and long-term 
customer value.
Swedbank and SpareBank 1 
entered a new partnership to 
create a leading Nordic investment 
bank: SB1 Markets. This increases 
industry expertise and strengthens 
our ability to serve customers 
across the Nordic region.
The mortgage credit institution 
Stabelo was acquired with the 
aim of further developing the 
mortgage offering and giving 
more customers access to 
our services.
We acquired Barclay’s shares in 
Entercard, strengthening our 
overall offering in cards and con-
sumer loans.
Through our collaboration with 
Econans, we help our customers 
make informed choices and pre-
pare their homes for the future.
A selection of key events in 2025
A valued and responsible brand 
Swedbank was named the most loved brand in 
the Baltic countries for the seventh consecutive 
year, and was also ranked as the most engaging 
and humane brand at the Baltic Brand Forum. 
We have also received significant recognition for 
our work in the area of equity. We are once again 
featured on Allbright’s Green List of companies 
with equitable leadership, while Equileap ranked 
Swedbank in Sweden fourth in their equity rank-
ing. Both reflect our long-term focus on creating 
a compassionate and inclusive culture.
S&P Global 
upgraded Swed-
bank’s credit rating to 
AA- long-term and A-1+ short-
term, with stable outlook and 
an expectation that we will 
continue to develop strongly 
with a solid capital base. In its 
assessment, S&P cites that 
Swedbank has strong gover-
nance, solid risk management 
and robust capitalisation. They 
also point out that we have an 
effective structure to prevent 
financial crime. 
Swedbank 
receives higher 
credit rating  
from S&P
Enhanced societal engagement 
In 2025, we continued to develop initiatives 
such as the Lyckoslanten magazine, Young 
Economy and other collaborations that pro-
mote learning and inclusion. We launched 
a new newsletter for school staff, and in 
connection with the Allowance Day initia-
tive, activities were carried out across the 
country, and the Institute for Financial 
Health published a new report on children’s 
finances. Together with the Savings Banks, 
we also established two national essay 
awards to promote research in the field of 
financial health and well-being. In Estonia, 
Latvia and Lithuania, Swedbank has 
donated EUR 30m over the past two years 
to establish foundations aimed at strength-
ening education, research and sustainable 
societal development.

Dear Reader, 
I am proud to present Swedbank’s Annual Report for 2025. Through our financial strength, 
proven business model and advisory services, we enable the many people and businesses to 
create a better future. We continue to be the most loved brand in the Baltic countries, and 
we have close to eight million private and corporate customers in our home markets. Managing 
their trust is the foundation of our business and crucial for the bank’s development over time. 
This responsibility pervades our entire business.
2025 was a year that required both responsiveness and for-
ward thinking. Geopolitical tensions affected the world around 
us, and the consequences of climate change became increas-
ingly apparent. Despite geopolitical uncertainty and trade 
­tariffs, the global economic situation was more resilient than 
expected. Inflation eased and central banks continued to lower 
interest rates. 
2025 was a successful year for Swedbank. Return on equity 
was higher than our target of 15 per cent. This is a strong 
result and proof that our business model works. For the finan-
cial year 2025, it is proposed that 70 per cent of the profit be 
distributed, which is in line with our dividend policy. The Board 
of Directors is also proposing an extra dividend in view of our 
strong capital position. As a sustainable and profitable bank, 
Swedbank gives back to society through its owners: savings 
banks, insurance companies, pension funds, fund manage-
ment companies, private shareholders and foundations.
During the year, we also further strengthened our internal 
gover­nance, risk control and compliance. This was recognised 
when the credit rating agency S&P Global raised Swedbank’s 
credit rating and highlighted in particular the bank’s improve-
ments in these particular areas.
Shortly after the turn of the year, Swedbank was informed that 
the US Department of Justice (DOJ) had concluded its multi-
year investigation of the bank without taking any further 
action. Earlier during year, the US Securities and Exchange 
Commission (SEC) made a similar announcement. This means 
that we are putting two more investigations into historical 
shortcomings behind us and can now devote even more atten-
tion to the future. 
From vision to reality and a new plan  
for the future
2025 marked both a significant ending and a new beginning 
for Swedbank. We delivered on Swedbank 15/25, the roadmap 
we presented in 2022 with a target to achieve a return on 
equity of at least 15 per cent by 2025. By focusing on strategic 
priorities, growth in selected segments and improved availa­
bility, we succeeded in achieving our target.
During the year, we presented our plan to continue delivering 
a sustainable return on equity of 15 per cent until 2027 – 
Swedbank 15/27. It starts with the customer and focuses on 
strengthening customer interactions, increasing volumes and 
continuing to improve efficiency. These three areas pervade 
work in all four of our Business Areas. 
Progress for our customers – in every meeting
Our customer promise is to make our customers’ financial 
lives easier with caring advice, intuitive service and by ­creating 
long-term value. It guides our work every single day.
To improve the customer experience and improve accessi­
bility, we have continued to invest in new technologies and 
platforms. During the year, we improved both the lending 
­platform and savings platform, as well as launched new func-
tions in the app and the advisory tools. The ultimate aim is to 
make it easy to manage everyday matters digitally.
We have worked systematically to reduce waiting times and 
increase availability for our customers in Sweden. Our branch 
opening hours for spontaneous visits have been adjusted to 
enable our employees to spend more time meeting customers 
in scheduled meetings and over the phone. This has resulted 
in ­significantly shorter waiting times in Sweden.
We made great progress in this area during the year. Towards 
the end of 2025, 86 per cent of customer calls in Sweden were 
being answered within three minutes. This is an improvement 
that reflects both increased availibility and efficiency, and is in 
line with our target.
During autumn 2025, we worked to further identify changes 
that can strengthen our customer focus and help us deliver 
on our strategic direction and on the Swedbank 15/27 plan. 
Decision-making must be moved even closer to those working 
close to our customers.
In Sweden, the increased availability and faster pace of the 
mortgage process have meant that we increased our market 
share of new loans, but there is more to do. The Premium and 
Private Banking concept has attracted more customers and 
increased inflows from both existing Swedbank customers 
and new customers. The corporate business is growing 
through local presence, sectoral expertise and a more proac-
tive approach. In Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, we are market 
leaders in both private and corporate markets. Continuous 
improvements are enabling us to strengthen our customer 
interactions, win more business and increase our efficiency.

Partnerships and structural steps  
for the future
We are continuously developing our strategic partnerships. 
The collaboration with the savings banks in Sweden creates 
a unique local strength in the Swedish market. During the year, 
we also further developed our Nordic collaboration through 
partnerships. Together with SpareBank 1, we formed a new 
Nordic investment bank in Sweden – SB1 Markets. This part-
nership will put us in a better position to meet the needs of our 
corporate customers through increased industry expertise, 
expanded equity analysis and equity trading. 
Structural steps have been taken, and two major transactions 
were completed in 2025. To complement our mortgage busi-
ness and at the same time be able to better meet the needs of 
younger and more digital customers, we acquired the mort-
gage institution Stabelo. Through the acquisition of Entercard, 
we have created the largest card business in the Nordic-Baltic 
region. Both transactions create new opportunities.
A stronger society starts with resilience
Social preparedness continued to be a priority during the year. 
Through our work on cybersecurity, payment infrastructure 
and stability, we contribute to resilience in Sweden, Estonia, 
Latvia and Lithuania. We have tackled fraud – we have 
enhanced our preventive work through investments in new 
technology and improved customer information. This is  
a long-term commitment.
A sustainable future requires action now
Sustainability is an integral part of our business strategy and 
of importance for sound, long-term profitability. As a bank, 
we have an important role to play in the transition to a more 
sustainable society. 
We finance energy-efficient properties and advise customers 
on sustainable renovation. There was high demand for sus-
tainable investments from our customers during the year. 
Nearly 40 per cent of the bonds arranged by Swedbank in 2025 
were classified as sustainable, and our Sustainable Asset 
­Registry has now exceeded SEK 165bn. In Sweden, we were 
named the most sustainable brand among banks by SB Insight 
in 2025. This gives us added strength to continue to drive 
change and help our customers make the transition.
200 years with a focus on financial health 
Swedbank has been around for more than 200 years, and this 
defines the business. Then, as now, the financial health of indi-
viduals has been close to our hearts. For us, financial health 
means having knowledge of your personal finances, a long-
term savings buffer, income that exceeds expenses, insurance 
that protects your finances and, if you borrow, margins. 
The Swedbank Institute for Financial Health enables us to 
enhance people’s knowledge of their private finances and con-
tributes to increased financial security. During the year, more 
than 110 000 children and young people in Sweden received 
training in private finance through the Young Economy initia-
tive. In Estonia, we opened a new future hub for education and 
advisory services, with activities that include teaching school-
children about household budgets and pensions. 
In Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, Swedbank has donated 30 
million euros to foundations aimed at strengthening educa-
tion, research and sustainable societal development. And in 
2026, we will be celebrating the 100th anniversary of Lycko-
slanten magazine! Through our work, we strengthen our 
­customers’ financial health.
We build Swedbank together
Let me conclude by extending my thanks to our customers. 
The trust you place in us enables us to continue to develop the 
bank. We take this responsibility very seriously. Thank you!
Running Swedbank would not have been possible without our 
employees. Your commitment and competence make a differ-
ence every day. Thank you! 
A big thank you to you, all of our shareholders, for choosing 
to invest in Swedbank. You are the ones who provide capital 
so that we can run our banking operations. Thank you!
Customers, employees, owners. Together we are building a 
bank that makes a difference. A bank that can work towards 
the vision of a financially sound and sustainable society. 
Swedbank stands strong. With our customers and our busi-
ness behind us, our values as a guiding star and our strategy 
as a map, we continue to move forward for sustainable growth, 
customer benefit and long-term value.
Our focus is on the future of our customers.
Stockholm, February 2026
Jens Henriksson
President and CEO

7 Swedbank Annual Report 2025

For more than forty years, the non-profit 
organisation Junior Achievement (JA) 
has been giving young people the oppor-
tunity to set up and run a business as 
part of their school work. Swedbank is 
proud to have been the organisation’s 
partner since 1985 – as a jury member, 
advisor and supporter for entrepreneurs 
of the future. 
Junior Achievement started with the 
ambition to inspire and train young 
people to develop their entrepreneurship 
and thereby also promote positive socie-
tal development. Since then, interest 
among students has grown every year  
– in total, more than 600 000 upper sec-
ondary school students have run over 
170 000 JA businesses. Many continue 
to be entrepreneurs even after upper 
secondary school.
Annika Sund launched the JA company 
Dalaklockan, which sold hand-painted 
Dala clocks, in her second year at upper 
secondary school in 1986. She is now 
marketing manager at the family-owned 
company Leksands Knäckebröd, which 
she runs together with her brother Peter 
Joon, who is CEO. 
“It was really educational to see the 
entire process from product concept to 
financial statements. Being able to run 
a business in practice made it so much 
more tangible than just reading about 
accounting and marketing in books. It 
gave me a good basic understanding of 
my future life in business, as well as 
a good starting point when I came to 
choose what I wanted to study next,” 
says Annika Sund.
It has been shown that having entrepre-
neurship on the timetable has positive 
effects, such as greater motivation to 
study, and also helping to reduce differ-
ences in classrooms. According to a 
study from Swedbank, former JA entre-
preneurs save more, in several different 
forms, and have better knowl-
edge of financial concepts 
and forms of saving.
Junior Achievement 
is now is a natural 
feature of everyday 
school life at many 
upper secondary 
and compulsory 
schools around 
Sweden. The “Fram-
tidskoll” theme day is 
an event at which Swed-
bank’s employees meet and 
train around 25,000 year nine stu-
dents across the country in personal 
finance, entrepreneurship and working 
life in general. At upper secondary level, 
a number of Swedbank’s employees act 
as mentors for JA companies, contribut-
ing their knowledge, experience and net-
works, in parallel with jury work in several 
districts. 
“It’s inspiring to see how JA 
is now engaging students 
from numerous study pro-
grammes, not just economics. 
There are amazing ideas coming out of 
both technology and natural science 
study programmes, and we can see that 
many are taking the next step in their 
entrepreneurship,” says Frida Svensson 
Söderlind, Team Manager in Growth & 
Start-ups at Swedbank and jury member 
for Junior Achievement.
Junior Achievement is extremely satis-
fied with developments so far, but 
believes there is much more to be done.  
“We want JA entrepreneurship to be 
available to everyone, all over the coun-
try and in all areas of upper secondary 
education,” observes Carsten Greiff, 
Head of Strategic Development at 
Junior Achievement.
Looking to the future, there is a clear 
desire to broaden participation to 
include more students from vocational 
programmes, where the step to running 
your own business upon completing 
your studies is often a short one. The 
ambition is to develop the support with 
adapted methods and tools so that 
teachers can integrate entrepreneurship 
into the teaching of vocational pro-
grammes. The organisation also wants 
to grow at compulsory school 
level through more success-
ful initiatives such as 
Framtidskoll, a lecture 
concept about per-
sonal finance for 
­students in year 9.
Together, Junior 
Achievement and 
Swedbank want to 
continue to build 
bridges between school 
and working life – and 
create better conditions for 
young people to understand 
finances, develop their entrepreneurship 
and actively shape their own future, 
whichever path they then choose.  
“Our long-term collaboration enables us 
to contribute to increasing knowledge of 
entrepreneurship and private finances, 
and thereby Swedbank’s vision to 
strengthen the financial health of society,” 
says Frida Svensson Söderlind.

From tied up to connected up – generational
succession at Väcklinge Södergård
When the Josefsson family was facing 
another generational succession at 
Väcklinge Södergård, located just out-
side Reftele in south-western Småland, 
discussions began about what the next 
step should be. The son Christoffer 
already had his own construction com-
pany, which was doing well. But when 
there wasn't enough time to work both 
with his own company and on the farm 
where he grew up, the decision eventu-
ally made itself. He would continue to run 
the family farm and invest in dairy cows.
“We needed to make a decision about 
the farm’s future investments for the 
next generations,” say Viktoria and 
Håkan Josefsson, who have run the 
farm themselves for over thirty years.
As the cows were standing tied up in 
stalls, a method of livestock farming 
that was being phased out, it was only 
a matter of time before the farm, which 
had served agriculture for ten genera-
tions, would have to be upgraded. The 
result was an investment in a state-of-
the-art farming facility, with an extra 
focus on animal comfort and climate­-
adapted operations.  
“It costs a lot at the moment, but if we 
have animals that are healthy and happy, 
it will pay for itself in the long run,” com-
ments Christoffer, who has himself been 
construction manager, joiner, farmer and 
much more in the new project.
Swedbank has been the family’s bank 
for generations, and it is now forestry 
and agriculture advisor Anna Hallakulle 
who manages the relationship. 
“These are long-term collaborations, we 
want to be there all the way. Not only to 
enable the generational change, but also 
to contribute to the future of agriculture. 
The family at Väcklinge Södergård had 
a well-considered plan that made it easy 
for us to sort out the financing,” she says.
Having an advisor who understands the 
conditions was crucial for the renova-
tion to become a reality.  
“It means a lot to meet someone who 
not only knows the industry, but shows 
faith in Swedish agriculture - even when 
the costings involve big sums and the 
market is volatile. In the plan to double 
production and invest in three milking 
robots, time and money were critical fac-
tors. We had a meeting with Swedbank 
in the autumn and the robots needed to 
be purchased before the end of the year 
to avoid an upcoming price increase. 
Speedy processing and a loan commit-
ment issued on time made all the differ-
ence in enabling us to move on,” says 
the Josefsson family.
The investment has brought a major 
boost to both animal welfare and the 
work environment on the farm. Previ-
ously, milking alone took almost six 
hours a day – this work has now been 
streamlined with connected monitoring. 
 With the aid of the automated robots, 
the entire process can be managed in 
around 30 minutes a day, despite the 
number of cows more than doubling. 
With the new facility in place and stron-
ger growth than was budgeted, the 
family has already decided on their next 
investment. It will be a fourth robot. The 
next step is to implement the genera-
tional succession, where Swedbank is 
also involved and providing support.
In focus
We’ve done what we 
believe in – and 
we’ve had a bank that has 
supported us all the way.

Our strategic direction
Swedbank empowers the many people 
and businesses to create a better future. 
We offer financial advice, service and 
products in our four home markets: 
Sweden, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. 
By doing so, we work towards our 
vision of a financially sound and 
sustain­able society.
Our purpose
When the first savings banks were founded more than 200 
years ago, the aim was to empower people to improve their 
financial security. It is in the savings bank movement that 
Swedbank has its roots, and it influences everything we do 
throughout our operations – every single day.
Our vision

This includes sustainability from an environmental, social, 
financial, regulatory and ethical perspective. We are convinced 
that Swedbank, together with our large customer base, can 
continue to create value and contribute to a society that is 
sustain­able in the long term.
Our customer promise
We are here for our customers at every stage of their lives. 
Our customer promise, “Together we will make your financial 
life easier”, means that we offer caring advice, intuitive service 
and long-term value – for our customers and for society at large.
Our values
“Open, Simple and Caring” – is the cornerstone of our 
­corporate culture. These values support our vision and guide 
us in our daily work and decision-making, as well as in our 
meetings with each other, our customers and stakeholders. 
We are an open and respectful bank where diversity is pro-
moted among employees and customers. Our ambition is to 
create an uncomplicated and caring banking experience for 
all ­cus­tomers, based on their individual needs.
Our foundation
The foundation of our business is the way we work together to 
ensure an attractive workplace with an inclusive culture where 
employees contribute and are held accountable. Our focus is 
on running an efficient and profitable bank, with a compliant 
financial services platform. To run our business responsibly 
and efficiently, we need a standardised, scalable and stable 
infrastructure. Our foundation is extremely important in enabling 
us to fulfil our purpose, vision and customer promise.

Our sustainability perspective
For Swedbank, sustainability is a precondition for long-term profitability. We work 
to integrate a sustainability perspective into the business – from lending and asset 
­management to advisory services and product development. As a financial institution, 
Swedbank plays an important role in the transition by managing capital and supporting 
customers in the development of a more sustainable economy.
Swedbank’s role in the climate transition
As a bank, we can make the biggest difference by directing 
capital towards investments and activities that contribute to 
reduced emissions and increased resource efficiency. Swed-
bank’s climate transition plan is based on long-term targets for 
2050. To work towards this overall commitment, we have set 
interim targets for the credit portfolio, assets under manage-
ment and Swedbank’s own operations. We are striving to 
­continue integrating our commitments into our lending, 
­investment decisions and governance models.
Overarching targets
Swedbank’s climate-related targets are based on achieving net zero emissions by 2050 and adapting the credit portfolio and assets under 
manage­ment to the 1.5-degree target.

Borrowing and financing
Swedbank operates under a sustainability framework that 
guides how the bank raises funding and finances projects that 
contribute to environmental and social sustainability. Swed-

updated during 2025 to ensure that it continues to be in line

port solutions. Social bonds finance projects in areas such as

a financial risk, especially in sectors such as agriculture, 
­forestry and construction, while new regulations are driving 
reporting requirements. 
Swedbank is involved in work to integrate nature and biodiver-
sity in the financial sector through partnerships such as the 
PRB Nature Community of Practice, the Swedish Biocredit 
­Alliance and research programmes such as Mistra BIOPATH.

business operations, as methodologies and our understanding 
of Swedbank’s impact and exposure to risks improve. Swed-
bank Robur has adopted a Nature Strategy based on a frame-
work from the investor initiative Finance for Biodiversity 
Pledge. The strategy clarifies, among other things, that targets 
should be set within the nature area and that dialogue should 
be conducted with portfolio companies. Read more about 
Swedbank Robur’s Nature Strategy on our website.

How we create value
Through financial advice, services and products, we create value for our customers 
and shareholders, and contribute to stability in society.
We make our customers’ financial lives easier 
We create value for our 7.3 million private customers and 
545 000 corporate customers in Sweden, Estonia, Latvia and 
Lithuania by offering loans, savings, payments, insurance 
and daily banking services. We are available around the  
clock, offering advice and service in person, by phone and 
via digital services.
The need for advice is growing among our customers and 
it is becoming increasingly important to offer products and 
­services that are tailored to their individual financial situation. 
Since the majority of our customers today prefer to manage 
their banking affairs digitally, our ambition is for all day-to-day 
transactions to be performed on the phone or through the 
internet bank, with personal support available when needed. 
To keep creating value for our customers, we must constantly 
improve our offerings and continuously develop more 
­customised services.
How Swedbank creates shareholder value
Swedbank’s ambition is to create a competitive return for 
shareholders in the long term. We aim to deliver a sustain­able 
return on equity of at least 15 per cent, which our business 
plan is designed to achieve.
Capital repatriation
To live up to Swedbank’s ambition to be a low-risk bank, we 
need to understand and price our lending correctly. Our margin 
must therefore be high enough to cover credit impairments. 
The margin must also cover our own expenses, fees to strengthen 
financial stability and a return on shareholders’ equity. 
Swedbank’s dividend policy is to distribute 60–70 per cent of 
the annual profit to shareholders. The remaining 30–40 per 
cent is used to finance growth, develop the bank and weather 
economic pressure in difficult times. 
Income
Our largest source of income is net interest income: the differ-
ence between interest income from lending and interest costs 
for borrowing and borrowing. The lending is financed through 
deposits from businesses and private customers and through 
funding from the capital market. Our second largest income 
source comprises fees for products and services such as 
asset management and payments. Income from asset man-
agement is generated from a fee on assets under manage-
ment and is therefore affected by the performance of the 
financial markets. Income from payments comes primarily 
from card fees, but also from businesses that use our 
card ­terminals.
Expenses
Our main expense items are staff costs and IT expenses. 
To meet demand from customers, satisfy requirements from 
govern­ment agencies and increase cost efficiency, we must 
continuously invest in our employees, services and systems.

Swedbank and taxes 
Swedbank is one of the biggest taxpayers in our home 
­markets, and as a major employer we pay significant amounts 
in social security contributions. This enables us to contribute 
to economic development, security and welfare in the coun-
tries where Swedbank operates. 
Business conduct is a central element of our business model, 
and transparent tax management is part of this commitment. 
Moreover, society’s expectations of companies and their 
responsibility are now greater than ever, not least from inves-
tors and other stakeholders. We therefore strive to be open 
and transparent with the taxes and charges we pay and report, 
and we work to maintain a high level of transparency in tax 
management in the countries where we operate. 
Swedbank shall neither participate in nor constitute a platform 
for improper tax arrangements or aggressive tax planning. 
We shall minimise the risk of the business being exploited 
for tax evasion.
Swedbank actively contributes its expertise and resources 
to the further development of well-balanced and effective tax 
­legislation by participating in expert groups and committees, 
both nationally and internationally. We also actively engage 
in international sharing of information in the field of tax as 
part of our commitment to combat tax evasion and promote 
­transparency.

Our business plan
In June 2025, Swedbank presented 15/27, our updated business plan to deliver 
a sustain­able return on equity of at least 15 per cent by 2027.
We have reached the key targets in our previous Swedbank 
15/25 business plan, which was presented in 2022. This was 
achieved through a consistent focus on our business priorities 
using our strategic direction as a guide. The aim was to 
achieve a return on equity of at least 15 per cent, supported 
by a number of KPIs: C/I ratio of 0.4, a CET1 capital buffer of 
200 basis points and growth in income exceeding growth in 
expenses by an average of 3 percentage points per year.
Based on these results, our Investor Day in June featured a pre-
sentation of Swedbank 15/27 – an updated plan with ­targets 
for 2027. The plan aims to produce a return on equity of at least 
15 per cent, maintain high credit quality and ensure the efficient 
use of capital, while creating long-term value for our customers, 
shareholders and society. With a tried and tested business 
model, clear priorities and a strong foundation, we are well 
positioned for continued sustainable growth and profitability.

Our long-term strategic targets
We focus on long-term value creation and have defined strategic targets to measure 
­success in line with Swedbank’s Strategic Direction.
As a major operator in the financial market, we have a major responsibility. Through our efforts to 
minimise our climate footprint and offer relevant investments, financing solutions and services

in the development of society and take responsibility for our role in the financial system by main-
taining a strong financial position, high asset quality and solid capitalisation. 
 
Customer satisfaction and brand trust 
We create customer value by offering relevant products and services based on our customers’ 
needs. Delivering a high level of customer value is critical for our long-term profitability as well

24/7 availability
It is our goal to always be there to help our customers. We work continuously to maintain  
a stable infrastructure and reliable digital solutions to ensure that products and services are

Engaged employees
Engaged and proud employees create a better customer experience, which in turn leads to more

Solid risk management and compliance
Solid risk management is reflected throughout our operations and helps us to make well-informed,

development.

The results for 2024/2025 for the six sectors in the credit 
portfolio are presented in comparison with the baseline year 
for the measurement period in question. The results are 
impacted by factors such as customers’ emissions, Swed-
bank’s exposure and the size of customers’ assets. For more

The emission intensity of mortgages has decreased by  
3 per cent since 2019. The reduction has taken place in both 
Swedish (–10 per cent since 2019) and Baltic (–17 per cent 
since 2019) portfolios. At the same time, higher growth in 
the Baltic property portfolio since the baseline year, with 
higher emission intensity, resulted in a smaller reduction 
in emission intensity at group level. 
For the commercial properties sector, emission intensity 
decreased by 24 per cent compared to the baseline year 
2019. Above all, emission intensity decreased in the Swedish 
property portfolio during the year. Since 2019, emission 
intensity has decreased by 27 per cent for the Swedish 
­portfolio and by 11 per cent for the Baltic portfolio. 
Emissions from oil and gas have decreased by 52 per cent 
since 2019, which means that the target for 2030 has already 
been met. This is a consequence of Swedbank having 
chosen to significantly reduce exposure to oil and gas 
extraction. The remaining exposure in the portfolio is to  
a few refineries. 
Emission intensity in power generation has decreased by 
65 per cent since 2019. The renewable part of the portfolio 
continued to grow during the year through new customers. 
In the Baltic countries, many customers have divested fossil 
assets and switched to renewable production, which also 
produced a positive outcome.
For the steel sector, the emission intensity has decreased 
by 21 per cent since 2019. This is due to increased exposure 
to companies with lower emissions intensity and to the fact 
that several customers reduced their emissions during 
this period. 
For the credit portfolio in the field of shipping, where the 
target is to fully align with the International Maritime Organi-
zation’s (IMO) most ambitious emission reduction trajectory 
by 2030 (0 per cent alignment delta), the alignment delta has 
decreased to 12.6 per cent, down from 40 per cent in 2022. 
This has been achieved through both a change in exposure in 
the portfolio and a general reduction in the emission intensity 
of vessels.

Promoting financial health and an
investment culture in the Baltic countries
Boosting people’s financial health is 
a long-term focus area for Swedbank. 
Every year, Swedbank uses the Financial 
Health Index to measure people’s finan-
cial capability and knowledge of every-
day finances, savings, loans and finan-
cial security. The survey is conducted 
in all of Swedbank’s home markets and 
aims to track developments over time 
and highlight areas for improvement. In 
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the report 
has become an important tool for identi-
fying the most central focus areas – 
with a particular emphasis on strength-
ening financial knowledge and 
increasing willingness to invest.
There are still challenges linked to long-
term savings and financial knowledge. 
To encourage regular savings and lower 
the threshold for new investors, in spring 
2025 Swedbank launched the Micro 
Invest service in Estonia, Latvia and 
­Lithuania. By rounding up card pay-
ments and investing the difference in 
pre-selected funds from Swedbank 
Robur, the service offers an easy intro-
duction to saving. At the end of the year, 
more than 88 000 users had joined 
Micro Invest – a clear example of how 
we can get more people to start saving 
regularly by making it easier.
As part of its efforts to improve finan-
cial health, Swedbank introduced the 
Investment School digital education 
platform in Latvia and Estonia in 2025. 
Available in local languages, the plat-
form is aimed at both new and more 
experienced investors who want to start 
investing or acquire more investment 
skills. It offers interactive video material, 
which is free of charge and available to 
all, and issues a certificate upon comple-
tion of courses and tests.
A virtual investment simulator enables 
Swedbank to offer a dynamic learning 
environment in which users in Estonia 
and Latvia can practise investing using 
real market data, with no risk of losing 
actual capital. The simulator includes 
equities from the US, Europe and the 
Baltic countries, and funds from Swed-
bank Robur. It is designed for those who 
want to investigate how to make their 
first investments, test different invest-
ment strategies and compete against 
other users. Gaming elements create 
engagement, and there is the facility to 
organise both private and open compe­
titions managed by Swedbank.
With initiatives such as Micro Invest 
and the Investment School, Swedbank 
is taking practical steps to increase 
willing­ness to invest and thereby give 
a boost to financial health in the Baltic 
countries. This work continues, with the 
aim of giving more people confidence in 
their financial decisions and the condi-
tions for building stable and sustainable 
finances in the long term.
For me, Micro Invest was a simple first step into 
saving. The tool is user-friendly – from registration 
to choosing funds. As I pay by card several times a day, 
I hardly notice the automatic investments, but at the 
end of the month I can already see results. It’s a way for 
me to slowly build up a secure financial future.

  Large customer base paves the way for  
high cost efficiency and profitability
Swedbank is a leader in all four of our home markets. With our 
roots in the savings banks movement, we have a long history 
in Sweden and the Swedish market. We also have a strong 
foundation in our three Baltic home markets, Estonia, Latvia 
and Lithuania. Markets that are growing rapidly and showing 
high growth potential. Swedbank has strategic partnerships 
with the savings banks in Sweden, SpareBank 1 SR-Bank in 
Norway, Aktia in Finland and Sydbank in Danmark, which fur-
ther strengthens our customer offerings. Our strong position 
across our four home markets provides a customer base of 
nearly 8 million customers, of which approximately 7,3 million 
private individuals, and 545 000 corporates. Our scale is the 
foundation for cost efficiency, and the large deposit base 
­provides stable and cost-efficient funding. 
2
  A low-risk bank with diversification  
and solid credit quality
Swedbank has a conservative approach to both lending and 
capital. Strict underwriting criteria and prudent risk manage-
ment supports solid credit quality, which in turn leads to low 
credit losses over time. Swedbank’s geographical footprint 
across the Nordic and Baltic countries, combined with broad-
based lending to both households and coporates, provides 
diversification enabling stable earnings potential. Swedbank 
Robur is the largest asset manager in Sweden and Baltic coun-
tries. Swedbank is also one of the largest within insurance in 
all markets. The maturing savings and insurance markets in 
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania has added additional growth in 
recent years. 
3
  Strong capital generation capability  
contributes to high returns
Our business model, broad diversification and low risk profile 
enable strong capital generation. Our capitalisation is strong and 
our CET1 capital exceeds the Swedish FSA’s capital requirement 
by 3 percentage points at year-end 2025 – well above our target 
of maintaining a buffer of 2 percentage points above the require-
ment. The return on equity amounted to 15.2 per cent during the 
year, compared with our target of a sustainable ROE of at least 
15 per cent. The Board of Directors propose to the AGM an ordi-
nary dividend of SEK 20.45 per share, representing 70 per cent of 
2025 net profit. On the back of the strong capital position, the 
Board also propose a special dividend of SEK 9.35 per share. 
Combined, this amounts to a total dividend of SEK 29.80 per 
share. In relation to the share price at the end of 2025, the pro-
posed dividend represents a dividend yield of 9.3 per cent. 
Trading on several markets
Swedbank has one share class, ordinary shares (A shares), 
which has been listed on Nasdaq OMX Stockholm’s Large Cap 
list since 1995. Swedbank’s shares are traded on a number of 
marketplaces, with Nasdaq OMX Stockholm having the highest 
turnover. On average, Swedbank shares were traded on 
Nasdaq OMX Stockholm at a value of SEK 587 million per trad-
ing day in 2025. The bank also has an American Depositary 
Receipt (ADR) programme that makes it possible to invest in 
Swedbank on the US OTC market through depository receipts.
Ownership, holding of own shares  
and convertibles
Swedbank had 1 132 005 722 shares in issue as of 31 December 
2025, of which the holding of own shares amounted to 
7 780 212. Based on the 1 124 225 510 shares outstanding, 
37.2 per cent was owned by foreign investors and 62.8 per 
cent by Swedish investors, of which 14.0 per cent was owned 
by individual Swedish investors.
The 2025 AGM authorised the Board of Directors to resolve to 
repurchase up to 10 per cent of the shares in issue to adjust 
the bank’s capital structure to prevailing capital requirements 
and settle share-based remuneration programmes. In order to 
trade financial instruments on its own account, the bank was 
authorised to repurchase up to 1 per cent of the shares in issue.
The Board was also authorised to issue convertibles that can 
be converted to shares. These convertibles are used to meet 
the Swedish FSA’s capital requirements, and the bank has 
­previously issued such notes on a regular basis.
Share-based remuneration programmes
Swedbank holds its own shares so that it can achieve objec-
tives such as securing the commitment in its performance­-
based remuneration programmes, with the aim of building 
long-term employee engagement at Swedbank.
In 2025, a total of 1 206 567 shares were transferred for these 
remuneration programmes, corresponding to a dilution effect 
of 0.11 per cent based on the number of shares outstanding 
as of 31 December 2025.
The 2025 AGM resolved to adopt new performance-based 
remuneration programmes. They are expected to result in the 
future transfer of approximately 1.58 million shares, corre-
sponding to a total dilution effect of about 0.14 per cent based 
on the number of shares outstanding as of 31 December 2025.

Increasing lending and deposit volumes. 
Lending volumes increased partly supported 
by acquisitions.
Swedbank mainly conducts business in the product areas of 
lending, deposits, fund savings and life insurance, and payments.
Loans to customers increased by SEK 82bn to SEK 1 882bn 
(1 800) during the year, corresponding to an increase of 5 per 
cent. Corporate lending in Sweden increased by SEK 25bn as 
a consequence of higher demand, primarily in the real estate 
sector. Lending to mortgage customers in Sweden increased 
by SEK 21bn to SEK 934bn (913), of which the acquisition of 
Stabelo in December contributed SEK 17bn, while the volume 
brokered by the savings banks in Swedbank Hypotek 
decreased by SEK 7bn during the year. In Baltic Banking, lend­
ing, including foreign exchange effects, increased to both pri­
vate customers and corporates, by a total of SEK 11bn. In local 
currency, the increase was 10 per cent and 12 per cent respec­
tively. Foreign exchange effects had a negative impact of SEK 
26bn on lending volumes, compared with 31 December 2025.
The Sustainable Asset Registry increased by SEK 37bn to SEK 
165bn (128) during the year. The increase is mainly attribut­
able to the financing of green buildings, followed by renewable 
energy. At the end of the year, the registry contained SEK 
157bn in green assets and SEK 8bn in social assets, financed 
by the bank’s sustainable bonds.
Total deposits from customers increased by SEK 15bn to SEK 
1 300bn (1 285). Deposits from private customers increased by 
SEK 25bn, of which SEK 7bn in the Baltic countries. In local cur­
rency (EUR), the Baltic countries increased by 9 per cent (EUR). 
Deposits from private customers in Sweden increased by SEK 
17bn. Corporate deposits decreased by SEK 6bn in the Baltic 
countries, however an increase of 2 per cent in local currency 
(EUR). Corporate deposits in Sweden decreased by SEK 3bn. 
Foreign exchange effects had a negative impact of SEK 31bn 
on total deposit volume, compared with 31 December 2024.
Total assets under management rose by 5 per cent during 
the year to SEK 2 565bn (2 433) as of 31 December. Of this 
amount, SEK 2 044bn relates fund assets managed in Swed­
bank Robur Fonder, of which SEK 1 892bn (1 802) is attribut­
able to Sweden, SEK 129bn (126) to the Baltic countries and 
SEK 23bn (20) to other markets. The rise was primarily due to 
the positive market development, but net inflows also contrib­
uted. The net flow during the year amounted to SEK 22bn (33). 
In terms of assets under management, Swedbank Robur 
Fonder is the largest actor in the fund market in Sweden, 
­Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Its market share in Sweden fell 
slightly an amounted to 21 per cent (22) as of 31 December. 
In Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, market shares also fell slightly 
to 39 (40), 37 (39) and 36 (37) per cent respectively.
Assets under management within Swedbank’s Swedish life 
insurance business increased by 9 per cent to SEK 448bn 
(412) as of 31 December. The market shares for premium pay­
ments in the first eleven months of the year were 45 per cent 
in Estonia, 29 per cent in Latvia and 21 per cent in Lithuania.
The total number of Swedbank cards in issue at the end of the 
year was 8.6 million, slightly higher than the end of the previ­
ous year (8.5). Entercard issued 1.4 million cards, of which 
0.6 million relate to cards issued for Swedbank and the 
­Savings Banks, and 0.8 million to other cards.
The quality of the mortgage portfolio in Sweden remains high 
and accounts for just over half of Swedbank’s total lending. 
From a historical perspective, mortgage-related credit impair­
ments have been very low. During the first part of the year, for­
borne loans increased after more repayment deferrals were 
granted but decreased towards the end of the year. Loans with 
late payments also reflected the same trend.
The total share of loans in stage 2, gross, decreased to 8.0 per 
cent (9.1). For personal loans the corresponding share was 
6.9 per cent (6.8) and for corporate loans it was 9.9 per cent 
(13.1). The decrease in loans in stage 2 is mainly explained 
by an improved macroeconomic outlook during the year. The 
share of loans in stage 3 gross decreased to 0.62 per cent 
(0.65), driven by both private customers and corporates.
Borrowing activity increased slightly in 2025
Swedbank’s borrowing activity increased slightly in 2025, 
mainly due to the acquisitions of Stabelo and Entercard during 
the year, which resulted in higher lending volumes. The volume 
of covered bonds in issue was slightly higher compared with 
2024, which reflects the development in the balance sheet in 
respect of deposits and lending. Swedbank’s total deposit 
­volumes have not yet been impacted by the expectation that 
deposits in the banking system would decline due to factors 
such as the Riksbank’s active phase-out of quantitative easing. 
However, corporate deposits in Sweden decreased slightly 
towards the end of the year. In 2025, Swedbank issued SEK 
170bn in long-term debt instruments, including capital instru­
ments in the form a fixed-term subordinated loan of SEK 6bn. 
The total issuance need for the full year 2026 is expected to 
be in line with the issuance volume in 2025, with a continued 
focus on covered bonds in SEK. The need for financing is 
impacted by the current liquidity situation, future maturities 
and changes in deposit and lending volumes, and is therefore 
adjusted over the course of the year. Maturities in 2026 
amount to SEK 110bn.
As of 31 December, short-term funding (commercial paper) 
amounted to SEK 251bn (265). Available cash and balances 
with central banks and reserves with the Swedish National 
Debt Office amounted to SEK 359bn (321) and the liquidity 
reserve to SEK 523bn (591).
The Group’s liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) was 184 per cent 
(201) and for USD, EUR and SEK it was 542, 289 and 108 per 
cent respectively. The net stable funding ratio (NSFR) was 
124 per cent (127).
Credit rating agencies S&P Global Ratings and Moody’s raised 
Swedbank’s credit rating during the year. S&P Global Rating 
upgraded the rating from A+ to AA, while Moody’s raised 
it from Aa3 to Aa2. Moody’s also changed the outlook for 
­Swedbank from stable to positive during the year.

Strong capitalisation
The Common Equity Tier 1 capital ratio was 17.8 per cent 
(19.8) as of 31 December. The total Common Equity Tier 1 cap­
ital requirement, including Pillar 2 guidance, was 14.8 per cent 
(15.2) of the Risk Exposure Amount (REA), which resulted in a 
Common Equity Tier 1 capital buffer of 3.0 percentage points 
(4.6). The change in the Common Equity Tier 1 capital require­
ment was mainly due to that the Board of Directors proposed 
the Annual General Meeting a special dividend along with a 
lower Pillar 2 requirement as a result of the Swedish Financial 
Supervisory Authority’s annual Supervisory Review and Evalu­
ation Process. Common Equity Tier 1 capital decreased to 
SEK 166.1bn (172.6) and was mainly affected by the profit 
and anticipated dividend, including proposed special dividend. 
The leverage ratio was 6.6 per cent (6.8). The leverage ratio 
requirement including Pillar 2 guidance is 3.2 per cent. During 
the year, REA increased by SEK 60.2bn to SEK 932.1bn (871.9). 
REA for credit risks rose mainly due to higher loss given default 
(LGD) for mortgages and for corporate loans, as part of Swed­
bank’s plan for model updates and due to increased volumes 
as well as the acquisition of Entercard. The increase was partly 
offset by ­foreign exchange effects, reduced risk for defaults 
and the implementation of capital requirement regulation 3 
(CRR3). REA for market risk was unchanged during the year.
REA for Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) increased by SEK 
1.8bn, mainly due to a revised calculation method with higher 
risk weights under CRR3 than under CRR. The annual update 
of REA for operational risk increased by SEK 38.1bn, mainly 
due to the transition to new regulations, CRR3, during 2025 
and that the three-year moving average of total income 
increased compared to last year. 
Investigations
During the third quarter, the U.S. Securities and Exchange 
Commission (SEC) announced that it has closed its investiga­
tion of the bank without enforcement. In January 2026, the 
bank was informed that the US Department of ­Justice (DOJ) 
had closed its investigation of the bank without encorcement. 
The Department of Financial ­Services in New York (DFS) is still 
investigating Swedbank. The bank cannot at this time deter­
mine any financial consequences or when this investigation 
will be completed.

Corporate Governance Report 2025
Swedbank plays an important role in society as a bank for the many people and businesses. 
We believe that a profitable bank creates value for its customers and contributes to a society 
that is sustainable for the long term. One prerequisite for this is that trust in the financial 
system and banks is maintained. In this context, a corporate governance model with 
­competent employees, a clear division of responsibilities, effective internal governance 
and control, robust risk management and compliance are important components. It is 
­imperative that a sound risk culture is maintained.
Swedbank works continuously to ensure that it has an appro-
priate corporate governance model with effective governance, 
control and risk management across the Group.
The Corporate Governance Report has been prepared in accor-
dance with the Swedish Annual Accounts Act and the Swedish 
Corporate Governance Code. 
Importance of corporate governance
Sound corporate governance means that the Group is gov-
erned effectively and responsibly based on Swedbank’s strate-
gies, targets and values. This is critical to maintain trust in 
Swedbank among shareholders, customers, employees, super-
visory authorities and other stakeholders, and to ensure effec-
tive and sound risk management and internal governance and 
control. Sound corporate governance forms the basis of effec-
tive and transparent internal and external information disclo-
sure. Decision-making processes shall be simple and transpar-
ent with clear lines of responsibility. There must be frameworks 
for not only internal governance and control, but also risk man-
agement, including clear rules and procedures to manage con-
flicts of interest. The culture in the bank shall be characterised 
by transparency, integrity, compliance and risk awareness. 
Swedbank’s values shall provide a foundation for day-to-day 
decision-making and the ongoing work of employees.
Regulations
Swedbank is a Swedish public banking company listed on Nasdaq 
Stockholm and falls under the supervision of the Swedish Finan-
cial Supervisory Authority (the Swedish FSA). Supervision essen-
tially covers risk management, governance and control. In addi-
tion, banking operations in other home markets fall under the 
supervision of local supervisory authorities and the European 
Central Bank (ECB). Banking is subject to extensive regulation.

2   Nomination Committee
The 2025 AGM decided on the principles for the appointment 
of the Nomination Committee prior to the 2026 AGM. These 
principles include that the committee shall be composed of six 
members: the representatives of the five largest shareholders 
as of the last business day in August 2025, and that wish to 
appoint a member, and the Chair of the Board. 
The Nomination Committee’s work is governed by an instruc-
tion approved by the 2025 AGM. The Nomination Committee’s 
task is to prepare and submit proposals to the 2026 AGM on 
the election of the Chair of the AGM, the members and Chair 
of the Board of Directors, and the auditor. The Nomination 
Committee will also submit proposals on the number of Board 
members, remuneration to the Board members and auditor 
appointed by the AGM, principles for how the Nomination 
Committee will be appointed prior to the 2027 AGM, and 
instructions on the Nomination Committee’s work prior to the 
2027 AGM. The instruction also states that the Board shall at 
all times have an appropriate composition distinguished by 
diversity and breadth in terms of the competence, experience 
and background of the Board members elected by the AGM. 
Gender parity is being pursued over time. The bank’s opera-
tions, stage of development and expected future direction and 
conditions in general are taken into account. The Board shall 
also have the support of its owners, at the same time that the 
need for independence in relation to the bank, the executive 
management team and the bank’s major shareholders shall 
be taken into account for the Board as a whole. 
The Nomination Committee takes note of and discusses the 
Board evaluation and has personal discussions with each 
Board member. The Chair of the Board is not present for these 
discussions with other Board members. The Nomination Com-
mittee also conducts a suitability assessment of proposed 
candidates and evaluates factors such as their experience, 
competence, reputation, potential conflicts of interest, inde-
pendence, and ability to devote sufficient time to the assign-
ment. Based on the Board evaluation, personal conversations 
with Board members and other information, the Nomination 
Committee discusses the size and composition of the Board.
No remuneration has been paid from Swedbank to the 
­members of the ­Nomination Committee.

3   The Board of Directors
The Board of Directors has overarching responsibility for 
Swedbank’s organisation, operations and management. Oper-
ations are carried out in a sustainable manner with a focus on 
the customer and sound risk taking to ensure the bank’s long-
term viability and to maintain trust in the bank.
The 2025 AGM elected eleven members of the Board. The Board 
also includes two employee representatives with two deputies. 
Swedbank’s Board meets the requirements of the Swedish 
­Corporate Governance Code in respect of its members’ indepen-
dence. All members except Göran Bengtsson and Rasmus Roos 
are considered independent in relation to the bank and the exec-
utive management team. All members are considered indepen-
dent in relation to the bank’s major shareholders. After the 2025 
AGM, the gender distribution was 45.5 per cent women and 
54.5 per cent men. The CEO, Deputy CEO, CFO and Board Secre-
tary attend Board meetings but are not members of the Board. 
The composition of the Board is presented on pages 62–68. 
The Policy on Diversity, Equity and Inclusion applies to the 
Board, see S1 Own workforce on page 125.
The Board’s obligations and division of responsibilities
The Board is the highest decision-making body after the AGM 
and the highest executive body. The Board is responsible for 
ensuring that the bank has an effective and appropriate organi-
sation and corporate governance. In accordance with its 
established rules of procedure, the Board decides on matters 
such as targets, strategies, operational frameworks and the 
business plan. The Board adopts operating policies, and veri-
fies that effective systems are in place to monitor and control 
operations. The Board is also responsible for compliance with 
laws and regulations, and ensures transparent and accurate 
information disclosures. 
The Board appoints, dismisses and evaluates the CEO and 
Deputy CEO, as well as the Chief Risk Officer (Group Risk), 
Chief Compliance Officer (Group Compliance) and Chief Audit 
Executive (Group Internal Audit), and decides on their remuner-
ation. The CEO and Chief Audit Executive are directly subordi-
nate to the Board.
The Board is responsible for ensuring that operations are 
organised in accordance with external and internal rules, so 
that accounting, treasury, operational risks and the bank’s 
­economic conditions otherwise are managed satisfactorily. 
The Chair of the Board has certain specific responsibilities 
according to the rules of procedure adopted by the Board. 
They include the following:
	
●Lead Board meetings and work, and encourage an open and 
constructive dialogue.
	
●Ensure that the Board is evaluated annually and that Board 
members receive the necessary training. 
	
●Oversee the CEO’s work, serve as a sounding board and 
­support for the CEO, and monitor that the Board’s decisions 
and instructions are implemented.
	
●Represent the bank and the Board vis-à-vis the owners on 
owner­ship issues, and on other material matters with 
­investors and other stakeholders.

The Board’s work
In 2025, the Board held 18 meetings. Board decisions were 
made unanimously and no dissenting opinions were noted on 
any matter during the year. Potential conflicts of interest for 
Board members are reported at each meeting and mean that 
the member participates in neither preparation, discussions 
nor decisions regarding the matter in question.
The Board regularly discusses business conditions and contin-
uously monitors the bank’s capital situation, credit risks and 
credit quality. The Board receives reports from the Board’s 
committees on an ongoing basis. Furthermore, the Board 
receives monthly reports from Group Risk and quarterly 
reports from other control functions (Group Internal Audit and 
Group Compliance), as well as on customer complaints and 
information security. 
In 2025, the Board of Directors maintained a strong focus on 
issues including the development of the bank’s services and 
Business Areas, geopolitical and macroeconomic develop-

The Board’s competence
The members of the Board are expected to continuously 
update and deepen their knowledge of Swedbank’s operations 
and regulations applicable to the bank. To this end, the Board 
establishes a training plan each year. During the year, the Board 
of Directors conducted training in areas such as payments 
(infrastructure, competition/market, development and future), 
market risks, civil defence, the Baltic markets and the RDARR 
(Risk Data Aggregation and Risk Reporting) regulations. 
New Board members also attend introductory training to 
acquire in-depth information about the organisation and oper-
ations, the control functions and the bank’s corporate gover-

annual seminar with in-depth reviews of one or more topical 
areas. The Board members also undertake training/in-depth

4   President and CEO
The President and CEO is responsible for managing the bank’s 
day-to-day operations and is the executive ultimately respons­
ible for ensuring that the Board’s strategic direction and other 
decisions are implemented and followed by the bank and 
its subsidiaries, and that risk management, governance, IT 
­systems, the organisation and processes are satisfactory. 
The CEO represents the bank externally on various matters, 
leads the work of the Group Executive Committee and makes 
decisions after consulting its members.
The CEO has the opportunity to delegate duties to subordi-
nates or Group committees, although ultimate responsibility is 
retained by the CEO. The Board’s directions on the CEO’s spe-
cial areas of responsibility are set out in documents including 
the Board’s Governance Policy and the instruction for the CEO. 
The CEO is responsible for ensuring that the Board’s decisions 
are implemented and that a process is in place to ensure that 
policies and instructions are followed in the organisation and 
are evaluated annually.
The CEO establishes Group-level rules on governance and 
internal control. To support the internal control, the CEO has 
a number of Group Functions, primarily Group Finance, Group 
Risk and Group Compliance. Monitoring is performed regularly 
through written reports and in-depth follow-up meetings with 
the heads of the various Group Functions and with the Busi-
ness Areas. For more information, see the Board of Directors’ 
report on internal control of financial reporting on page 61. 
The CEO is also responsible for ensuring that the Group has 
a strategy for competence management.
Group Executive Committee (GEC) and other committees 
Swedbank’s GEC comprises the CEO together with fourteen 
other executives. Many of the executives have direct business 
responsibility, and the GEC therefore plays an important role 
as a forum for sharing information and ideas. The GEC nor-
mally meets on a weekly basis. One of the purposes of the 
weekly meetings is to ensure a uniform overview and transpar-
ency in matters of importance to the bank and the Group. 
The Group Executive Committee consists of fifteen members:
	
●the CEO, 
	
●the Deputy CEO, 
	
●the CFO,
	
●the Heads of Swedish Banking, Premium and Private 
­Banking, Baltic Banking and Corporates and Institutions, 
	
●the Head of Group Products and Advice, and
	
●the Heads of Group Credit, Group Channels and Techno­
logies, Group Risk, Group Compliance, Group Human 
Resources and Facility Management, Group Brand and 
­Communication and Group Legal. 
Both the CEO and subordinate heads are assisted by Group com-
mittees that gather expertise when preparing various matters. 
With a few exceptions, the committees have no collective deci-
sion-making authority. Decisions are made by the chair of each 
committee, who will typically be a subordinate manager to the 
CEO, or the decision is escalated to the CEO.
In addition to the Group Executive Committee, other committees 
include:
– Group Asset Allocation Committee (GAAC), 
– Group Risk and Compliance Committee (GRCC), 
– Group IT Investment Committee (GIIC), 
– Group Financial Crime Committee (GFCC), 
– Group Product Oversight Committee (GPOC), and 
– Group Executive Sustainability Committee (GESC).
The GAAC is led by the CFO. The purpose of the GAAC includes 
to coordinate the financial management of capital, liquidity, 
financing and tax issues. 
GIIC is led by the CIO. The GIIC plans and prioritises the 
Group’s strategic IT investments and ensures that they are in 
line with the bank’s strategy. 
The GRCC is led by the Chief Risk Officer in collaboration with 
the Chief Compliance Officer. The purpose of the GRCC includes 
to ensure uniform management of non-financial risks, including 
compliance risk, and to contribute to a sound risk culture. 
The GFCC is headed by the Head of Group Products and Advice. 
The GFCC ensures appropriate and effective management of 
the Group’s risks related to money laundering, terrorist financ-
ing and financial sanctions, as well as complete and uniform 
implementation of the Group’s internal rules on money launder-
ing and terrorist financing, as well as financial sanctions.
The GPOC is led by the Head of Group Products and Advice. 
The purpose of the GPOC is to ensure a Group-level overview 
of the product and service offering in the areas of savings, 
insurance, payments, loans, cards and accounts, and to 
­provide support for decisions relating to them.

Internal control and risk management
The foundation for effective risk work is a well-implemented, 
sound and consistent risk culture. The Board of Directors 
defines the framework for the Bank’s risk work and risk culture 
through the Policy on Enterprise Risk Management. The 
Group’s risk management is based on the principle of three 
lines of defence.
First line of defence – risk management by the  
business operations
The first line of defence has ultimate responsibility for risk 
management and consists of all risk management activities 
carried out by the business in Business Areas, Product Areas 
and Group Functions. The business operations take, or are 
exposed to, risks and are responsible for continuous and 
active risk management. The operations own the risks within 
their respective area of responsibility and are also responsible 
for ensuring that structures for internal control and reliable 
­processes are in place so that risks are identified, assessed, 
managed, monitored, reported and kept within the boundaries 
of the Group’s risk appetite and in accordance with the risk 
management framework. First line responsibilities also 
include establishing a governance structure to ensure 
­comp­liance with external and internal requirements.
Second line of defence – independent  
control functions 
The second line of defence consists of the independent 
­internal control functions Group Risk and Group Compliance.  
Within their respective areas of responsibility, these functions 
are responsible for the risk management framework, which 
covering all risk types in the Group. The framework determines 
how risks are identified, assessed, measured, managed, moni-
tored and reported. The second line of defence also monitors 
and assesses whether effective risk management processes 
and controls are being implemented by relevant risk owners. 
The second line of defence challenges and validates first line’s 
risk management activities, controls and analyses the Group’s 
material risks and provides the CEO and Board with indepen-
dent risk reporting. 
The second line of defence is organisationally independent of 
the first line and is not operationally involved in the business 
activities or the unit it monitors and controls.

Swedbank has an independent Internal

The Chief Audit Executive is appointed

The purpose of Group Internal Audit’s 
reviews is to create improvements in

the bank’s activities and Group companies under the supervi-
sion of a financial supervisory authority as well as other Group 
companies that the Board of Directors considers material from 
time to time are the purview of Group Internal Audit. The 
assignment is based on a policy established by the Board and 
is performed using a risk-based methodology in accordance 
with internationally accepted standards issued by the Institute 
of Internal Auditors (“IIA”). Group Internal Audit prepares an 
annual risk analysis and an audit plan that are approved by the 
Board and can be revised and updated as required. Audit 
reports are submitted to management and the conclusions, 
together with the measures that will be taken and their status, 
are compiled in quarterly reports and presented to the Group 
Executive Committee, the Audit Committee and the Board.
6   External auditor
The external auditor is elected annually by the AGM and inde-
pendently reviews the bank’s financial statements to determine 
whether they are materially accurate and complete and provide 
a fair view of the bank’s financial position and results. The 
auditor also ensures that the accounts are prepared in accor-
dance with current laws and recommendations. The auditor 
also reviews the administration of the Board and the CEO.
According to the Articles of Association, the bank shall have 
no less than one and no more than two authorised public 
accountants. A registered auditing firm may also be elected as 
auditor. PwC was appointed as auditing firm at the 2025 AGM, 
and the Chief Auditor is Authorised Public Accountant Anneli 
Granqvist. The external auditor presents the auditor’s report 
and describes the audit work at the AGM. 
In 2025, the external auditor reported to the Audit Committee 
on six occasions. The auditor also participated in one Board 
meeting during the year, at which a summary report of the 
year’s audit was presented in full. The auditor has met on a 
regular basis with the Chair of the Audit Committee, the Chief 
Audit Executive, the executive management team and other 
operational managers. Swedbank’s interim reports are 
reviewed by the bank’s auditor. The Sustainability Report has 
also been reviewed by the external auditor. Remuneration to 
the Group’s auditor is reported in Note G14. The Audit Commit-
tee evaluates the auditor annually to ensure that its objectivity 
and independence cannot be questioned. The auditor affirms 
its independence annually in the auditor’s report.
Group structure 
An effective operating structure is essential to the bank’s gov-
ernance. The Group structure provides a framework for various 
roles, functions and reporting channels within the bank. The 
bank’s Group structure is divided into Business Areas, Product 
Areas and Group Functions.
Business Areas
The bank’s operations are conducted in four Business Areas: 
Swedish Banking, Premium and Private Banking, Baltic Banking 
and Corporates and Institutions. The Heads of the Business 
Areas are directly subordinate to the CEO. They have over­
arching responsibility for their Business Area’s operations 
and report on an ongoing basis to the CEO. 
The responsibilities of the Head of each Business Area 
include:
	
●Implement the Group’s strategies, prepare business plans 
for each Business Area, and ensure that these are imple-
mented and reported to the CEO.
	
●Create and maintain reporting and escalation procedures 
to raise issues for information or decisions at CEO or 
Board level.
	
●Ensure that policies and instructions are implemented  
within the Business Area.
	
●Customer offering and customer satisfaction.
	
●Integrate sustainability aspects into business decisions 
and working methods.
	
●Profitability and financial stability within the Business Area.
	
●Monitor, follow up and manage the Business Area’s assets, 
liabilities and profitability.
	
●Maintain a sound internal control system to ensure that risks 
are identified and managed in accordance with the bank’s 
risk appetite.
	
●Effective implementation of the bank’s corporate gover-
nance model within the Business Area.

The Board of Directors’ report on 
internal control of financial reporting
The Board of Directors is ultimately responsible for ensuring that the Group’s financial statements 
comply with external regulations, and is also responsible for monitoring the Group’s internal 
control of financial reporting (ICFR). ICFR at Swedbank refers to the processes and controls 
that are implemented to ensure reliable financial reporting. ICFR is based on the Committee of 
Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO). In order to maintain, develop 
and adapt internal controls, limit risks and support sound decision-making and governance of 
the organisation, Swedbank applies COSO through the following five integrated components:
1. Control environment 
– the Board of Directors and executive management 
establish the foundation for internal control
Swedbank’s internal control of financial reporting is rooted in 
the bank’s organisational structure and division of responsibili-
ties, as well as governance documents in the form of policies 
and instructions adopted by the Board and the CEO. 
2. Risk analysis 
– risk assessment based on materiality and complexity
Risk management is an integrated part of business activities. 
Every manager has a primary responsibility for effective risk 
management and risk assessment in their operations and in 
the Group’s financial reporting process. To identify and create 
an understanding of the risks in the Group’s financial reporting 
process, Group Finance conducts a risk assessment of finan-
cial reporting risks at a Group level regarding materiality and 
complexity. The risk assessment is used to decide which pro-
cesses and activities should be covered by the framework.
3. Control activities 
– controls at different levels
To ensure reliable financial reporting, controls are performed 
at various levels in the Group. Group Finance is responsible for 
identifying the controls to be covered by the financial reporting 
framework. The controls are categorised according to the ICFR 
framework’s structured controls as follows: Group-level con-
trols, controls at the process/transaction level and general 
IT controls.
4. Compliance 
– follow-up and evaluation
The controls included in the ICFR framework are regularly 
­evaluated by the control owners through self-assessment. 
The results from the self-assessment are used to assess the 
reliability of the Group’s financial statements.
5. Communication 
– analysis and reporting
The results from the self-assessment are compiled and anal-
ysed by Group Finance in order to assess the outstanding risk 
of material misstatements in the Group’s financial reporting. 
The results from the analysis are reported to Swedbank’s CFO 
and the Board’s Audit Committee on a quarterly basis.
Work started in 2024 to develop risk assessments for internal 
controls for the primary risks related to sustainability reporting. 
Furthermore, key controls were identified for sustainability and 
taxonomy reporting. This work continued during 2025 and addi-
tional key controls have been developed for sustainability and 
ESRS reporting. Internal control of sustainability reporting (ICSR) 
is integrated into ICFR, and reporting takes place annually.

	 BP-1    General basis for preparation of sustainability statements 
Swedbank’s sustainability report is part of the Board of Directors’ report and has 
been prepared in accordance with the Swedish Annual Accounts Act for Credit 
Institutions and Securities Companies (ÅRKL) and the Swedish Annual Accounts 
Act (ÅRL). Reporting is prepared for the Group on the same consolidation basis 
as the financial statements. The sustainability report is prepared at Group level 
and all subsidiaries, including Swedbank’s subsidiaries Swedbank AS Estonia, 
Swedbank AS Latvia and Swedbank AB Lithuania, are included in the consolida-
tion. It also constitutes Swedbank’s report to the UN Global Compact (CoP).
The sustainability report covers activities upstream and downstream in the 
value chain, as well as Swedbank’s own operations. 
Swedbank has used the option to omit confidential and sensitive information 
relating to information security and the prevention of financial crime. Omissions 
have been made on pages 138 and 145. Swedbank has not disclosed information 
regarding intellectual property rights, know-how or the results of innovation.

	 SBM-1    Strategy, business model and value chain
Swedbank is a leading financial actor with four home markets: Sweden, Estonia, 
Latvia and Lithuania. The Group has a full service offering through products, ser-
vices and advice in the areas of financing, savings, investments and payments. 
Swedbank provides financial services to 7.3 million private customers and 
545 000 corporate customers. The bank’s main customer segments are private 
customers, corporate customers, tenant-owner associations, the public sector 
and financial institutions. The business is organised in four Business Areas: 
Swedish Banking, Baltic Banking, Corporate & Institutions and Premium & Private 
Banking, as well as a number of Group Functions tasked with supporting 
­
Swedbank’s vision is “a society that is financially sound and sustainable” with 
the ambition to contribute to a society that is sustainable from environmental, 
­
-
grate sustainability into its strategy and business model, thereby helping to 
create business opportunities, meet customer demands for products and ser-
vices, strengthen risk management, and enable attractive financing in the capital 
market. It is also an important factor in attracting employees with the right com­
petencies. Overall, the sustainability efforts are assessed to drive long-term value 
creation for shareholders.
The transition to a sustainable society requires efforts from many different 
actors, each with their own specific roles and responsibilities. The financial 
sector plays an important role in this context, through its opportunity to influence 
how capital is allocated, which investments receive financing and how risks are 
priced. By directing capital towards long term sustainable activities and integrat-
ing climate and sustainability risks into credit assessments, the financial sector 
can help accelerate the transition and strengthen financial ­stability. Swedbank 
develops relevant products and services for both private ­individuals and compa-
nies, acts as an advisor as companies and the public sector make the transition, 
and thereby provides capital and creates incentives that drive the transition to 
a more sustainable economy.
A broad customer base creates the conditions for achieving change and creat-
ing business value. Swedbank strives to reduce its own carbon footprint and offer 
products and services that support customers’ financing and investment needs 
in a sustainable direction. The focus is on minimising climate impact and energy 
consumption, promoting actions in the areas of equity, diversity and inclusion, 
and fighting financial crime. By ensuring a strong financial position, high credit 
and asset quality, and good capitalisation, Swedbank assumes responsibility for 
its role in the financial system.
