Sustainability in the value chain
As a major credit institution, Swedbank is a key actor in the markets in which the 
Group operates. Swedbank develops and distributes products and services with 
a sustainable focus. The Group also designs financial incentives and terms and 
conditions to encourage change, and applies active selection when selecting 
customer engagement.
As a major financial operator and employer, Swedbank also has a responsi­
bility to work actively on relevant environmental matters and social sustainability, 
as well as to conduct responsible business and combat financial crime. To con-
tribute to the broader sustainability transition, Swedbank is also engaged in vari-
ous ways in local communities and the social debate to influence the direction of 
the discussions for the benefit of the industry, customers and society at large. 
Position statements
Swedbank has adopted two Group-wide position statements with regard to arms 
and defence as well as climate change and nature. They are applied to all mar-
kets in which Swedbank operates and are publicly available on Swedbank’s web-
site. The position statements cover financing and investments when Swedbank 
makes investment decisions for financial products as well as capital market 
­services, for example, when Swedbank arranges bonds or commercial securities. 
Indirect investments, such as funds managed by third parties or investment 
­decisions based on a discretionary mandate, are not covered.
The position statement for arms and defence specifies conditions for the pro-
vision of financing and investment services to the arms and defence sector. With 
due reference to risks associated with the unlawful use and distribution of arms 
that would violate international human rights and international humanitarian law, 
Swedbank excludes companies that produce, maintain or trade in controversial 
arms and nuclear arms. 
In its position statement for climate change and nature, Swedbank has speci-
fied various types of restrictions on fossil fuels, including coal, peat, oil and gas. 
The business model and the value chain’s involvement 
of and impact on stakeholders 
Swedbank’s business model and value chain have been developed to deliver 
­customer value, which forms the basis of the Group’s existence and continued 
operations. The Group’s offering and service are built on the basis of customers’ 
expectations and preferences. Customer insights are collected through surveys 
and customer dialogues. This provides information about customers’ views 
on sustainability matters, not only in terms of the Group’s position statements,  
brand and capital generation, but also on demand for sustainable products, 
­service and distribution. 
Value creation
With a focus on sustainable value creation, Swedbank strives to offer services 
that enhance customers’ profitability and contribute to long-term stability. One 
element of this is the continued development of a robust infrastructure and reli-
able digital performance. This is crucial to ensure that products and services are 
available and function as expected, even in a rapidly changing operating environ-
ment where risks and requirements change. Good risk management is expected 
to support operations and contribute to informed and sound decisions being 
made that are well balanced in relation to risk, return and market situation. This 
is important to maintain trust and deliver long-term value to customers and 
­investors, and to remain a stable actor in the financial system. 
Stakeholders 
Swedbank engages in dialogue with investors, owners and other actors in the 
capital market to better understand expectations and needs related to long-term 
sustainability. These dialogues are important for identifying relevant opportuni-
ties and managing potential risks. At the same time, this is an area in a state of 
constant development, which places demands on transparency, adaptability and 
close dialogue with market actors and other stakeholders. 
In addition to collaboration with external parties, the work on employee rela-
tions and the internal work environment is central. Particular focus is placed on 
creating an attractive and inclusive workplace with a focus on long-term skills 
supply. In order to identify areas for improvement in internal work, employees are 
involved by such means as employee surveys, the results of which are discussed 
within the respective teams and through dialogues with employee 
­representatives.

Lending
To support a sustainable transition, Swedbank has developed a diversified  
range of financing products and services for customers. 
Private customers are offered different types of loans, such as:
­	Green mortgages for properties with an approved energy class or 
­environ­mental certification in accordance with the Group’s criteria.
•	Green car loans and car leasing for low-emission vehicles.
•	Solar panel loans for the installation of solar panels.
­	Energy loans for energy-saving measures in homes in Sweden. 
Corporate customers are offered loans such as:
•	Green loans to companies when financing environmentally sustainable 
­activities in accordance with established criteria, such as energy- and 
resource-efficient properties with a lower environmental impact.
•	Sustainability-linked loans that can be used for general business purposes 
rather than a specific purpose. The interest rate on the loan is linked to how 
well the company performs in relation to the metrics specified for the 
­company’s sustainability work. Loans are followed up by means of regular 
­performance reporting during the term of the loan.
•	ESG-related bonds where corporate and institutional customers are offered 
an opportunity for assistance in issuing green, social, sustainability and 
­sustainability-linked bonds in the capital market.
•	Sustainability-related advice and analysis in the field of sustainable financing. 
Sustainable Asset Register
Swedbank’s Sustainable Asset Register is a collection of the Group’s green and 
social assets that meet established criteria in the Swedbank Sustainable Funding 
Framework. 
•	Green assets: Financing of assets that contribute to environmental sustain-
ability, such as renewable energy production, energy-efficient buildings and 
sustainable ecosystem management.
•	Social assets: Financing that contributes to positive social effects, such  
as the promotion of socio-economic development and inclusion.
Swedbank Sustainable Funding Framework
The sustainable borrowing and financing framework enables the Group to issue 
green and social bonds. It was updated during the year to ensure that it continues 
to be in line with prevailing recommendations, market practice and Swedbank’s 
business model, as well as investors’ requirements and expectations.
Swedbank’s Sustainable Asset Register continued to grow during the year, 
especially in the green buildings segment. The increase is explained by more 
mortgages to private individuals and loans to commercial real estate companies 
and housing associations that meet specific sustainability criteria. The growth is 
also partly driven by improved data availability, such as energy performance cer-
tificates, which enables the identification of financing for buildings that meet the 
criteria in the Sustainable Funding Framework. Renewable energy financing also 
increased during the year, as Swedbank continues to support the expansion of 
renewable energy sources and the broader energy transition across the Group’s 
home markets.

Stakeholder dialogue
	 SBM-2    Interests and views of stakeholders
Swedbank’s stakeholders
Swedbank has a regular dialogue with its main stakeholder groups: customers, 
employees, owners and investors, as well as society and the world around us. In 
addition to these, a dialogue is also maintained with other stakeholders, including 
government agencies, municipalities and regions, regulators, pension and asset 
managers, analysts, journalists, trade unions, students, foundations, non-profit 
organisations, interest groups, trade associations, associations, schools and 
­universities, suppliers, subsidiaries, savings banks, competitors, ratings agencies 
and indices, and auditors. 
Customers
Swedbank uses aggregated data from ongoing customer surveys to proactively 
develop products and services based on customers’ needs. Customers can con-
tact the bank on specific matters using the Group’s five-step customer complaint 
process. The employee who receives the customer complaint is responsible for 
ensuring that it is handled internally and reports back to the customer. Swedbank 
also has specially appointed customer ombudsmen. 
Employees
Swedbank encourages ongoing dialogue and an open feedback culture in the 
­various entities within the Group. To assess and follow up on how employees 
­perceive their work situation, employee surveys are conducted on a regular basis. 
The outcomes of these are important contributions to the identification of 
strengths, impacts, risks and opportunities for possible measures. The results 
are discussed within each unit. Group HR & Facility Management is responsible 
for communicating the results to the Group Executive Committee to support 
strategy development and improvement initiatives. Development reviews with 
line managers are also an important channel for safeguarding the interests of 
employees. Employees are also represented by two employee representatives 
and two deputies on the Board of Directors, appointed by Finansförbundet and 
Akademikerföreningen respectively. These representatives are involved in the 
Board’s work on the strategy and business model. 
Owners and investors
Swedbank maintains an ongoing dialogue with current and potential owners 
and investors. This dialogue covers issues such as business ethics, responsible 
corporate governance, financial stability, capital and risk management, and the 
management of ESG-related targets as well as risks and opportunities. The feed-
back from these stakeholders is key to developing the business and ensuring the 
Group’s relevance in the market. A sound financial system is a prerequisite for 
Swedbank’s long-term existence. Good profitability and returns enable the Group 
to contribute to the benefit of society through investments and initiatives in 
­various forms of social engagement.
Society and the world around us
Swedbank interacts continuously with stakeholders in society, the world around 
us, and both regulatory authorities and decision-makers. A dialogue is maintained 
both directly with government agencies and with industry organisations such as 
Finance Sweden’s Sustainability Council, the European Savings and Retail Banking 
Group (ESBG), the European Banking Federation (EBF) and other relevant groups. 
Most dialogues take place with Swedish government agencies such as the 
­Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority, but also with EU institutions such as the 
European Commission. The purpose is to monitor the development of regulatory 
frameworks and contribute to policy design for effective regulatory frameworks 
that give banks good opportunities to strive for a more sustainable society. Swed-
bank also monitors media reporting on sustainability in all home markets, which 
is taken into account in the way improvement work is to be ­carried out.

Insights from the stakeholder dialogue and its relationship  
to the strategy and business model
Swedbank’s strategy and business model aim to meet stakeholder expectations 
from several different perspectives in both the short and long term. The develop-
ment and adjustment of Swedbank’s strategy and business model are under-
pinned by external and internal analysis. The external analysis includes several 
stakeholders and aspects that affect the strategic choices that Swedbank 
makes. Aspects evaluated include market developments, regulatory changes, 
customer insights and different types of trends, which form the basis of identify-
ing opportunities and risks to take a position on. The purpose of the internal anal-
ysis is to identify Swedbank’s strengths and weaknesses, including those linked 
to the Group’s current position and the resources and competences that the 
Group possesses. Together, these analyses form the basis of strategic choices 
and decisions going forward. 
The business strategy is reviewed annually with the existing and changed 
views and requirements of stakeholders in mind, as well as other internal and 
external factors that may affect Swedbank’s strategic choices. In 2025, there 
was a particular strategic focus on further enhancing the customer experience, 
increasing accessibility and reduce waiting times in Sweden to meet customer 
expectations. This has resulted in Swedbank revising its distribution model in 
Sweden by establishing a uniform service model. Adjustments were also made 
to relevant regulatory changes that affect the business model and strategy, such 
as regulations for internal credit risk models and changed requirements and 
­regulations in the area of payments. 
Swedbank participates in initiatives such as SAMLIT and the financial intelli-
gence centre, and actively collaborates with government agencies and other 
stakeholders to combat money laundering, terrorist financing and fraud. This 
work is based on the ongoing sharing of information and a strategic dialogue, 
which strengthen the resilience of the financial system. 
For the years ahead, Swedbank is planning several steps to further boost its 
work and proactively address the interests of stakeholders. This includes focus-
ing on personalised customer experiences, simplified processes and continuing 
to strengthen the customer offering. 
 In the double materiality assessment, the opinions of stakeholders are taken

The results of the double materiality assessment support strategic analysis 
in the area of sustainability. They are used to validate the adopted strategy and 
as input into the annual review of the strategy, and also to identify any need for

Interests of consumers and end-users 
	 S4 SBM-2    Interests and views of stakeholders 
Data protection
It is important that the Group’s customers feel confident about how their personal 
data is used and protected. The Code of Conduct clarifies the commitment in 
respect of data protection, including the fundamental right to the protection of 
personal data. Swedbank is committed to protecting personal data and the rights 
of individuals by complying with the GDPR requirements for information, trans-
parency and the rights of individuals to their personal data. In this way, the Group 
ensures that both legal obligations and customers’ fundamental human rights to 
data protection are upheld. Customers’ data and privacy are also protected by 
Swedbank’s information security procedures and Swedish legislation on banking 
confidentiality. 
Information security 
Information security is a central element of Swedbank’s work to build trust with 
the Group’s customers. Swedbank’s strategy and business model are continu-
ously evolving, and as they evolve, security initiatives are adapted to support the 
operation and create value for customers. This is how information security is 
integrated into the overall business operation.
One example of the Group’s customer-oriented security work is the third-party 
audited report SOC2, which Swedbank issues to corporate customers and part-
ners when necessary. This is to provide increased transparency regarding the 
Group’s controls linked to security and availability. The report is an important tool 
to help customers with their own risk assessments and reinforce confidence in 
Swedbank’s operation. 
Swedbank undertakes targeted customer communication to share insights 
on the cybersecurity situation, answer questions about the Group’s security 
­architecture and discuss shared security challenges. These events strengthen 
the relationship, create a platform for proactive collaboration and build a shared 
safety culture. 
Financial health
Swedbank respects universal human rights in all markets in which the Group 
operates. The Board of Directors has adopted a Group-wide sustainability policy 
that clarifies work on social sustainability, the promotion of human rights, fair 
working conditions and long-term social engagement. 
In line with this, Swedbank values its stakeholders’ perspectives and main-
tains an active dialogue with both customers and various stakeholders in society 
in order to better understand and prioritise their needs and expectations. Through 
digital and physical lectures, advisory meetings, events and regular surveys, 
Swedbank seeks to promote financial inclusion and take into account the needs 
of stakeholders in individual activities.

The material impacts, risks and opportunities identified in Swedbank’s materi­
ality assessment 2025 are presented in the table below. For each sustainability 
topic, there is a description of sub-topics and the reason why the topic was 
deemed to be material. The information also includes where in the value chain 
each material impact, risk or opportunity has been identified. The Time ­horizon 
for when each identified impact, risk and opportunity is expected to have an 
effect is also specified. The information also includes whether Swedbank has set 
measurable, outcome-oriented and time-bound targets for material sustain­ability 
topics in order to assess progress. 
As part of Swedbank’s risk work, an ESG risk and materiality assessment is 
conducted to identify activities that may have a material financial impact. The 
ESG risks deemed to be material form the basis of the financial risk assessment 
in the double materiality assessment, and are integrated into the Group’s estab-
lished risk management processes and taken into account in the credit strategy. 
Swedbank’s ambition is to continue its work to integrate the results of the double 
materiality assessment more clearly into the annual Group-wide strategy review 
process and other relevant internal processes and reports. The purpose is to 
reuse the insights from the analysis to enable strategic decisions and systemati-
cally integrate current and future impacts of the Group’s material sustainability 
topics into operational work. 
Swedbank’s ESG risk and materiality assessment is based on climate and 
environmental scenarios provided by the Network for Greening the Financial 
System (NGFS). Based on these scenarios, it is estimated that the risk of credit 
impairments will increase in the short to medium term, as a consequence of 
companies’ and individuals’ increased costs for greenhouse gas emissions and 
energy use. The forecast underlines the inherent complexity of being able to navi-
gate and reliably quantify in the prevailing uncertainty related to different ambi-
tions regarding the pace of the climate transition. Apart from the area of climate 
risk, Swedbank has not systematically evaluated the financial effects of material 
risks and opportunities on the Group’s financial position, results and cash flow 
during the current year. 
A Group-wide analysis of the resilience of the strategy and business model in 
relation to material impacts, risks and opportunities remains to be carried out for 
Swedbank. Work on increasing resilience to climate risks been established in the 
Baltic countries and has been started for the Group. The process established in 
the Baltic countries includes both qualitative and quantitative ­analyses to enable 
these risks to be managed effectively. For further information, see chapter E1 Cli-
mate Change on page 99. 
Changes in the 2025 materiality assessment
The results of this year’s materiality assessment show differences compared 
to the previous year. Biodiversity and ecosystem services is a new sustainability 
area that has been identified as material in the environmental area. This is due 
to a further development of the materiality assessment methodology for 2025, 
which involved a deeper analysis of the Group’s business relationships and 
sector exposure. Analysis tools applied had been adapted in parallel to address 
the thematic areas in ESRS as well as indirect business relationships, in accor-
dance with updated reporting requirements. The impact assessment identified 
an indirect negative impact on biodiversity linked to Swedbank’s corporate 
­lending, which means that the topic is classified as material for 2025. 
Furthermore, there have been changes in the results among the sub-topics 
identified. Two new sub-topics, Information security and Financial health, have 
been added within the Consumers and end-users category.
At the same time, some sub-topics have been re-evaluated. For the area Own 
workforce, the sub-topic Other work-related rights has been deemed to be no 
longer material. The same change applies to the area of Business conduct, where 
the sub-topic Protection for whistleblowers is no longer deemed to be a material 
sub-topic.
These changes are largely a result of improved methods for identifying 
and assessing impact materiality and risk, as the Group’s operational risk 
­assessment has been applied in the double materiality assessment for 2025. 
There is additional information about the materiality assessment on page 85.

Swedbank’s double materiality assessment
	 IRO-1    The process to identify and assess material sustainability topics
In order to further develop the double materiality assessment, Swedbank con
ducted its third double materiality assessment in 2025. This enhanced assess-
ment was conducted making greater use of aids such as quantitative data and 
customised tools. The following sections describe Swedbank’s method and 
­process to define the Group’s double materiality assessment.
As in the previous year, the materiality assessment was conducted in accor-
dance with the principle of double materiality. To produce the assessment, a 
double materiality assessment is conducted, a process that identifies and analy-
ses sustainability topics based on the two perspectives of impact materiality and 
financial materiality. The result of the double materiality assessment shows 
which sustainability topics are most relevant for Swedbank and should therefore 
be prioritised in the Group’s sustainability work and reporting.
Swedbank has developed an analysis method in accordance with ESRS and 
EFRAG’s guidance. Assumptions have been applied where complete information 
was missing, for example in mapping the value chain, assessing the time horizon 
for impact and managing data availability and related uncertainties. For the 
reporting of material sustainability topics, Swedbank has chosen to apply the 
time horizons used in the Group’s existing risk framework: short term 1–3 years, 
medium term 3–10 years and long term 10 years or more. The analysis is based 
on separate assessment factors for each perspective, which are described 
below.
Impact materiality
Impact materiality refers to the organisation’s actual and potential impact 
on people and the environment, both positive and negative. Actual impact 
refers to areas identified through the Group’s analysis and due diligence 
process. Potential impact refers to areas that may be relevant, but for 
which sufficient data or evidence is not yet available. The assessment of 
potential impact includes likelihood, which is evaluated on the basis of 
how often a given event is expected to occur. For example, an event that 
is expected to occur once a year on average is deemed to have a high 
­likelihood, while an event that is expected to occur once every 10–20 
years is deemed to have a low likelihood. 
Financial materiality
Financial materiality refers to how external sustainability-related factors 
can impact the organisation financially, in the form of risks and/or 
­opportunities. 
Current methods used to assess financial materiality have primarily 
been developed for risk management associated with climate change, an 
area in which Swedbank has been working for a long time. Methods to 
assess risks linked to other sustainability topics and the assessment of 
business opportunities linked to sustainability topics are primarily quali-
tative at present.

1   Analysis of business context
The value chain mapping forms the basis of the double materiality assessment, 
and it includes all of the Group’s home markets: Sweden, Estonia, Latvia and Lith-
uania. As Swedbank is a financial company, it can be assumed that the most rele-
vant parts of the Group’s value chain regarding sustainability topics may be found 
downstream, where material impacts, risks and opportunities arise primarily 
though business relationships, for example via lending to the Group’s customers. 
Upstream in the value chain, sustainability topics are linked primarily to activities 
such as purchasing processes and capital acquisition. Within the company’s own 
operations, the role as employer is key to the analysis. Based on these insights 
and in order to support the ongoing analysis, the Group’s operations are divided 
into four different analysis units based on underlying activities:
•	Lending
•	Assets under management
•	Payments (new for 2025)
•	Own operations, including purchasing
2   Identification of materiality
At an early stage of the analysis, a gross list of sustainability topics was drawn up 
that were deemed to be potentially material. This was based on the sustainability 
topics defined in ESRS combined with insights from the Group’s stakeholder 
­dialogue. 
The 2023 materiality assessment included dialogues with both internal and 
external stakeholders, which yielded valuable insights. External stakeholders, 
including investors, customers, suppliers, researchers and voluntary organisa-
tions, were consulted in order to identify relevant sustainability topics. 
In 2024 and 2025, the dialogue was extended to include internal stakeholders 
based on the topics previously identified in consultation with external parties. 
Internal stakeholders include employees, trade union representatives and ­internal 
subject matter experts. 
In addition to the stakeholder dialogue, various sources relevant for the finan-
cial sector were used, such as reports from voluntary organisations, industry sur-
veys, research findings and indices such as the Sustainability Accounting Stan-
dards Board (SASB), as well as tools such as the Portfolio Impact Analysis Tool 
developed by UNEP FI (United Nations Environment Programme Finance Initia-
tive), ENCORE and Bioscope. Swedbank also based its approach on the opera-
tion’s significant activities based on earnings from the credit portfolio, invest-
ments and payment solutions. The way in which the Group’s costs are distributed 
across different Business Areas was also taken into consideration. 
3   Assessment of materiality
The sustainability topics identified as being potentially material were progressed 
for a materiality assessment. All sustainability topics were subjected to the same 
assessment method, regardless of whether or not they had been identified as 
being potentially material. 
In 2025, internal stakeholders, such as subject matter experts and representa-
tives from different Business Areas and Group Functions, were consulted in work 
to assess impacts, risks and opportunities for the sustainability topics identified 
as being potentially material through the gross list. A series of workshops took 
place with representatives from different Business Areas and Group Functions, 
to assess and describe which sustainability topics are material in the Group’s 
value chain. 
Material impact
The seriousness of actual and potential impacts was assessed on the basis of 
scale, scope, irremediability and likelihood. The outcome of the assessment is 
the average value of scale, scope and irremediability and, if applicable, multiplied 
by the likelihood of impact, in accordance with the method described previously. 
This result formed the basis of the prioritisation of the areas, with the threshold 
value to be classified as material impact set at two. There is no specific process 
in the double materiality assessment for monitoring material impact. 
Financial materiality
Risks and opportunities identified as potentially material in the gross list were 
evaluated by applying criteria for financial impact and likelihood. For financial 
materiality, the outcome of the financial impact assessment is multiplied by likeli-
hood. The outcome of the assessment formed the basis of the prioritisation of 
the risks and opportunities identified. A threshold value of two was applied to 
determine which ones should be classified as financially material.
Swedbank has taken into consideration the links between impact and financial 
materiality by investigating, for example, how Swedbank, through lending to the 
property sector, contributes to greenhouse gas emissions and can thus be 
exposed to risks linked to climate adaptation, or whether lending to energy effi-
ciency solutions might constitute an opportunity. 
In risk-based planning, ESG risks are prioritised annually in an internal calcula-
tion application. This includes identifying and considering risks using both a top-
down and bottom-up perspective, and has both a long-term and short-term per-
spective. As ESG risk is a driver of other risks, it is prioritised in the same way as 
other risk types. Risk-based planning supports the organisation in proactively 
considering relevant and material risks, in order to better perform in line with the 
Group’s strategy and targets, and to stay within the established risk appetite. The 
process of identifying, assessing and managing ESG risks is also an integral part 
of the Group’s operations, and the results are used as input to the Internal Capital 
Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP), in which material risks can be stress-
tested within the framework of the evaluation. At present, Swedbank does not 
have a process for integrating identified impacts into the established risk man-
agement process. Material risks are, however, included in the risk management 
process. This means that even if some impact areas have been assessed as 
being material, they are not managed systematically as risks within the frame-
work of the existing risk management process. 
Swedbank has not at present integrated material opportunities into a general 
governance process. 
Changes, validation and decisions
The outcome of the 2025 double materiality assessment differs in part from the 
corresponding assessment in 2024. This is generally due to greater access to 
quantitative data as a source, such as sector classification of the credit portfolio 
and the results of employee surveys. The use of quantitative data and the use of 
tools adapted for CSRD, such as the Portfolio Impact Analysis Tool developed by 
UNEP-FI, have made it possible to conduct a more granular assessment that is 
specific to Swedbank’s operations. See section SBM-3 Material impacts, risks 
and opportunities and their interaction with strategy and business model on page 
81 for a comprehensive list of material sustainability topics. The implementation 
of CSRD is still at a relatively early stage and this, combined with the proposed 
updates to the regulations, means that Swedbank still sees a need for continued 
methodological development of the double materiality assessment.

In the assessment, the environment-related sustainability topics of pollution,

Process to assess climate change
	 E1 IRO-1    Description of the processes to identify and assess material 
climate-related impacts, risks and opportunities
The procedure to identify and assess material sustainability issues related to 
­climate was divided into four analysis units:
•	Loans: Swedbank’s credit portfolio. 
•	Assets under management: Swedbank’s investments, primarily through 
­Swedbank Robur Fonder.
•	Own operations, including purchasing: Swedbank’s operations in the form of 
energy consumption of properties, business travel and purchasing of IT and 
office supplies. 
•	Payments: Swedbank’s provision of payment services.
The analysis is also divided into three parts: i) impacts, ii) risks and iii) opportuni-
ties. The identification of material climate-related impacts, risks and opportuni-
ties is largely based on the Group’s emission volumes. As the majority of Swed-
bank’s emissions originate from lending and assets under management, it means 
that Swedbank’s work focuses on these areas. For an overview of Swedbank’s 
emissions, see section E1-6 Total greenhouse gas emissions on page 107.
Impact
Lending
Swedbank has assessed positive and negative climate-related impacts related to 
the credit portfolio. To assess the Group’s positive impact, an analysis was con-
ducted of the Group’s Sustainable Asset Register, and of related impact reporting 
as presented in the Swedbank Sustainable Bond Impact Report. 
To assess negative impacts from Swedbank’s credit portfolio, emissions were 
analysed at sector level. Initially, an analysis of Swedbank’s credit portfolio was 
performed using the Portfolio Impact Analysis Tool developed by UNEP-FI. The 
results of the analysis were compared with the Group’s calculations of emissions 
by sector. For a number of emission-intensive sectors, Swedbank has decided on 
emission reduction targets by 2030 in accordance with the Paris Agreement’s 
1.5-degree scenario. The sectors have been selected on the basis of potential 
or actual climate impact, the size of Swedbank’s financing and the availability 
of ­reliable data. There is additional information on sectors selected in section  
E1-4 Targets, on pages 102–104. 
Assets under management
Swedbank Robur Fonder is committed to reducing its carbon footprint and can 
have an indirect or actual impact on climate change by allocating assets to 
investments that have an impact on the climate, as described in the fund man-
agement company’s Climate Strategy. Material positive impacts on climate 
change have been assessed within the framework of the investment process 
in each fund. 
To identify and assess potential and actual negative impact, Swedbank Robur 
Fonder uses indicators in the Sustainable Financial Disclosure Regulation 
(SFDR). These indicators state the Principle Adverse Impact (PAI) and are 
designed to measure and report the impact that investments can have on sus-
tainability factors, including climate change. The climate impact from invest-
ments in funds is followed up by measuring the carbon footprint of the fund 
­holdings. This method follows recommendations from the Net Zero Investment 
Framework and is applied to all fund capital. Carbon footprint measurements 
are followed up at least on an annual basis. 
Own operations and payments
As Swedbank has low emissions from its own operations, this unit is not material 
from a statutory requirement perspective. The same assessment was performed 
for payments, as Swedbank’s payment services are largely provided through pay-
ments with low climate emissions. 
In order to identify and assess potential or actual impact in its own operations 
and in the supply chain, Swedbank has conducted a review of Scope 1, Scope 2 
and Scope 3 emissions. An analysis has also been conducted using the ENCORE 
tool of those sectors from which Swedbank makes purchases that can have an 
impact on climate change. As part of Swedbank’s procurement process, a review 
is also conducted of the supplier’s geographical location, which is relevant as, for 
example, energy sources and infrastructure may vary from region to region. 
Research-based estimates of emissions from different payment methods, such 
as cash, cards and mobile payments, have been used in the analysis of the cli-
mate impact of payment services. The results show that cash payments generate 
higher emissions compared to cards and digital alternatives. As a large propor-
tion of Swedbank’s customers use card payments, the negative climate impact 
from the Group’s payment services is deemed to be low. To assess financial 
materiality, a risk assessment was conducted in accordance with the established 
operational ESG risk methodology for own operations including purchasing and 
payments, together with a qualitative assessment of opportunities based on the 
criteria applied to other ESG-related topics. No analysis of physical and transition 
risks has been conducted or scenario analyses applied. 
Risk
Lending
Methods to identify and assess climate risks
Climate change is characterised by both an increased risk of acute hazards and 
potentially irreversible long-term environmental degradation. The risks need to be 
managed in the near future, even though the majority of the risk is likely to materi-
alise in the long term. There is also considerable uncertainty around what mea-
sures the world’s countries will take, as well as the timing and extent of mea-
sures. This means that different types of methods are needed to assess the 
financial impact on Swedbank, including an enhanced analysis in which different 
scenarios and outcomes are examined in economic and financial terms. An 
enhanced analysis is also needed of the Group’s customers, to identify both 
immediate and future potential risks in the Group’s lending at micro level. Meth-
odologies to assess the financial materiality for financial actors such as banks, 
i.e. establishing a clear and measurable link between climate risks and credit risk, 
are still at an early stage of development, which means that there is material 
uncertainty in the outcome.
In its report on the management and supervision of ESG risks, i.e. environmen-
tal, social and governance risks, the European Banking Authority (EBA) presents 
a set of risk assessment methods, all with a focus on climate risks. These are: 
(1) the risk framework method, which focuses on how ESG risks impact a bank’s 
risk profile through standard risk indicators and includes scenario analysis 
and stress tests; 
(2) the exposure method, which focuses on how exposed individual counter­
parties are to ESG factors; and 
(3) the portfolio alignment method, which focuses on how aligned a bank’s credit 
portfolio is with global sustainability targets.

Swedbank has developed methods in all three categories, and these are 
described in the text below.
The risk framework method – forward-looking risk identification 
and ­assessment
i) Scenario analyses
Climate change, and the transition made to meet the threat of climate change, 
may give rise to risks for Swedbank, primarily through the credit risk arising from 
lending. As part of the Group’s ESG risk and materiality assessment of climate 
risks, scenario analyses are conducted (please note that scenario analyses are 
separate from the double materiality assessment). All scenarios have been 
developed by Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), and the 
­scenarios used are: 
(a) Net-Zero 2050, which entails an immediate and orderly transition with an 
increase of 1.4°C in the average temperature by 2100. 
(b) Delayed transition, which entails a delayed and disorderly transition with an 
increased transition risk and an increase of 1.7°C in the average temperature 
by 2100.
(c) Current policies, which entails increased physical climate risks and an 
increase of 3.0°C in the average temperature by 2100. 
The scenarios contain both global and national variables, for example GDP, infla-
tion and carbon price, that are relevant drivers for the identification and assess-
ment of risks where the Group has its assets. For the assessment of physical 
risks, variables for economic damage relating to floods, heatwaves and droughts, 
which in Swedbank’s real estate lending are supplemented with geodata, which 
shows real estate lending in particularly vulnerable areas. 
The NGFS scenarios have different narratives that contain quantitative vari-
ables and assumptions, as well as descriptions of different time horizons for 
transition and physical scenarios with varying degrees of natural disasters. 
Guided by Swedbank’s ESG risk framework, relevance assessment and the mate-
riality map prepared by the Sustainable Accounting Standards Board (SASB), as 
well as the Group’s own industry and sustainability experts, identification takes 
place of the sectors that are exposed to different climate risk drivers. Examples 
of these drivers include greenhouse gas emissions, energy management and 
physical climate risks. An expert assessment is then conducted to assess nega-
tive financial impacts for Swedbank in different scenarios in terms of, for exam-
ple, increased expected credit impairments and potential operating losses. 
Swedbank’s Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (IKU/ICAAP) 
examines the long-term effects of the transition to climate neutrality in a ten-year 
scenario. 
The climate scenarios presented have not affected the Group’s financial state-
ments for 2025. Climate risks are primarily expected to materialise in the finan-
cial statements as credit risks and credit impairments. In the Group’s assess-
ment of expected credit impairments that are not captured by traditional models 
and historical statistics, probable credit risks resulting from the climate scenarios 
have not yet been considered sufficiently quantifiable and material for ­specific 
provisions. 
ii) Stress tests
As part of the ICAAP, three-year scenario-driven stress tests are conducted, 
­integrating both physical risks and transition risks. 
Exposure methodology – ESG analysis of corporate customers with 
a focus on climate-related risk
In the credit process, corporate customers are assessed from a sustainability 
perspective with the aim of ensuring that risks are managed satisfactorily and 
that the customer’s operations are aligned with Swedbank’s values and guide-
lines. The ESG analysis tool uses a quantifiable methodology based on the mate-
riality map developed by SASB, which is now part of the International Financial 
Reporting Standards (IFRS). This methodology makes it possible to focus on the 
most material ESG factors for each industry. By providing industry-specific and 
customer-specific ESG scores, the new tool will enable Swedbank to manage 
ESG risks in lending operations at both customer and portfolio levels. The ESG 
score is a result of: 
(i) The identification of exposures to ESG factors (e.g. greenhouse gas emis-
sions, energy efficiency, physical risk) in each sector based on the customer’s 
­primary economic activity. 
(ii) The assessment of the customer’s ESG management capability based on 
a questionnaire. The assessment results in an ESG score and a classification 
of corporate customers into the categories of high, medium and low ESG risk. 
The portfolio alignment method – Swedbank measures financed 
­emissions and has adopted climate targets for the credit portfolio 
that are aligned with the 1.5-degree target
Swedbank’s climate targets for the credit portfolio primarily aim to create busi-
ness that is sustainable in the long term by supporting customers in reducing 
their climate impact while also reducing the climate risks in the portfolio. At the 
same time, the targets serve as a tool for the Group to reduce its exposure to 
­climate risks, by directing the credit portfolio towards activities that are aligned 
with the target of limiting global warming to 1.5°C. 
Methods to identify and assess climate risks
Swedbank uses a combination of methods to identify and assess transition risks 
and physical risks in its lending. As described earlier, an ESG risk and materiality 
assessment is conducted, identifying which activities are deemed to be able to 
have a potential material financial impact. For example, for the real estate portfo-
lios (property management and housing), transport and manufacturing sectors, 
transition risks are analysed based on stricter regulations and increased costs of 
carbon emissions in the short to medium term. The physical risks are analysed 
through a methodology developed by SMHI in which a broad spectrum of climate­-
-related events were investigated, including the IPCC’s high-emission scenario 
(Representative Concentration Pathways RCP 8.5), in which emissions continue 
to accelerate and global warming stabilises at just under four degrees. The identi-
fication of properties that are more sensitive to the impact of the physical risk 
events of climate change is undertaken by evaluating the development of physi-
cal risk indicators in the different scenarios in different geographically ­specified 
areas.
For 2025, 4 per cent of lending against collateral in properties in Sweden was 
deemed to have heightened sensitivity to physical risk, of which 3 per cent was 
sensitive to acute physical risk. In the Baltic countries, 1.2 per cent of lending 
against collateral in residential properties was deemed to have heightened sensi-
tivity to physical climate risks for 2025. The indicator for rising sea levels has not 
been calculated for the Baltic countries. 
Climate risks in the short, medium and long term 
The scenario analysis that forms the basis of Swedbank’s ESG risk and material-
ity assessment uses NGFS scenarios that extend to 2050. In the “Delayed Transi-
tion” scenario, the focus is on 2030, when transition risks suddenly increase rap-
idly and sharply. In the “Current Policies” scenario, the focus is on the effects in 
the latter part of the scenario, when the physical risks have reached a signifi-
cantly higher level compared with other scenarios. This also captures potentially 
significant risks that lie far in the future. The ICAAP’s internal forecast, which 
examines the effects of Swedbank’s strategy and plans, extends ten years ahead 
to 2034, with annual effects and extended analysis of metrics for 2023, 2028 and 
2033. In the short term, in this case three years, Swedbank has, as part of the 
ICAAP, investigated what a stressed transition could mean in terms of profit­
ability and capitalisation, including an assessment of increased credit risks. 
Definition of short, medium and long term 
From a risk identification perspective and to determine what is material, a defini-
tion is used in which the long term extends over 10 years (in accordance with the 
double materiality assessment). The NGFS scenarios used in the Group extend 
until 2050 and thus cover the long-term perspective. Among the scenarios are 
“Delayed transition”, in which the greatest risks materialise in the medium-term 
perspective, i.e. in the range of 4–10 years. Swedbank’s strategic planning has 
a five-year horizon and a tactical planning horizon of 1–3 years, where the latter 
represents the short-term perspective. 
The expected lifetime of different parts of Swedbank’s lending is described 
below. 
Transition risk: Swedbank has loans of approximately SEK 580bn to compa-
nies and tenant-owner associations that are reported to have a heightened transi-
tion risk. Property-related lending, including tenant-owner associations, accounts 
for 70 per cent. The average term of property-related lending has an average 
remaining term of 9 years. For most other sectors, the term is between 0 and 3 
years, with a clear emphasis on 1 year. The only longer term is noted for “Produc-
tion of electricity” (exposure SEK 15bn), which has a term of 3 years.
Physical risk:Swedbank has loans with collateral in residential properties of 
approximately SEK 1 062bn. The loans in the portfolio that have a heightened 
physical climate risk (approximately 4 per cent) have an average remaining term 
of just over 23 years. Loans with collateral in commercial properties in Sweden 
amount to approximately SEK 170bn. The loans that have a heightened physical 
climate risk have an average term of 11 years.

are a cornerstone of the Group’s low risk profile. Scenario analysis and stress 
tests provide the basis for customer dialogues aimed at promoting customer 
transition and enabling proactivity in strategies and plans.

and office environments, are deemed to be non-material. Nor have material cli-
mate risks been identified in the Group’s supply chain. With regard to lending, the

and ­ecosystems
	 E4 IRO-1    The process to identify and assess material  
sustainability topics
The process to identify and assess material sustainability issues related to bio­
diversity and ecosystems was divided into four analysis units: lending, assets 
under management, payments and our operations including purchasing. Bio­
diversity was assessed to as be material in lending operations and indicated 
an indirect potential negative impact.
Assessing impacts, risks and opportunities linked to biodiversity in the bank-
ing sector is still at an early stage. There is a lack of scientifically based, sector­-
specific guidelines, universally quantifiable metrics and quality-assured data for 
customers in relation to biodiversity.
As a consequence of this, Swedbank’s focus has been on assessing potential 
rather than actual impact, and the Group has applied available and adapted analy-
sis tools to the extent possible. In addition to this, qualitative assessments have 
been conducted based on industry exposure in relation to relevant quantitative 
and qualitative input data. There has also been collaboration with internal experts 
and researchers on the subject. The assessment was conducted in accordance 
with the requirements of the double materiality assessment, the process for 
which is described on pages 86–87. 
Lending
Impacts
To analyse impacts in this area, Swedbank used the Portfolio Impact Analysis 
Tool developed by UNEP FI (United Nations Environment Programme Finance 
­Initiative). A potential negative impact on the loss of biodiversity was identified 
indirectly through the value chain via the Group’s corporate lending. In order to 
identify the sectors with the greatest potential negative impact, a more detailed 
analysis of the loan portfolio’s exposure was conducted using the analysis tools 
ENCORE and Bioscope. The assessment included Swedbank’s indirect contribu-
tion to the direct causes behind loss of biodiversity, including climate change, 
changes in land, freshwater and sea water, direct exploitation of species, invasive 
species, and pollution, as well as the impact and dependencies on ecosystem 
services. The assessment does not, however, include analysis of impacts on the 
state of species or impacts on the spread and state of ecosystems through land 
degradation, desertification and soil sealing. 
Swedbank has identified dependencies on ecosystem services with a specific 
focus on the downstream value chain. ENCORE has been used to assess these 
dependencies, with a focus on mapping them without evaluating their current 
or expected disruption status. 
Risk
The risk assessment of the area is part of the risk-based planning process, in 
which a prioritisation of ESG risks is carried out annually. Swedbank assesses 
material risks caused by loss of biodiversity and ecosystems for relevant risk 
types. The analysis is based on scenarios from the Network for Greening the 
Financial System (NGFS). The development of physical and transition events 
at a macroeconomic level is considered in these scenarios and used in sector 
analyses. To conduct the assessment, an impact assessment is conducted for 
­certain sectors based on their dependence on ecosystem services. An impact 
and dependency analysis based on geographical information was conducted for 
biodiversity and ecosystems, with a focus on financed properties located in key 
biotopes, nature reserves and Natura 2000 areas. The assessment criteria for the 
sector analysis are based on the WWF Biodiversity Risk Filter’s five-point scale 
and guidance from the Task Force on Nature-related Financial Disclosures 
(TNFD). The NGFS scenarios do not specifically include systemic risks, such as 
large-scale ecosystem collapses. The scenarios do, however, include increased 
average temperatures as well as increased frequency of heavy rainfall, drought 
and heatwaves. These events have been taken into consideration in particular 
for the agricultural and forestry sector.
Opportunity
The analysis of business opportunities was based on the Group’s framework for 
assessing business opportunities in relation to NGFS stipulated scenarios, and 
was conducted in collaboration with representatives from different Business 
Areas and Group Functions.

Assessment of impacts

To identify and assess indirect contributions from the Business Area to the direct

on biodiversity and ecosystems.

Own operations

Process to assess business conduct 
	 G1 IRO-1    The process to identify and assess material  
sustainability topics
Working with a high standards of business conduct is fundamental for all bank-
ing operations and a material sustainability area for Swedbank. Swedbank oper-
ates in a highly regulated sector in all four of the Group’s home markets, with 
a commitment to maintain financial stability. Based on Swedbank’s double 
­materiality assessment method, aspects related to business conduct have been 
analysed based on Swedbank’s business context and established risk analysis 
models for banking operations. In identifying and assessing material impacts 
and financial materiality, internal experts within relevant units with legal expertise 
provided their opinions and assessments. Swedbank has identified positive 
impacts related to its own operations where the foundation for business conduct 
is laid through processes and procedures for a sound corporate culture and busi-
ness ethics. Through the provision of financing solutions, investments and finan-
cial advice, Swedbank involves stakeholders in the upstream and downstream 
value chain. In the earlier stages of the value chain, business relationships with 
suppliers were identified as a material sustainability area that places demands 
on ethical standards and conscious risk management in the purchasing process. 
Through its business activities, the banking sector is exposed to risks linked to 
financial crime in the form of corruption and bribery, money laundering, terrorist 
financing, violation or circumvention of financial sanctions, tax evasion and 
fraud. Corruption and bribery as well as the entity-specific disclosure of financial 
crime were therefore identified as material sustainability areas for Swedbank 
linked to business conduct. Any deficiencies in these processes and controls can 
have a negative impact on society, but also financial consequences in the form of 
damaged trust and sanctions for Swedbank.

	 GOV-1    Role of the Board of Directors and the CEO1

Swedbank’s Board of Directors (“Board”) is the highest decision-making body 
after the AGM and the highest executive body, with overarching responsibility 
for the Group’s governance. The Board sets the Group’s targets and strategies, 
ensures that they are appropriate for the business, and that they are imple-
mented, followed-up and evaluated. Furthermore, the Board is responsible for 
governing and supporting the business by adopting policies, ensuring effective 
systems and processes for follow-up and control, and regularly evaluating risk 
management to ensure that it is effective. The Board is responsible for ensuring 
compliance with laws and regulations and keeps itself informed about changes 
in the external environment and relevant rules for business conduct. 
 The Board’s responsibilities are based on external and internal regulations. 
The internal regulations, such as policies adopted by the Board and instructions 
adopted by the CEO, define the division of responsibilities within the Group and 
are tools for the Board and the CEO in their controlling roles. Among other things, 
the Board has adopted a Sustainability Policy in which it is stated that the Board 
has an overarching responsibility to ensure that Swedbank’s strategies are well 
adapted to its business operations, that the Group has adequate and effective 
governance structures and control processes in place, that these processes are 
applied consistently throughout the organisation and that they are integrated 
with Swedbank’s risk framework and risk management. The Sustainability Policy 
also states that the Board shall ensure that the organisation and management of 
Swedbank’s business operations are characterised by sound internal control. To 
assist it in this work, the Board has established four committees, that amongst 
other address sustainability matters.
In addition the Board has adopted a Policy on Diversity, Equity and Inclusion, 
as this is a fundamental prerequisite for robust corporate governance. The Board 
has also adopted a Code of Conduct that sets out the framework for how employ-
ees are expected to conduct Swedbank’s business and relationships, and serves 
as the Group’s ethics policy. Swedbank’s internal regulations and related gover-
nance documents describe in more detail how employees should act with trans-
parency, trust and integrity. 
All of Swedbank’s policies and instructions are reviewed and adopted on an 
annual basis. The Board approves Swedbank’s annual report and, at least quar-
terly, interim reports on the Group’s financial position and development, and can 
thus evaluate and follow up on business operations and sustainability work. In 
addition, the Board also receives monthly reports from Group Risk as well as 
ongoing information from the CEO, Group Executive Committee, The Board’s 
committees and quarterly reports from Group Compliance in order to oversee 
and govern the ­business in respect of issues including conflicts of interest and 
corruption. 
Composition of the Board of Directors
The Board members appointed by the AGM do not work operationally at Swed-
bank. The composition of the Board should be characterised by diversity with 
regard to age, geographical origin and both educational and professional back-
ground, in order to promote independent viewpoints, sound decision-making and 
critical questioning. There is a 29-year age difference between Swedbank’s 
youngest and oldest board members. The members’ educational backgrounds 
vary and include, for example, economics, law, sociology, political science and 
mechanical engineering.
Efforts shall be made over time to achieve an even gender distribution. An 
even gender distribution means that at least 40 per cent of Board members 
should be of each gender. The gender distribution on the Board is 45.5 per cent 
women and 54.5 per cent men. The number of independent Board members is 9 
out of a total of 11 members, which corresponds to 81.8 per cent. The Board also 
has two permanent employee representatives appointed by the local branch of 
the Finansförbundet trade union. The local branch of the Finansförbundet trade 
union and the local branch of the Akademikerförbundet trade union also appoints 
one deputy each. In October 2025 the deputy appointed by the Finansförbundet 
trade union resigned and a replacement will be elected in connection with the 
AGM 2026. The employee representatives mainly contribute expertise in the area 
of labour law, including matters of working conditions and equal treatment. 
The members have experience from various sectors, such as banking and sav-
ings banks, insurance and pensions, macroeconomics, business, the real estate 
sector, private and corporate customers, forestry and agriculture, digitalisation 
and artificial intelligence, savings including securities, and lending. The members 
also have work experience from senior positions, including Sweden’s Prime 
­Minister and Minister of Finance, CEO and senior position in the real estate 
sector, CEO of a savings bank and President and CEO of an international corpo-
rate group. Moreover, the members have experience in different geographical 
regions such as Sweden and the Baltic countries. The Board also possesses 
expertise in the areas of digitalisation and AI, corporate governance, ethics, law 
and sustainability, with special expertise in the field of work against financial 
crime, anti-­corruption and risk management.

established several committees with the task of preparing matters in various

 The CEO is responsible for Swedbank’s position statements in respect of the 
armaments industry and climate change, as well as instructions to support the 
implementation of the Group’s policies. Swedbank’s position statements specify 
how sustainability is integrated in business decisions, and are more operational 
than Swedbank’s policies. 
In addition to the Group Executive Committee, there are a number of commit-
tees that gather expertise when preparing various matters. With a few excep-
tions, the committees have no collective decision-making authority. Decisions 
are made by the chair of each committee, or the decision is referred to the CEO. 
As can be seen from the sustainability governance map, the committees estab-
lished include the following:
The Group Asset Allocation Committee is tasked with managing the Group’s 
financial risks. Sustainability factors must be considered across all risk types and 
also in all risk management. The CFO is the chair and decision-maker of the com-
mittee. Depending on the nature of the matter, the committee may make a recom-
mendation before a decision is referred to an appropriate body, such as the Chief 
Risk Officer, the CEO or the Board.
The Group Risk and Compliance Committee is tasked with mapping and com-
municating a holistic view of the Group’s non-financial risks, and also ensuring 
consistent and appropriate governance within the risk area and contributing to a 
sound risk culture. Sustainability factors must be considered in all risk types and 
in all risk management. The Head of Group Risk chairs the committee. Depending 
on the matter in hand, the Head of Group Risk or the Head of Group Compliance is 
the decision-maker in the committee. Depending on the nature of the matter, the 
Group Risk and Compliance Committee may make a recommendation to refer 
a decision to an appropriate body, such as the CEO or the Board.
The Group Executive Sustainability Committee is tasked with ensuring effec-
tive management and governance of the sustainability perspective within the 
Group. The CFO is the chair and decision-maker of the committee. Depending 
on the nature of the matter, the committee may make recommendations before 
a decision is referred to an appropriate body or function, such as the CEO. This 
committee, together with the Group Operational Sustainability Committee and its 
two sub-committees, was established during 2025 in connection with a reorgani-
sation within Swedbank, which saw it replacing the previous equivalent commit-
tee in order to ensure that sustainability is integrated more effectively into the 
Group’s core business operations and governance processes. The purpose of the 
Operational Sustainability Committee is to translate strategy and sustainability 
plans into concrete action by coordinating between units and following up on 
ongoing initiatives. The sub-committees include the Sustainability Framework 
Committee, which supports the organisation with structured analysis and recom-
mendations in individual matters within the framework of the Group’s sustain­
ability policy framework.
This structure aims to ensure that Swedbank manages sustainability matters 
at several levels, with clear decision-making paths and a common direction, in 
order to strengthen the Group’s long-term work on responsible banking. 
Swedbank uses reporting channels that are already in place for information to 
the Board and the CEO relating to impacts, risks and opportunities, and manages 
relevant information through these. In addition, Swedbank has an independent, 
separate whistleblowing function, which enables whistleblowers to report irregu-
larities openly or anonymously alongside the usual reporting channels. 
The Board, the CEO and relevant committees are regularly informed about mate-
rial impacts, risks and opportunities by relevant units. These aspects are taken into 
account at an overall level in the annual review of the Group’s business strategy. 
The CEO is responsible for executing, implementing and following up on the 
Board’s adopted strategies and ensuring that Swedbank develops in line with the 
strategic direction, including the area of sustainability. To ensure progress, both 
the CEO and Swedbank’s Business Areas, Product Areas and Group Functions are 
followed up through sustainability-related key performance indicators (KPIs).
Swedbank’s internal regulations and associated processes govern how the 
Board of Directors, CEO and Group Executive Committee exercise supervision of 
the setting of targets and monitor progress towards these targets. Sustainability 
work is a regular item on the Board of Directors’ and CEO’s agenda, ensuring that 
the sustainability perspective is integrated into decision-making.
Swedbank’s extensive internal regulations cover all of the Group’s areas of 
operation and regulate issues such as the handling of information, reporting and 
escalation. Swedbank’s internal regulations and associated processes also 
govern how special controls and procedures are applied to manage impacts, 
risks and opportunities, and how these are integrated with other internal func-
tions, as well as how the Board of Directors, CEO and Group Executive Committee 
exercise supervision of the setting of related targets and monitor progress 
towards those targets. Among other things, regular employee surveys are con-
ducted, the results of which are important contributions to the identification of 
strengths, impacts, risks and opportunities for possible measures. The results 
are discussed within each unit, and Group HR & Facility Management is responsi-
ble for communicating the results to the Group Executive Committee to support 
strategy development and improvement initiatives. The two employee represen-
tatives on the Board of Directors are also involved in the Board’s work on the 
strategy and business model. Another example of the way in which sustainability 
work is translated into practice is how Swedbank’s Business Areas identify cli-
mate-related opportunities through analyses of how the transition affects differ-
ent sectors, and integrate the results into strategic planning. Based on Swed-
bank’s double materiality assessment method, aspects related to business 
conduct have also been analysed based on Swedbank’s business context and 
established risk analysis models for banking operations. Working with high stan-
dards of business conduct is fundamental for Swedbank’s banking operations. 
Swedbank’s sustainability work is therefore regularly included on the agenda 
of the Board of Directors and the CEO, which ensures that the perspective is 
included in decision-making. This includes managing sustainability-related 
impacts as well as risks and opportunities by means of, for example, integrating 
sustainability into the range of financial products and services.
Management of sustainability matters

by the Board of Directors and the CEO
The Board and the CEO, including relevant committees, are regularly informed 
about material impacts, risks and opportunities by relevant units. As part of work 
to determine the outcome of the Group’s materiality assessment, the Board’s 
committees (Remuneration and ­Sustainability Committee and Audit Committee) 
and the CEO are informed about the dual materiality assessment process, the

At an overarching level, impacts, risks and opportunities are taken into account

Interpretation and implementation
The reporting requirements under the EU Taxonomy are under development and 
form part of the EU’s Omnibus proposal for sustainability, which aims to simplify 
and coordinate sustainability legislation. Swedbank works continuously to imple-
ment changes in the EU taxonomy and are discussing interpretation issues and 
industry practice on an ongoing basis within Finance Sweden’s working group. 
This year’s reporting is presented in accordance with the Omnibus Delegated Act, 
but further analysis and implementation resulting from the new directive will 
­continue next year, as Swedbank also continues to assess the FAQs published in 
December 2025. Swedbank hopes that additional guidance on requirements and 
definitions will be published in the coming year. Swedbank does not apply the 
materiality-exemption related to non-assessed exposures, which allow financial 
undertakings to omit assessing taxonomy-eligibility or taxonomy-alignment of 
certain KPIs and holdings, nor exposures included on a voluntary basis in the 
report 2025, but intends to evaluate the possibility in 2026. 
Alignment with the EU Taxonomy, including KPIs, is monitored on a quarterly 
basis by Swedbank’s Business Areas. By supporting the Group’s customers in 
developing sustainable operations and energy-efficient housing, as well as 
making sustainable investments, the ambition is to improve the KPIs. Swedbank 
has started to update customer processes and develop new products, for exam-
ple to be able to demonstrate the Taxonomy alignment of an individual loan. 
Increasing the proportion of environmentally sustainable assets is an important 
element of Swedbank’s climate work. The Group has decided on climate targets 
for financed emissions by 2030 in several sectors, including commercial proper-
ties and mortgages. Sustainability-related climate targets are presented on 
page 78.
The EU Taxonomy plays a central role in identifying the activities of Swed-
bank’s customers that can contribute to achieving the climate targets. Increasing 
Taxonomy­-aligned assets and assets under management is important for Swed-
bank to be able to ensure that the targets are achieved. Within Swedbank’s assets 
under management, a number of funds in the ­product range have committed to 
maintaining a minimum proportion of Taxonomy­-aligned investments. The EU 
Taxonomy will serve as one of several tools for monitoring the sustainability 
­performance of these assets.
Loans collateralised by residential immovable property
The acquisition and ownership of property by households is an activity covered 
by the EU Taxonomy. The majority of Swedbank’s assets that are covered by the 
regulation consist of loans collateralised by residential immovable property. 
Housing accounts for a significant part of the EU’s energy consumption and 
greenhouse gas emissions, which can be reduced through increased energy 
­efficiency. Swedbank contributes to the financing of energy efficiency improve-
ments in residential properties and is dependent on high-quality energy data.
The EU Taxonomy sets different requirements for a loan collateralised by 
­residential immovable property to be classified as Taxonomy-aligned, depending 
on when the building was built. For buildings built before 31 December 2020, the 
primary energy requirement of the property must be within the top 15 per cent of 
the national housing stock or have energy class A. 
Swedbank’s energy requirements are based on threshold values developed on 
behalf of Fastighetsägarna for loans collateralised by residential immovable 
property in Sweden. Corresponding information was used for loans collateralised 
by residential immovable property in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. 
For buildings built after 31 December 2020, the requirement is instead that the 
primary energy requirement must be at least 10 per cent below the threshold for 
near-zero energy buildings.
To meet the requirements to not cause significant harm to the Climate Change 
Adaptation target, Swedbank conducted climate risk assessments for loans col-
lateralised by residential immovable property, in accordance with the same meth-
odology used in the Pillar 3 report. Loans collateralised by residential immovable 
property are reported as Taxonomy-aligned when the property both meets the 
energy requirements and the climate risk assessment indicates low risk. Data for 
the climate risk assessment has been obtained from an external supplier. Work is 
under way to develop these assessments.
CSRD companies
Financial companies rely heavily on customers and counterparties reporting in 
accordance with the EU Taxonomy, so that they can fulfil their own reporting obli-
gations. Swedbank’s reporting thus reflects the companies’ reporting in terms of 
both scope and alignment. Information from corporate customers’ sustainability 
statements has been obtained from an external supplier. 
Corporate lending accounts for 26 per cent (24) of Swedbank’s assets, of 
which only 2 per cent (2) are CSRD companies. 
Assets under management in CSRD companies constitute 36 per cent (35) of 
total assets under management. Assets under management in global portfolios 
with holdings outside the EU and assets under management with an investment 
focus on small and medium-sized enterprises, which do not report under the EU 
Taxonomy, contribute to lower Taxonomy alignment.
Data availability and quality
The absence of a central external database for corporate sustainability informa-
tion and the inadequate quality of external data pose difficulties in collecting 
quality-assured data regarding KPIs from corporate customers and energy 
perfor­mance of properties. Inadequate availability and quality of data affects 
Taxonomy alignment and thereby the KPIs GAR and Green ratio for assets under 
management. At present, Swedbank has not been able to obtain data for all data 
points requested, for example “use of proceeds” in connection with corporate 
loans.
52 per cent (55) of Swedbank’s loans collateralised by residential immovable 
property do not have valid energy performance certificates, which limits the 
­ability to demonstrate Taxonomy alignment. The system of energy classes is not 
harmonised, which is why, for example, in Sweden there are higher requirements 
than in many other EU countries for a property to be assigned energy class A, 
and thus meet the requirements of the EU Taxonomy.

Strategy and business model
	 E1 SBM-3    Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their 
­interaction with strategy and business model 
The climate transition poses major challenges, while it can also represent new 
business opportunities for both Swedbank and its customers. The Group’s ambi‑
tion is to be a key actor in the transition by financing sustainable solutions, for 
example through projects that inceases the energy efficiency of buildings. Swed‑
bank works to direct financing and investments towards sustainable activities, 
complemented by dialogue, advisory services and follow-up. 
Within Swedbank’s total credit portfolio, where the real estate sector accounts 
for approximately 80 per cent, the focus is on supporting the energy transition. 
By requesting energy performance certificates and offering commercial property 
customers support with the implementation of sustainable energy solutions, and 
the Group may be able to enhance their ability to upgrade existing properties. 
Swedbank is also reviewing its product and service portfolio in order to better 
meet market demands for sustainability and innovation.
Within asset management, efforts to mitigate climate change form an important 
starting point. This includes excluding holdings with significant climate impact 
in line with established criteria for fossil‑related sectors, and actively directing 
­capital towards companies considered well‑positioned for the climate transition.
Identified climate-related risks 
Risk identification and evaluation of climate-related risks are carried out annually. 
It is primarily in the credit portfolio where transition risks in the short term have 
been assessed to be material for the Group. Among the sectors where Swedbank 
has identified significant transition risks are the energy sector, property manage‑
ment, transportation, forestry and agriculture, as well as manufacturing. A list of 
all risk drivers and their financial impact on different parts of the Group’s lending 
would be very extensive. Some examples of events that could increase the 
Group’s transition risk in lending include:
•	New or amended policies and legislation aimed at mitigating climate change.
•	Significant increases in energy prices with an impact on economic stability. 
•	New or changed technology that limits climate change. 
•	New or changed behaviours among consumers and investors to support 
­climate change mitigation. 
Resilience analysis
Swedbank’s work to increase resilience to climate risks includes both qualitative 
and quantitative analyses to manage climate risks effectively within the credit 
portfolio. The qualitative assessments indicate that greenhouse gas emissions 
and energy factors will have a less negative impact on the business model and 
strategy over a horizon of 1-5 years. Based on the scenario analysis and the 
stress tests conducted as part of Swedbank’s Internal Capital Adequacy Assess‑
ment Process (ICAAP), the conclusion is that the Group’s resilience to climate-­
related risks is good. The ICAAP includes:
•	A ten-year scenario in which Swedbank simulates its capital situation given 
a transition in accordance with the Group’s climate targets. The result shows 
that both profitability and capitalisation remain strong.
•	Three-year macroeconomic stress tests integrating both physical risks and tran‑
sition risks. The results show that the Group’s resilience to both stressed transi‑
tion risks and stressed physical risks in terms of extensive flooding is good. 
The ICAAP covers Swedbank’s consolidated situation, with the exception of the 
Group’s wholly owned insurance company, which is included only as an equity 
holding. The ICAAP covers both operational activities and the value chains for 
lending and savings. No material climate-related risks have been excluded from 
the ICAAP in respect of the value chains. The processes for the ten-year scenario 
analysis and the three-year stressed scenarios are under development, and the 
quantitative results are derived from a number of assumptions based on Swed‑
bank’s strategy, plans and hypothetical scenario developments. It is assumed 
that the trend in the macroeconomic scenario will follow the long-term trend,
