Climate Transition Plan
	 E1-1    Transition plan for climate change mitigation
The Swedbank Climate Transition Plan is based on the Group’s strategy and 
focuses on selected customer segments and areas. One important element of 
the plan is Swedbank’s position statement on climate and nature, which specifies 
various types of restrictions on fossil fuels, including coal, peat, oil and gas.
One key element of Swedbank’s Climate Transition Plan is the Group’s over­
arching target of achieving net zero emissions by 2050 by aligning the credit port­
folio and assets under management with the 1.5-degree target of the Paris 
Agreement. In this area Swedbank is working to adapt the business model by 
steering financing and investments towards sustainable activities and through 
dialogue, advice and follow-up. This is reflected in the aim to increase sustain‑
able financing to support new business opportunities. The biggest ­climate 
impact occurs via customers, which means that customers making the transition 
is a key component of the Group’s work to reduce emissions. Swedbank’s ability 
to achieve set climate targets depends on the ability of customers to make the 
transition. This is why the Climate Transition Plan places particular emphasis 
on this.
The Swedbank Climate Transition Plan was published in 2024 and has been 
approved by the CEO and reviewed by the Board of Directors. It will be updated 
and adapted as climate work develops and new legislation emerges, and will 
strive to ensure that the right conditions are in place to achieve the Group’s 
­climate targets. 
Progress in the implementation of the Climate Transition Plan is monitored by 
reviewing set targets, primarily by measuring financed emissions. Swedbank is 
not currently conducting a quantitative analysis of or follow-up on the actions 
that contribute to reduced emissions. The Climate Transition Plan is not currently 
an integral element of the financial planning process. Swedbank has not identi‑
fied material operating or capital expenditure specifically for the Climate Transi‑
tion Plan; these expenses are an integral part of Swedbank’s running costs. 
Swedbank’s share is not excluded from the EU Paris‑aligned Benchmarks.

Assessment of customers’ climate transition plans
In 2025, Swedbank developed its methodology for assessing the climate transi‑
tion plans of corporate customers. The assessment focuses on four areas: tar‑
gets and metrics, implementation plan, financing and governance. The method 
has been used during the year to evaluate large corporate customers in sectors 
where Swedbank has set 2030 targets for reducing financed emission intensity.
This assessment enables Swedbank to better understand customers’ pre‑
paredness for the climate transition and evaluate whether their plans are aligned 
with the 1.5-degree scenario. The assessment is also used to better understand 
how customers’ climate transition plans relate to the Group’s own climate targets. 
The majority of customers evaluated were deemed to have credible transition 
plans. A credible climate transition plan means that the customer has a targets in 
line with the Paris agreement, clear strategies to achieve its targets, effective 
governance and reporting, and investments and decisions that follow the plan. 
Less than one third are deemed to lack sufficient commitment in their transition 
plan or have significant deficiencies in the plan. Swedbank engages in dialogue 
with, advice to and follow-up on improvement measures for these customers.

excluding discretionary mandates. Actions have been taken during the year to 
exclude business operations, include investment objects and engage with hold‑
ings with the aim of reducing the greenhouse gas emissions of managed funds. 
Swedbank Robur Fonder has excluded operations in the fossil sector (coal, oil 
and gas) in accordance with its exclusion strategy. Daily checks are conducted

accounts for 70 per cent of financed scope 1 and 2 emissions from Swedish fund

Prerequisites for climate actions
Swedbank’s ability to implement actions to address climate change, in terms of 
both mitigation and adaptation, depends on the availability of resources, where 
capital is a decisive factor. By operating profitably, the Group can ensure stable, 
cost-efficient financing. This in turn enables Swedbank to support its customers 
in the transition, for example by offering loans for investments in sustainable proj‑
ects and technologies that reduce emissions and promote the climate transition. 
Internal expertise in sustainability also plays a central role. Employees with 
in-depth knowledge of climate topics help drive the effectiveness of Swedbank’s 
climate actions. Swedbank follows industry practice and adapts to changing reg‑
ulations and market trends. Finally, access to data is crucial for strategy develop‑
ment and operational decisions. Data gives the Group insight into current emis‑
sion levels, identifies risk areas and opportunities, and helps to measure progress 
towards Swedbank’s targets. By analysing data, Swedbank can make more 
informed decisions that strengthen commitment to long-term sustainability. 
All in all, this means that Swedbank is highly dependent on these resources in 
order to successfully implement its climate strategies. 
Swedbank has identified actions based on adopted strategies, which are fol‑
lowed up annually. These actions aim to contribute to the climate targets, which 
in turn aim to reduce negative impacts, strengthen positive ones and make use of 
business opportunities. Swedbank does not conduct quantitative follow-up on 
how each action contributes to these. Swedbank has not identified any signifi‑
cant capital or operational expenditures for the measures beyond the resources 
already integrated into the regular financial planning.
Targets
	 E1-4    Targets related to climate change mitigation and adaptation
The Swedbank Climate Transition Plan is based on a commitment to achieve net 
zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 at the latest, in line with the 1.5 degree 
target of the Paris Agreement. To achieve this overall commitment, the Group has 
set interim targets for 2030 for the credit portfolio, assets under management 
and Swedbank’s own operations. The targets aim to manage climate-related 
impacts, risks and business opportunities with a focus on the downstream value 
chain. ­Targets for the credit portfolio cover all of Swedbank’s home markets, 
while targets for assets under management cover the Swedish fund manage‑
ment activities. The ­climate targets are aligned with the governing documents 
established for this area.
Emissions from own operations are not material in relation to indirectly 
financed emissions downstream. At the same time, Swedbank considers it 
important to also reduce its own emissions and has therefore set specific targets 
for this. More information about the targets for each part of the operation is 
­presented below.
Targets for the credit portfolio
Swedbank has set climate targets that cover six sectors within the credit port­
folio. The targets have been set based on the Net Zero Banking Alliance (NZBA) 
framework. The selection of sectors is based on several criteria: climate impact 
(high-emission sectors according to NZBA), Swedbank’s exposure to each sector, 
the degree of homogeneity of the sectors, which is important in order to enable 
a common methodology and objectives, as well as access to relevant data and 
established calculation methods. In 2022 and 2024, Swedbank published 
method reports externally on the website, which further explain the selection 
of sectors for which targets are set.
The climate targets are Group-wide and have been approved by the CEO and 
reviewed by the Board of Directors. The targets are followed up through annual 
KPIs that are set for the CEO and then broken down to the heads of each Busi‑
ness Area at unit level. The CEO’s targets are reported to the Board of Directors, 
while the results of the targets at unit level is reported to the CEO. Progress 
towards the climate targets for the different sectors is also followed up in the 
Group’s sustainability committees: the Group Operating Sustainability ­Committee 
and the Group Executive Sustainability Committee. 
 Swedbank maintains an ongoing dialogue with its stakeholders. Insights from 
these dialogues are used broadly when Swedbank develops its targets, although 
stakeholders are not involved in setting the targets.
The Group continuously reviews the climate targets to encourage the align‑
ment of the credit portfolio with the 1.5-degree target of the Paris Agreement. 
Swedbank is also involved in several partnerships, memberships and networks, 
including the EEMI (Energy Efficient Mortgage Initiative), the PCAF (Partnership 
for Carbon Accounting Financials) and the Poseidon Principles.
The targets are set on the basis of scientific reduction trajectories, which are 
based on how much the sector needs to reduce its emissions in order to be 
aligned with a temperature increase that does not exceed 1.5°C. Apart from this, 
Swedbank has not used any more scenarios or defined and quantified actions.

Scope of the targets
The climate targets cover 81 per cent of Swedbank’s gross carrying amount and 
72 per cent of Swedbank’s total credit portfolio. For financed emissions, the tar‑
gets cover 39 per cent of customers’ Scope 1 and 2 emissions. When customers’ 
Scope 3 emissions are included, they cover 18 per cent of the credit portfolio. 
Swedbank’s climate targets are designed to cover the most relevant emissions 
Scopes by sector. Based on this division, i.e. customers’ Scope 1 and 2 emissions 
for all sectors as well as Scope 3 emissions for oil and gas and the automotive 
industry, the targets cover 45 per cent of financed emissions.
There are several reasons why the targets cover a lower proportion of financed 
emissions than Swedbank’s total credit portfolio. Swedbank’s mortgage and real 
estate portfolio is deemed to have a relatively low emission intensity compared 
to other sectors, while it also represents the majority of the Group’s credit port­
folio volume. Swedbank also has relatively low exposure to the majority of 
­sectors defined as carbon-intensive in the NZBA framework, such as coal 
(no exposure) and oil and gas (only low exposure to refineries remains). 
Swedbank continuously reviews the climate targets and their scope.
External factors that can affect the outcome of the ­targets 
Swedbank’s ability to achieve its climate targets within the credit portfolio is 
strongly linked to customers’ transition. Several factors are driving this transition, 
including the emergence of green technology that is gradually reducing the costs 
of sustainable solutions, stricter regulations and policy measures such as the EU 
ETS (European Union Emissions Trading System), increased demand for sustain‑
able products and services, and growing pressure from investors on financed 
companies to reduce their emissions. 
Many of the sectors where Swedbank has adopted climate targets are also 
dependent on society’s transition as a whole. This includes, among other things, 
the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy. If Swedbank is to achieve its 
climate targets, it is a requirement that fossil fuels are phased out in each sector. 
The development of new technology is also crucial, especially for the steel and 
shipping industry, which are highly dependent on the development of new tech‑
nologies for the production of fossil-free steel and new types of fossil-free ves‑
sels. In the real estate sector, development is also largely due to national shifts in 
the countries’ energy mix, as well as the introduction of regulations or incentives 
for energy performance certificates, improved energy efficiency and the phasing 
out of fossil energy sources.

Target: Reduce the financed emission intensity (kgCO2e/m2) by 39 per cent 
by 2030 and 89 per cent by 2050 compared to 2019
The target covers customers’ Scope 1 and 2 emissions and includes loans to house­
holds with collateral in residential properties and tenant-owner associations.
The outcome for 2025 reflects a 3 per cent reduction in the sector’s emission 
intensity for the property portfolio, compared with the baseline year 2019. 
The emission intensity decreased for both the Swedish (–10 per cent) and Baltic 
(–17 per cent) property portfolios. At the same time, higher growth in the Baltic 
property portfolio since the base year, characterized by a higher emission intensity, 
has resulted in a more modest reduction in emission intensity at Group level. Devel‑
opments are affected by factors such as the pace of the energy transition in the 
countries in which the Group operates, as well as controls and incentives that affect 
the willingness and ability of households to produce energy performance certifi‑
cates, improve energy efficiency and phase out fossil energy sources. These exter‑
nal factors lie largely beyond the bank’s direct ability to influence and introduce 
increased uncertainty in the progress toward the target. In summary, this means that 
there is a risk that the bank may not fully achieve the target by 2030.
For the Swedish mortgage portfolio, the future trend is primarily dependent on 
continued energy efficiency improvements in the property portfolio, an increased 
proportion of single-family houses with energy performance certificates, and the 
phasing out of fossil heating sources. Among single-family houses in Sweden, the 
transition takes place through investments made by individual households. In order 
for households to bear the cost of energy efficiency improvements, training and 
­support can serve as enablers.
Financed emissions from mortgages in the Baltic countries have continued to 
decrease. This reduction is being driven by increased coverage of energy perfor‑
mance certificates and improved energy efficiency in the mortgage portfolio. Swed‑
bank has continued to support customers in the mortgage portfolio to make more 
sustain­able choices by developing special offers linked to more energy-efficient 
properties. At the same time, Swedbank is dependent on the transition in the coun‑
tries’ energy systems, which also faces other challenges in the Baltic countries (e.g. 
in terms of energy security). Other challenges in transitioning the Baltic mortgage 
portfolio are low energy efficiency of the property portfolio combined with depen‑
dency on national support programmes to carry out renovations. These structural 
conditions affect the ability to accelerate emission reductions going forward and 
may therefore also impact the achievement of the target.

Targets for assets under management
In its Climate Strategy, Swedbank Robur Fonder has adopted two overarching 
­climate targets: to be in line with the Paris Agreement’s 1.5-degree target by 2025 
and to achieve net zero emissions by 2050. The fund management company has 
also adopted three interim targets and five carbon dioxide targets. The interim 
targets cover three focus areas and the carbon dioxide targets cover five asset 
classes within the fund portfolio. Discretionary mandates is not covered by the 
climate targets, as it is the customers themselves who determine the investment 
focus and targets for their portfolio. Fund capital in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania 
is covered by separate climate targets for each fund management company.
Swedbank Robur Fonder’s Climate Strategy has been approved by the CEO of 
Swedbank Robur Fonder. The targets for net zero emissions follows the Paris 
Aligned Investment Initiative: Net Zero Investment Framework (NZIF). This is in 
line with best practice in the fund industry. To set carbon dioxide targets for equi‑
ties and corporate bonds, Swedbank Robur Fonder has used the International 
Energy Agency’s (IEA) Net Zero 2050 scenario. This scenario describes how 
global emissions will decrease given factors such as growth in GDP, population 
growth and policy changes. In its process to develop the climate targets, Swed‑
bank Robur Fonder analysed several climate scenarios, and chose to use IEA 
NZ2050. The baseline year 2019 has been chosen on recommendations from 
Net Zero Asset Manager (NZAM), and Swedbank Robur Fonder believes that even 
though the portfolio composition will change over time, the baseline year is gen‑
erally representative of the portfolio in the future. If major changes are made in 
the portfolio, the baseline year will be adjusted. For other asset classes, targets 
for either Sweden or the EU have been used as a starting point and with 2024 as 
the baseline year, and just like for equities and corporate bonds, Swedbank Robur 
Fonder considers the baseline year to be representative of the portfolio in the 
future. Carbon dioxide targets are expressed as an intensity metric so that it is 
possible to distinguish the change in carbon dioxide for underlying holdings in 
relation to the change in total assets under management. Swedbank Robur 
Fonder has not made any assumptions about how the portfolio will develop. 
The targets have not been audited by an external party. There is additional infor‑
mation about calculations and measurement on pages 119–121.
In the beginning of the year Swedbank Robur Fonder changed unit for its 
carbon dioxide target for equities and corporate bonds. The previous metric, 
which used weighted average carbon intensity, was replaced by carbon footprint. 
Furthermore, a new target was adopted for climate solutions for equities and cor‑
porate bonds, which is aligned with the NZIF framework. Swedbank Robur Fonder 
also adopted carbon dioxide targets for sovereign bonds, municipal bonds, 
regional bonds and mortgage bonds which means that the carbon dioxide tar‑
gets now includes almost the entire fund capital. These targets are expressed 
using the same intensity metric as for equities and corporate bonds, with the 
exception of mortgage bonds, which is expressed in total emissions. This has 
affected the baseline value, but not the long-term climate targets or how they are 
to be achieved. Moreover, Swedbank Robur Fonder adopted a new target called 
Port­folio Alignment for the asset classes equities, credits and mortgage bonds. 
The emissions covered by Swedbank Robur Fonder’s targets are also included in 
Total greenhouse gas emissions, E1-6. 
Swedbank Robur Fonder’s targets are followed up annually. The results are 
examined by the fund management company’s Sustainability and Corporate 
Gover­nance team, and also by the CEO. The results are published externally in 
Swedbank Robur’s annual Climate and Nature Report. Any changes in method­
ology or targets are approved by the CEO.
Swedbank Robur Fonder conducts ongoing dialogue with its stakeholders. 
Insights from these dialogues are used broadly when Swedbank Robur Fonder 
develops its targets, although stakeholders are not involved in setting the targets.

Data quality
The quality of the emissions reporting is affected by limitations in the underlying 
data, which are presented in the tables for the credit and investment portfolios. 
Data quality is assessed in accordance with the PCAF method. The scale ranges 
from 1, which represents verified reported data (highest quality), to 5, which 
­indicates that no emission data is available, resulting in the use of standardised 
­calculations (lowest quality).
Data quality varies between Scope 1, 2 and 3. Scope 2 generally reports the 
highest data quality, while Scope 3 has the lowest. This is primarily due to the  
fact that Swedbank’s credit portfolio includes many smaller companies, where 
access to reported and verified emission data is limited. Compared to the credit 
portfolio, the investment portfolio has higher data quality, as it is based to 
a greater extent on reported data from companies with more highly developed 
processes for climate reporting.
As reporting requirements are strengthened, for example through the CSRD, 
Swedbank expects to have access to more complete and reliable emission data 
from the Group’s customers. This will reduce the need for estimated values, 
which in turn increases the accuracy and transparency of the reporting of 
­emission over time. At present, a large proportion of the emissions calculations 
is based on standard values.

Total greenhouse gas emissions have increased between 2024 and 2025. This is 
primarily due to an increase in the Group’s Scope 3 emissions within Category 15 
for financed emissions.
Within the credit portfolio, the increase of nearly 10 million tCO2e is mainly

Credit portfolio 
The table below presents emissions per scope (1, 2 and 3) for Swedbank’s credit 
portfolio, allocated by sector. Also shown is the data quality according to the 
PCAF method, as well as the volume and proportion included in the emission 
­calculations. Financed emissions from the credit portfolio relate to loans to 
the public and credit institutions and granted but not utilised loan commitments, 
as well as contingent liabilities. Calculations have not been performed for credit 
institutions and consumer loans due to a lack of available data. 
Swedbank uses different methods to calculate financed emissions. A top-down 
method is used for agriculture and forestry. For corporate loans, a company­-
based method is used, which accounts for the majority of the reported emis‑
sions. For motor vehicles, properties and shipping, asset-based methods are 
used, in which emissions are calculated based on the specific characteristics 
of each asset class. A more detailed description can be found in the section 
­Calculation methods below. 
The financed emissions from the credit portfolio for 2025 amounted to 
27 527 425 (17 550 932) tCO2e, which corresponds to an increase of 57 per cent 
compared to 2024. The majority of the increase is due to Swedbank improving 
the quality of the underlying data used for the emissions calculations, by relying 
to a greater extent on reported emissions data from corporate customers instead 
of basing the calculations on proxies. For some companies, the reported emis‑
sions are considerably higher than ­previous standardised calculations.
The majority of emissions (Scope 1, 2 and 3) come from corporate lending, 
98 (97) per cent. In corporate lending, the high-intensity manufacturing industry 
is the sector that generates the most emissions. The largest increase during 
the year has been in the retail and wholesale sector, mainly in wholesale and  
retail trade. 
For the agriculture, forestry and fishing sector, negative emissions from Swed‑
ish forestry are included in Scope 1. In total, this amounts to 343 748 (412 067) 
tCO2e. The calculations for the forestry sector include both emissions and carbon 
sequestration from the forest. Since the data is reported at an aggregated level, it 
is not possible to distinguish between emissions and sequestration. This results 
in the total reported emissions showing a negative value. 
2 (3) per cent of total emissions come from the private segment, which mainly 
consists of mortgage lending.

Calculation methodology
Calculation methods for calculating Swedbank’s total emissions in Scope 1, 2 
and 3 are presented below. The method for calculating emissions is based on the 
GHG Protocol. These calculations are also used to follow up on the ­climate tar‑
gets that are presented under Targets, E1-4. The metrics have not been validated 
by an external body.
Scope 11
The calculations use emission factors from internationally recognised databases 
such as IPCC, AIB, BEIS and the UN. When activity data was not available, 
assumptions were made regarding vehicle fuel based on emissions from an 
“average vehicle”. For Swedbank’s smaller branches, as well as for Stabelo and 
Entercard, average emissions have been allocated based on the number of 
employees and/or office space, using the Group’s estimated emissions per full-
time employee (FTE) and per square metre of office area. As there is good access 
to activity data from Swedbank’s main operations, it is reasonable to use an allo‑
cation method to cover the relatively few units that have not delivered activity 
data. The method is based on the GHG Protocol, and has been chosen because 
the GHG Protocol is the most widely acknowledged method internationally. 
Scope 21
When calculating location-based Scope 2 emissions, Swedbank has robust 
reporting of activity data in respect of purchased electricity, district heating and 
district cooling for its main operations. Electricity purchases (kWh) are separate 
from grid charges. For Swedbank’s smaller branches, as well as for Stabelo and 
Entercard, average emissions have been allocated based on the number of 
employees and/or office space, using the Group’s estimated emissions per 
­full-time employee (FTE) and per square metre of office area.
The emission factors come from internationally recognised databases such 
as IPCC, BEIS, AIB, CIBSE and the UN. Emission factors for contract-based elec‑
tricity are sourced from electricity suppliers’ Environmental Product Declarations 
(EPDs) or supplier-specific electricity mixes. In cases where the emission factors 
include biomass, the percentage share of biomass is not disclosed separately. 
Biogenic emissions are calculated only for district heating in Estonia and for 
­certain transport fuels. Biogenic emissions are not reported separately.
When calculating market-based Scope 2 emissions, emission factors corre‑
sponding to energy purchased (or not purchased) through contractual instru‑
ments are applied. Contractual instruments include energy attribute certificates, 
direct energy contracts, power purchase agreements (PPAs) and supplier-spe‑
cific emission rights. Contractual instruments represented 43 per cent of total 
consumption in 2025. The percentage of sales related to contractual instruments 
is zero per cent, since Swedbank does not sell energy. In the calculation, U&We 
has assessed whether the contractual instruments presented meet the estab‑
lished quality criteria. Where contractual instruments did not meet the quality cri‑
teria, or where contractual instruments were not purchased, market­-based Scope 
2 emissions have been calculated using residual factors. Scope 2 emissions are 
calculated based on operations in branches and buildings where Swedbank has 
operational control.
Scope 3
Scope 3 emissions from own operations1
Scope 3 emissions for climate targets for own operations have been calculated 
based on activity data such as quantity/weight of purchased products, passen‑
ger kilometres, hotel nights and waste weights. No spend calculations have been 
performed for reporting in 2025. The emission factors come from internationally 
recognised databases such as IPCC, BEIS, CIBS, UN and individual suppliers. 
Swedbank cannot quantify the proportion of Scope 3 data based on primary data 
from suppliers and business partners in the value chain. 
Scope 3 emissions from Category 15 Investments
Swedbank has developed an internal calculation tool based on the PCAF standard 
(Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials) to calculate financed emissions 
for the credit portfolio. PCAF is used for the credit portfolio to follow the industry 
standard for calculation methods, and to be able to assess the relevance of 
­different parts of the lending portfolio.
The calculations are based on the following formula: 
1)	 Swedbank performs an annual calculation in the Our Impacts calculation tool, which is provided by the software developer EcoOnline. Access to the platform is administered by U&We, which 
also performs quality control of input data, market-based energy certificates and calculations. Calculation is carried out in accordance with the World Business Council for Sustainable Develop‑
ment and World Resources Institute’s (WBCSD/WRI) Greenhouse Gas Protocol (GHG Protocol); Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard. Calculation of greenhouse gases in the Our 
Impact platform quantifies all seven Kyoto greenhouse gases where applicable, and measures them in units of carbon dioxide equivalents, CO2e. The seven gases are carbon dioxide (CO2), 
methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFC), nitrogen trifluoride (NF3), sulphur hexafluoride (SF6) and perfluorocarbons (PFC). The global warming potential (GWP) of each 
gas is applied.
Financed emissions = Emissions X Attribution factor 
Emissions = Emissions from an underlying company or an asset 
Attribution factor = Swedbank’s financed share of the company’s or asset’s 
total value.
Swedbank has further expanded the scope of its calculations and developed new 
methodologies. This year, in addition to estimates of financed emissions for the 
credit portfolio, Swedbank also made estimates for Swedbank’s investments in 
government entities. Swedbank Robur Fonder’s Scope 3 emissions for their 
investments were also added. Swedbank also estimated its facilitated emis‑
sions.The method for calculating financed emissions related to mortgages and 
commercial real estate has been improved, including a change in the source of 
electricity emission factors from the European Energy Agency (EEA) to the Inter‑
national Energy Agency (IEA), which is assessed to provide greater accuracy. 
As a result of this methodological change, the base year 2019 has also been 
updated.
Overall, Swedbank has developed asset-based methods for properties, Motor 
Vehicles and Shipping, and a calculation method at company level defined as 
Corporate Loans. A top-down method at country level has been defined for 
financing relating to agriculture and forest ownership by private individuals in 
Sweden.
The calculations do not generally include emission removals at company level. 
Emission sequestration is applied for private individuals in the Swedish forest 
sector, as described below in the relevant section.
For counterparties Scope 2 emissions, the market‑based method is used as 
the primary approach.
Restatement rules
Swedbank has defined rules for restatements that describe which types of 
events should trigger a restatement of financed emissions for the baseline year, 
as well as a significant threshold to be subject to restatement. In accordance 
with the defined rules, financed emissions shall be restated in connection with:
•	Structural changes within the Swedbank Group, such as acquisitions and 
divestments.
•	Significant changes in the methodology for estimating greenhouse gas (GHG) 
emissions.
•	Improvements in the accuracy of emission factors or activity data (for 
­example more detailed information on emission factors per energy source).
•	Discoveries of defects that are deemed to be material, individual or collective.
•	The addition of new Scope 3 categories.
The climate targets and financed emission data reported for the baseline year 
need to be updated if the historical data changes are material and in line with the 
above principles. The impact is considered significant if the upward or downward 
impact exceeds five per cent for any sector/portfolio for which climate targets 
are set. Swedbank may choose to restate the baseline year for changes that are 
deemed less significant in order to ensure the consistency, relevance and compa‑
rability of the reported data over time.
Mortgages and Commercial real estate 
Mortgages are defined as loans to private individuals or tenant-owner associa‑
tions for the acquisition of housing. Commercial real estate include all loans to 
property management companies related to the acquisition of properties for 
­revenue-generating activities such as retail, offices, industrial properties and 
apartment buildings. In accordance with the PCAF standard an asset‑based 
­calculation method is used which covers Scope 1 and 2.
Calculation methodology
Calculations of financed emissions for property consist of two components: 
the attribution factor and the building’s emissions.
The attribution factor is equal to the property’s loan-to-value ratio determined at 
the baseline market value and, for loans opened after 2019, the value of the loan.
The building’s emissions are expressed as the amount of kgCO2e per year that 
the building’s energy consumption generates and includes assets that are 
deemed to generate emissions. The methodology for calculating the building’s 
emissions depends on data availability. In Sweden, for the most accurate calcula‑
tions, information is used on heated surface, energy consumption from the

Energy Performance Certificate (EPC), heat source and an emission factor for 
each type of energy, as well as an estimate of the energy consumption of resi‑

the respective EPC and building type-specific estimates of energy consumption 
from PCAF are used. For calculations in the Baltic countries, estimated EPCs are 
also used, including EPCs that expired up to ten years ago. The assumption is 
that expired EPCs are still representative and provide useful information even 
after the expiry date, as it is better to have some form of energy-related figure 
than just an average based on property type. When such data is unavailable or 
incomplete in both Sweden and the Baltic countries, estimated figures are used 
for heating area and estimates from PCAF based solely on property type.
Motor Vehicles
Motor vehicles are defined as financing for passenger cars, light commercial 
vehicles (vans), motorcycles and heavy goods vehicles. Tractors are excluded 
due to a lack of accurate data on which to base the calculations. In accordance 
with the PCAF standard an asset‑based calculation method is used which covers 
Scope 1 and 2 emissions from motor vehicles.
Calculation methodology 
Calculations of financed emissions for motor vehicles consist of two compo‑
nents: the attribution factor and the vehicle’s emissions. The allocation factor is 
equal to the financing provided for each motor vehicle, divided by the vehicle’s 
market value at the time the loan originates. A vehicle’s emissions are expressed 
as the amount of emissions per year that the vehicle generates. The emissions 
are generated either as tailpipe emissions or emissions linked to electricity con‑
sumption. For the best data quality, the vehicle’s exhaust emission intensity per 
kilometre is used in combination with the vehicle’s annual mileage. In cases 
where information on tailpipe emissions is unavailable, Swedbank retrieves esti‑
mates from the PCAF database. These estimates are based on vehicle attributes 
such as make/model, vehicle type and fuel type. For Scope 2 emissions, data is 
retrieved from PCAF in all cases. When specific annual mileages for the vehicle 
are unavailable, the metric is derived from the PCAF database.
Shipping
The calculation methodology for shipping refers to loans with vessels as collat‑
eral for companies operating in shipping-related industries. The scope is limited 
by data availability, as only vessels larger than 5 000 GT (Gross Tonnage) are 
required to report emission data according to the International Maritime Organi‑
zation’s regulations. The methodology covers Scope 1 emissions and upstream 
Scope 3 emissions from vessels, and applies an asset‑based calculation 
approach.
Calculation methodology
Calculations of financed emissions for shipping consist of two components: 
the attribution factor and the vessel’s emissions. The attribution factor is equal 
to the financing provided for each vessel divided by the vessel’s market value 
at the start of the loan. Vessel emissions are expressed in tonnes of CO2e that 
a vessel’s fuel consumption generates each year. Exact emission calculations 
for vessels are based on the fuel emission factor for each fuel type and the 
respective fuel volume consumed during a given year. The emission factor 
reflects a vessel’s engine type, size and type of vessel, and differs between the 
different fuel types, such as heavy fuel oil, marine gas oil, liquefied natural gas, 
biofuel, methanol, etc.
Agriculture and forestry 
Financed emission calculations for the agricultural industry and parts of the 
­forestry portfolio are carried out using a top-down approach based on National 
Inventory Reports for each country and sector. This top‑down approach is chosen 
because the Business Loan Method overestimates the Group’s financed emis‑
sions, based on comparative analyses, country‑level statistics, and anecdotal 
farm‑level assessments. The scope of agricultural calculations is defined as 
­sectors related to dairy, livestock farming, mixed agriculture, crop cultivation 
and other agriculture. The scope of forestry calculations is defined as activities 
related to forestry and applies only to private individuals in Sweden. For other 
activities related to forestry, the Business Loan Method is applied.
Calculation methodology
For agriculture, top-down emissions include a country’s territorial emissions cov‑
ering Scope 1 and 2 emissions. Scope 1 covers greenhouse gas emissions from 
agricultural activities and greenhouse gas emissions from organic soil on arable 
land and grassland. Scope 2 emissions come from the energy used for stationary 
and non-stationary machinery. Scope 3 is added from other sources and only 
includes emissions linked to the production of mineral fertiliser used by the 
­agricultural industry in Swedbank’s core markets. 
The calculation method for financed emissions from forestry uses a top-down 
approach based on values from the National Inventory Report. These values 
include the forest’s carbon sequestration. Since the values from the report are 
only reported as an aggregated figure, it is not possible to distinguish the total 
emissions from the carbon sequestration. This means that customers assessed in 
accordance with the forestry method have negative values for financed emissions.
As PCAF does not currently provide a specific methodology for the forestry 
sector, this method has been chosen as the most appropriate short-term solution. 
PCAF is currently developing a calculation method for agriculture and forestry.
Corporate loans
The calculation method for corporate loans use a company-based method and is 
applied to all corporate loans, unless a loan is ­covered by one of the other meth‑
ods. The method covers customers’ Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions. It is important 
to note that the portfolio’s Scope 3 emission data is still incomplete, as the under­
lying companies are still improving their Scope 3 coverage and calculation 
­methods. PCAF calculations only include upstream emissions.
Calculation methodology
Calculations of financed emissions for corporate loans consist of two compo‑
nents: the attribution factor and the company’s emissions. The attribution factor 
is Swedbank’s loan amount to the company divided by the company’s total 
assets (as proxy for total debt + equity). The asset value used is based on 
whether the company’s or the group’s emission information is used. Customer emis‑
sions data is obtained either from clients’ public disclosures or provided bilaterally 
by the clients, or alternatively estimated using region‑specific and sector‑specific 
proxy information supplied through PCAF. The customer’s reported figures, both 
financial and related to greenhouse gas emissions, are based on the latest avail‑
able full-year data, where the latest data is no more than 24 months old.
Deviations from PCAF
The Group has chosen to make certain deviations from the PCAF standard based 
on data availability or data quality. The deviations relate either to the methods 
themselves or to assumptions. Swedbank has chosen to use its own methods for 
sea vessels, the agricultural industry and properties in Sweden for tenant-owner 
associations and assets with available EPCs. The methodology applied to sea 
vessels follows the annual ship-level data required by the IMO. The methodology 
applied to agriculture and private individuals involved in the forestry sector in 
Sweden follows top-down estimates using National Inventory Reports, market 
share and financing information. The methodology applied to properties in 
Sweden for tenant-owner associations and assets with available EPCs follows the 
guidance produced by Finance Sweden. The calculation for tenant-owner associ‑
ations has been developed to avoid duplication. The main deviations related to 
certain assumptions are that, for Corporate Loans, Swedbank uses the company’s 
asset value to calculate the attribution factor as a proxy for the company’s equity 
and debt values due to limited internal data availability; that, for Commercial Real 
Estate, no updated property value is currently obtained when a loan is modified 
owing to existing limitations in internal data‑management systems; and that, for 
Motor Vehicles, Swedbank treats leasing agreements in the same way as lending 
in accordance with the PCAF methodology for motor vehicles.
Next steps
Swedbank continues to develop its calculations and reporting of financed emis‑
sions, by such means as improving data quality and methodological aspects. 
Swedbank is committed to continuing to provide transparency and comparability 
in this area by describing its calculation methods.
Scope 3 emissions from assets under management
Calculations of financed and intensity-based emissions in investments
Investments are covered by the GHG Protocol, Scope 3 Category 15 (invest‑
ments). Swedbank Robur Fonder has not signed PCAF itself, but is part of Swed‑
bank’s commitment and thus complies with PCAF’s standards for the asset 
classes for which there is a method. The most recently available data is used in 
the calculations. The calculations included in this annual report are described 
below. 
Equities and corporate bonds
The calculation for equities and corporate bonds is based on PCAF’s standards.

Scope 3 emissions from facilitated emissions 
Calculations of facilitated emissions from the debt capital market
Facilitated emissions refer to emissions arising from capital market transactions 
in which Swedbank acts as a facilitator, but not a direct investor, in the debt capital 
market. These emissions are calculated according to a standardised methodol‑
ogy developed by PCAF, Part B. The calculation is based on the following formula:
Facilitated emissions = annual emissions × attribution factor × weighting factor
Annual emissions refer to the company’s total greenhouse gas emissions during 
the year. The attribution factor refers to Swedbank’s share of the financing in 
­relation to the company’s total value. The weighting factor is a fixed factor that 
reflects the level of responsibility for facilitated transactions. PCAF has set this 
at 33 per cent for all covered capital market issuances.

Shipping
Swedbank has adopted a Group-wide climate target for the shipping portfolio in 
order to integrate climate considerations in the Group’s loan decisions on financ‑
ing for shipping. The target means that the shipping portfolio shall achieve 0 per 
cent alignment delta by 2030 compared to the International Maritime Organiza‑
tion’s (IMO) reduction trajectory “striving for”. A 0 per cent alignment delta means 
that the portfolio is fully aligned with the reduction trajectory selected. 
The target is based on the Poseidon Principles, which is a global framework 
for integrating climate considerations into loan decisions on financing for ship‑
ping. The reduction trajectory is based on the IMO’s most ambitious climate tar‑
gets for the sector, including achieving net zero emissions by 2050. However, the 
reduction trajectory is not yet fully aligned with the 1.5-degree scenario. Swed‑
bank is committed to following developments in the methodology for climate tar‑
gets in shipping and to revising the target when improved reduction trajectories 
are available through the Poseidon Principles.
The portfolio’s alignment delta is based on the AER measured in g CO2e/
tonne-nautical mile, and is part of the reporting that takes place through the 
Poseidon Principles. The target includes vessels covered by the Poseidon Princi‑
ples (vessels equal to or greater than 5 000 gross tonnage). The target covers the 
vessels’ emissions from a “well-to-wake” perspective, which means that emis‑
sions within Scope 1 and upstream Scope 3 from fuel consumption are included. 
The target covers the most relevant greenhouse gases, carbon dioxide (CO2), 
methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O), as well as Swedbank’s operations in all 
home market countries. 2022 was chosen as the baseline year due to data avail‑
ability and given that it reflects a year without the impact of Covid-19 restrictions. 
Further details regarding the calculations and the measurement against the 
target can be found on pages 103–104 and 119.
Climate targets for asset under management 
The objective for net zero emissions follows the Paris Aligned Investment Initia‑
tive: Net Zero Investment Framework (NZIF). This is in line with best practice in 
the fund industry. To set carbon dioxide targets for equities and corporate bonds, 
Swedbank Robur Fonder has used the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Net 
Zero 2050 scenario. This scenario describes how global emissions will decrease 
given factors such as growth in GDP, population growth and policy changes. In its 
process to develop the climate targets, Swedbank Robur Fonder analysed several 
climate scenarios, and chose to use IEA NZ2050. 
The baseline year 2019 has been chosen on recommendations from Net Zero 
Asset Manager (NZAM), and Swedbank Robur Fonder believes that even though 
the portfolio composition will change over time, the baseline year is generally 
­representative of the portfolio in the future. If major changes are made in the 
port­folio, the baseline year will be adjusted. For other asset classes, targets for 
either Sweden or the EU have been used as a starting point and with 2024 as the 
baseline year, and just like for equities and corporate bonds, Swedbank Robur 
Fonder considers the baseline year to be representative of the portfolio in the 
future. Carbon dioxide targets are expressed as an intensity metric so that it is 
possible to distinguish the change in carbon dioxide for underlying holdings in 
relation to the change in total assets under management. Swedbank Robur 
Fonder has not made any assumptions about how the portfolio will develop. 
The targets have not been audited by an external party. ­Further details regarding 
the calculations and the measurement against the target can be found on pages 
105–106.
Climate targets for own operations
The target covers Scope 1, 2 and 3. Scope 3 categories included are: business

other countries in which Swedbank operates (Norway, Finland, China and the 
USA). 2019 was chosen as the baseline year to reflect a year ­without the impact 
of Covid-19 restrictions. 
Swedbank cannot specify what proportion of the target applies to each Scope,

Strategy and business model
	 E4 SBM-3    Material impacts and their interaction with the strategy  
and business model
Reversing the loss of biodiversity is an important aspect of environmental 
sustain­ability, where the financial sector has a key role to play through its 
manage­ment of indirect impacts on nature-related losses. 
Swedbank is deemed to have a potential indirect negative impact on biodiver‑
sity downstream in the value chain. This is primarily due to the Group’s lending 
to corporate customers whose activities may result in the loss of biodiversity. 
At present, Swedbank cannot assess whether or exactly which activities can 
cause a negative impact on areas with sensitive biodiversity, including land deg‑
radation, desertification, soil sealing and on threatened species. The background 
to this is that scientifically based guidelines for the banking sector and estab‑
lished measurable indicators to assess the Group’s impact through its custom‑
ers’ operations are still under development. Swedbank has not identified any 
parts of its own operations that have a significant impact on biodiversity. 
Transition plan for biodiversity
	 E4-1    Transition plan and consideration of biodiversity and ecosystems 
in strategy and business model
Swedbank has not yet adopted a transition plan for biodiversity or evaluated 
the resilience of its business strategy. The Group does, however, see a need to 
take biodiversity and ecosystems into account to a greater extent in the future 
strategy and business model. 
As measurement methods are developed and there is an increased under‑
standing of Swedbank’s impact, the Group will be able to take nature and bio­
diversity into account to an increasing extent in its operations. 
Policies
	 E4-2    Policies for biodiversity and ecosystems
Swedbank has adopted governance documents that serve as important guide‑
lines and rules for the Group’s work to manage material negative impacts relating 
to biodiversity. These documents comprise Swedbank’s Sustainability Policy and 
Position on Climate change and Nature. The governance documents do not 
­specifically address direct impact factors that contribute to loss of biodiversity, 
impact caused, tracking of activities that cause negative impacts along the value 
chain, monitoring of biodiversity status or its societal impacts. Swedbank has at 
present not adopted a specific policy for the protection of biodiversity and eco‑
systems that covers customers’ operational facilities that are owned, leased or 
managed in or near areas with sensitive biodiversity.

Actions
	 E4-3    Actions and resources for biodiversity and ecosystems 
Swedbank’s Sustainability Policy emphasises that healthy ecosystems are 
­crucial for economic and social resilience and for long-term value creation. Swed‑
bank’s ambition is to work on integrating nature and biodiversity into the financial 
sector, and the Group is involved in various collaborative initiatives and research 
projects that focus on biodiversity. 
During the current reporting year, Swedbank has not explicitly integrated 
­original and traditional knowledge or nature-based solutions into its actions 
to combat the loss of biodiversity. Nor does Swedbank apply compensation 
for biodiversity. 
Swedbank has not identified significant capital or operating expenditure for 
the measures in addition to the resources already integrated in routine financial 
planning. 
Nature and biodiversity credits
To contribute to increased knowledge of innovative economic incentives for pre‑
serving and developing biodiversity, in 2023 Swedbank purchased the first Swed‑
ish biodiversity credits in a pilot project with Orsa Besparingsskog. The biocredits 
have been developed as part of a research project at the Swedish University of 
Agricultural Sciences. Since then, Swedbank has further developed expertise in 
this area and been active in discussions with both private and public actors about 
biodiversity credits. 
In 2025, Swedbank’s activities included participation at round table discus‑
sions on natural credits organised by the European Commissioner for Environ‑
ment, Water Resilience and a Competitive Circular Economy. Swedbank has also 
joined the Swedish Biocredit Alliance to contribute to the development of a credi‑
ble and transparent biocredit market. The Group is also working continuously to 
increase internal awareness of nature and biodiversity within the Group through 
various events. 
Partnerships and knowledge sharing
In accordance with Swedbank’s Sustainability Policy, the Group participates in 
international initiatives, including in the area of biodiversity. Through involvement 
in industry forums, collaborations and research projects, the aim is to contribute 
to the development of best practice and the establishment of global standards. 
In 2025, Swedbank continued to participate in several initiatives focusing on 
biodiversity. The purpose of this is to increase collaboration with relevant actors 
and to jointly address challenges linked to the loss of biodiversity. These initia‑
tives include skills-building programmes through the Principles for Responsible 
Banking (PRB Nature Working Group, now known as the PRB Nature Community 
of Practice). The initiative aims to support banks in their work on nature and bio‑
diversity by such means as publishing guidelines and reports on best practice. 
By providing tools and insights, the initiative facilitates the sharing of knowledge 
within the banking sector. The PRB Nature Community of Practice is an interna‑
tional programme involving banks and stakeholders from all over the world, 
including Swedbank, which became an active reference group member in order 
to promote the sharing of experience. 
Swedbank is also involved in Mistra BIOPATH, a research programme that is 
investigating how biodiversity can be integrated into financial decision-making. 
In addition to collaborations with various stakeholders, Swedbank’s work in 
2025 focused on internal analysis and planning for the future. The results of the 
dual materiality analysis form the basis of continued development and in-depth 
work in this area. The next step involves a more precise identification of drivers 
behind the loss of biodiversity in Swedbank’s corporate lending. The intention is 
to establish a basis for addressing these issues through informed actions. One 
key aspect going forward is to improve data availability and deepen the analysis. 
Targets and metrics
	 E4-4    Targets for biodiversity and ecosystems
Swedbank does not report any measurable outcome-based targets to follow up 
on the effectiveness of policies and measures in this area, nor does the bank 
report comparisons over time. It is important to enhance the work going forward 
to increase the understanding of the drivers behind potential negative impacts. 
It is essential to enable targeted actions and develop relevant metrics to assess 
results and appropriateness. Developing this understanding is a key element of 
the work that lies ahead.

	 S1 SBM-3    Material impacts and opportunities and their interaction  
with the strategy and business model1
Swedbank’s employees are crucial to the Group’s operations, culture and suc-
cess. The Group-wide strategy clarifies the importance of attracting, retaining 
and developing a dynamic workforce to ensure that future operational and com-
petence needs are aligned with the strategy and business model. In both the 
strategy and the business model, working conditions and equal treatment are 
important areas for creating an inclusive climate at the workplace.
Working conditions
Good working conditions with a focus on occupational health and safety are one 
way of contributing to employees’ well-being, engagement and performance. In 
the area of health and safety, Swedbank works in a structured way with a focus 
on an open and transparent dialogue between manager and employee, as well as 
a sustainable work-life balance. Swedbank strives to offer an open and flexible 
work environment that promotes collaboration and the sharing of knowledge. 
The workplace concept Swedbank at work is a strategic tool in achieving this and 
creating an attractive, inclusive and accessible workplace. Everyone working at 
Swedbank’s workplaces must be offered a safe, secure and inclusive work envi-
ronment, both the employed and non-employed workforce. As a starting point, 
Swedbank’s terms of employment and benefits apply only to individuals 
employed directly by Swedbank. 
Swedbank operates in markets and in an industry where forced labour, child 
labour and human trafficking are not common. It is, however, possible that other 
factors may have a negative impact on the employees in Swedbank. In the finan-
cial sector, health and safety risks are mainly related to the organisational and 
social work environment, such as high workload, unfavourable working hours and 
cognitive and emotional stress. This applies primarily to employees in custom-
er-facing roles and becomes visible through increased sick leave. Against the 
background of the organisational and social aspects, Swedbank has chosen to 
focus on these areas in its health and safety work. For further information about 
Swedbank’s actions in the area of health and safety, see section S1-4 Actions on 
page 127.
Equal treatment and opportunities for all 
Swedbank promotes an environment that encourages employees to take respon-
sibility for their own development. Employees are offered various opportunities 
to develop the competences for both their existing and future roles.
Swedbank strives to create a culture based on inclusion and accountability 
culture in which the Group’s values – open, simple and caring – aim to create 
a high level of engagement among employees, who are guided by supportive 
coaching and leadership. Principles of diversity, equity and inclusion are key in 
processes that aim to prevent discrimination and promote equal opportunities. 
The Group has zero tolerance of discrimination, harassment, sexual harassment 
and bullying. The opportunity to develop and pursue a career should be the same 
for all employees, regardless of factors such as age, gender and ethnicity. It is 
important for Swedbank to be an attractive employer, as the Group depends on 
competent and motivated employees. By actively working with issues of diver-
sity, equity and inclusion from a customer, employee and community perspective, 
Swedbank can strengthen its position in this area. The targets of an even gender 
balance in managerial positions and equalised pay gaps reinforce this ambition.

●Swedbank has zero tolerance of bullying, harassment, sexual harassment and discrimi-
nation. The Group and its employees may not discriminate or harass on grounds of 
gender, transgender identity or expression, sexual orientation, age, ethnicity, skin colour, 
ethnic or social origin, genetic characteristics, language, national minority affiliation, 
wealth, birthright, functional disability, religion or other beliefs, political views or other 
opinions.
	
●All employees shall have equal opportunities for development and careers, and an 
­inclusive work environment must be created where differences are viewed as an asset 
and contribute to commercial value.
	
●The Board of Directors, boards of subsidiaries and top management must reflect 
­diversity in terms of, for example, gender, age, geographical origin and educational 
and professional background.
	
●The policy is not based on external standards or initiatives from third parties, but refers 
to laws, rules and trade union agreements, which constitute a minimum level.

The policies are based on internationally recognised human rights regulations 
and include, among other things, the prohibition of discrimination, child labour 
and forced labour, and the right to a safe work environment and statutory terms 
and conditions. There are processes for whistleblowing, managing discrimina-
tion and harassment, as well as systematic health and safety work and diversity 
initiatives. 
In order to increase inclusion and diversity, training programmes, workshops 
and regular communication initiatives are carried out to clarify the responsibility 
of managers to promote a respectful culture and combat inappropriate 
behaviour. Swedbank has a key activity plan for equity, diversity and inclusion. 
The area is headed by the Group Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Lead, with addi-
tional diversity managers in each home market. Since 2022, Swedbank has 
established a Chief Diversity Officer role within the Group Executive Committee, 
a rotating two-year responsibility aimed at strengthening this work within the 
business operations and accelerating the Group’s proactive work on diversity, 
equity and inclusion.
Work to prevent discrimination and harassment is a priority issue. The regular 
employee surveys ask questions about how inclusive the workplace is perceived 
to be and whether employees experience discrimination or harassment. Surveys 
also include questions about how aware employees are of how they should act if 
they observe any instances of discrimination or harassment. 
Swedbank continuously monitors trends in areas such as equal treatment, 
gender balance in managerial and senior roles, levels of sick leave, parental leave, 
age distribution and equal pay for equal work. This is broken down at unit level 
and for each home market. Information about the Group’s policy and the proce-
dures used in the event of discrimination or harassment is available to all employ-
ees on the intranet. Swedbank also has networks and associations that strive to 
raise and work on issues for marginalised groups. For further information about 
processes and measures, see section S1-4 on page 127.
Communication with employees 
 S1-2    Processes for engaging with own workforce and employee 
­representatives about impacts 
Swedbank communicates continuously with employees via several channels and 
has established procedures for contact with both employees and employee rep-
resentatives. These procedures promote an open feedback culture and ensure an 
ongoing exchange of information. Dialogue with employees takes place primarily 
through the line manager, as well as via internal communication in various channels, 
such as the intranet and newsletters, and through physical and digital meetings.
Work Environment Directive
According to Swedbank’s Work Environment Directive, managers are responsible 
for ensuring a continuous dialogue with employees about their well-being and 
work situation through regular individual discussions. If the individual discus-
sions reveal an issue that may have a negative impact on the employee’s work 
environment or health, the manager takes measures in accordance with the 
­manager’s responsibility and the Work Environment Directive. 
Forum for employee representatives
Swedbank engages in continuous dialogue with employee representatives in vari-
ous forums. In 2007, Swedbank established a Group-wide European Works Coun-
cil (EWC), which is a cross-border forum for information and consultation with 
employee representatives from different European countries where Swedbank 
operates. The forum is there to deal with cross-border issues such as major 
organisational changes, HR policy issues and various business strategy initia-
tives. Swedbank’s CEO and CFO participate regularly in these meetings. In the 
Swedish operation, there is an ongoing dialogue with representatives from trade 
union organisations and health and safety officers, in accordance with the collec-
tive agreements. 
Swedbank’s co-determination model is based on the trade unions being 
involved at an early stage, and being given good insight and the opportunity to 
influence decisions regarding changes in operations that may affect the Group’s 
employees. The dialogue takes into account the views of the employee represen-
tatives, bringing the employees’ perspectives into Swedbank’s decision-making 
processes. Group HR & Facility Management is responsible for the area of trade 
union relations. Swedbank’s employees are also represented on Swedbank’s 
Board of Directors by two employee representatives and two deputies. 
Employee surveys 
One of the tools for engaging employees is the regular employee survey (People 
Pulse), which is conducted by Group HR & Facility Management. The survey gives 
employees the opportunity to express their views on the operation and work 
environ­ment through various questions, while also enabling an evaluation of 
employees’ engagement and how well they perceive, understand and deliver in 
accordance with Swedbank’s strategically important areas. The employee survey 
contains questions about whether Swedbank is perceived as an inclusive work-
place and whether the employee experiences discrimination or harassment. 
A selection of questions focuses on equal treatment based on grounds of 
­discrimination to provide an insight into whether certain employee groups are 
at greater risk of being subjected to unfair treatment.
With an average response rate of 85 per cent, the survey provides valuable 
information for leaders and teams to identify and determine actions for the fol-
lowing period. This feedback is also shared and discussed regularly by both the 
Group Executive Committee and the Board of Directors. The results of employee 
surveys are compiled in indices, two of which, the Engagement Index and the 
Sustainable Employee Index, constitute KPIs that are regularly followed up at 
a Group-wide level. High and stable results in these indices indicate strong 
engagement among employees, and that the work environment is perceived  
to be good and sustainable. 
In addition to the insights provided by the employee surveys, Swedbank also 
works actively to create forums where different perspectives can be highlighted. 
There are internal employee networks, such as Swedbank Women in Tech and the 
LBTQ+ GLaS network, which serve not only as platforms for networking and shar-
ing experiences, but also as important channels for identifying and discussing 
challenges or barriers that employees may encounter. 
Meetings for dialogue 
Twice a year, the Group Executive Committee and employees meet in a so-called 
Town Hall meeting, where Swedbank’s CEO and the Group Executive Committee 
present developments at Swedbank and answer employees’ questions.
Processes to remediate negative impacts  
and reporting channels
	 S1-3    Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for own 
workforce to raise concerns 
Swedbank has established procedures to manage and address potential material 
negative impacts. This includes systematic health and safety work to identify 
health and safety risks and take appropriate actions to deal with situations that 
arise and to work preventively. For further information on health and safety work, 
see section S1-4 Actions in respect of impacts, risks and opportunities on 
page 127. 
Swedbank’s employees are encouraged to act ethically, assume responsibility 
and, if necessary, take action against any irregularities. Swedbank has several 
channels through which employees can alert the Group to irregularities and have 
them investigated. If irregularities are confirmed after an investigation has been 
completed, Swedbank will take appropriate action at individual or group level to 
address the situation. This may include, for example, actions under labour law 
to stop behaviour or supportive actions to help the victim. 
Reporting of irregularities 
All employees can report suspected irregularities to their manager or, if neces-
sary, to another unit with responsibility, as well as via an internal incident report-
ing system. 
Swedbank’s Group-wide whistleblower process encourages employees and 
other stakeholders to report suspicions of serious irregularities in operations. 
Swedbank follows up on reports and cases received via the whistleblower func-
tion. Checking availability and direct dialogue with the whistleblower ensures that 
the process is working well. Information about the whistleblower process may be 
found in the Group’s Code of Conduct, which is available to all employees. There 
is no data on whether employees trust the whistleblower process. A more com-
prehensive description of the whistleblower function and the process around it 
may be found in G1-1 Whistleblower function on page 143. 
Irregularities can also be raised through the trade union organisations, the 
employee representatives from Swedbank’s European Works Council or the 
health and safety officers, depending on the country and local legislation. The 
trade union organisations with which Swedbank has collective agreements may 
also demand compensation if Swedbank were to breach its obligations under 
collective agreements. 
A specific process for evaluating whether any compensation is sufficient has 
not been established.

Actions
	 S1-4    Taking action on material impacts, and approaches  
to pursuing material opportunities
Swedbank has established processes to reduce the risk that the Group’s busi-
ness practices cause or contribute to negative impacts for employees. Examples 
of these processes are systematic health and safety work, the whistleblower pro-
cess and the salary equity mapping process. Internal controls, and in some cases 
double decision-making processes, have been established to prevent conflicts of 
interest and corruption. Swedbank has a number of governance documents that 
support these processes. They are updated regularly to respond to changes in 
operations, legislation and the operating environment. Based on the Group’s 
employee-related policies, a number of measures were taken during the year 
within the bank’s own operations. Measures are taken to promote responsible 
business operations that are sound in the long term. In 2025, the focus has been 
on the following measures:
Working conditions:
•	Health and safety in Swedbank’s home markets 
 — Dialogues 
 — Health and Safety Committee
 — Health and safety inspection
Equal treatment and equal opportunities for all
•	Equal pay for equal work
•	New skills development programmes
Swedbank has not identified significant capital or operating expenditure, either 
financial or non-financial, for the actions in addition to the resources already 
­integrated into routine financial planning. 
Working conditions
Health and safety work in Swedbank’s home markets
In 2025, implementation of systematic health and safety work in the Baltic coun-
tries was completed, with the aim of achieving Group-wide occupational health 
activities. This involves the implementation of a health and safety committee, 
quarterly management team meetings on the psychosocial work environment 
and a regular, structured dialogue between manager and employee about the 
work situation and well-being. During the year, Swedbank offered a seminar on 
mental health at the workplace to all employees in the Group, with the aim of 
increasing knowledge and understanding of the importance of mental health. 
In Sweden, Swedbank provides nationwide occupational health support. In the 
Baltic countries, the corresponding needs are met through health insurance 
­policies for employees. 
Dialogue as part of health and safety work 
One key element of preventive and systematic health and safety work is the 
­managers’ regular and close dialogue with each employee about their own work 
situation, atmosphere at work, work-life balance, health and well-being. System-
atic health and safety work takes place locally in each operation’s management 
team, and is based on a Group-wide health and safety agenda that focuses on the 
organisational and social work environment and indications of potential health 
and safety risks. The health and safety agenda is based on, among other things, 
the results of employee surveys, incident reporting, sick leave figures, staff turn-
over and circumstances inside or outside the operation that may affect employ-
ees. The work of management teams on the health and safety agenda forms the 
basis of risk assessments, measures and preventive work, and entails uniform 
work for sustainable employees in all operations, in all home markets. 
Health and Safety Committee
Swedbank’s health and safety committee is a Group-wide group consisting of 
business managers, employee representatives and representatives from the 
Group Executive Committee. The committee’s task is to follow up on local health 
and safety work at a central level and to collaborate between the different opera-
tions in the Group. The health and safety committee holds quarterly meetings at 
which follow-up takes place in the form of each Business Area reporting its larg-
est health and safety risks, together with action plans with associated activities. 
Follow-up focuses on the results of the operations in the Sustainable Employee 
Index, consisting of questions that reflect the Group’s largest health and safety 
risks, sick leave figures, staff turnover and health and safety-related incidents. 
The Sustainable Employee Index is also followed up as a KPI at management 
level in the Group Executive Committee. Sick leave figures, in the form of both 
long-term and short-term absence, are also monitored by the Group Risk unit. 
The results of the Group’s health and safety targets during the year show that 
Swedbank has a good work environment.
Health and safety inspection as an action in health and safety work
In collaboration with employee representatives, an annual health and safety 
inspection is conducted for each workplace, involving a systematic review to 
investigate how the physical work environment and workplace design are per-
ceived and support day-to-day work and health. After a health and safety inspec-
tion, deficiencies are risk assessed and measures are taken. These inspections 
are followed up twice a year at central level. The results for 2025 showed a 
reduced number of serious and critical health and safety risks at the Group’s 
branches, which is partly due to intensified systematic health and safety work 
to address risks in accordance with the action plan.
Related KPIs are reported in S1-14 table showing health and safety indicators, 
S1-6 table showing staff turnover and Note G13.9 table showing sick leave on 
page 244.
Equal treatment and opportunities for all 
Swedbank has established a strategic framework for diversity, equity and inclu-
sion that aims to operationalise Swedbank’s Policy on Diversity, Equity and Inclu-
sion. The framework clarifies how different initiatives create value for customers, 
employees and society. It also describes specific targets to be achieved and 
emphasises the importance of both business and HR processes as well as gover-
nance, communication and culture in order to achieve the desired results in this 
area. The framework covers the whole Group and is reviewed annually. The 
framework is available on the intranet for all employees.
Work to integrate an accessibility perspective has been strengthened, with the 
aim of creating a workplace in which all employees are given equal opportunities 
to contribute and develop. One example is the environment in the office premises, 
which should support inclusion, well-being and various accessibility needs in 
order to provide employees with the conditions to perform their work efficiently.
Swedbank measures and evaluates equal opportunities and anti-discrimina-
tion initiatives via the employee survey. The Group follows up on data regarding 
gender and age, based on personal identity numbers. Gender balance in senior 
roles, at managerial level and in managerial positions is systematically followed 
up to ensure transparency and drive the trend towards more equal representa-
tion. Other grounds for discrimination in Swedbank’s Policy on Diversity, Equity 
and Inclusion are not requested in the survey.
For further information on Swedbank’s policies, see section S1-1 Policies for 
own workforce on page 125.
To increase awareness and engagement throughout the organisation, employ-
ees have been offered a number of seminars and training sessions on inclusion, 
diversity and equity. Related KPIs are reported in sections S1-6, S1-9, S1-15 and in 
Note G13.9. 
Equal pay for equal work
Equal pay for equal work means that pay is determined on a fair basis for all 
employees. In order to deliver in accordance with the Group’s strategy for an 
inclusive and equal workplace, Swedbank’s remuneration strategy is designed to 
attract and retain a workforce with diversity, competence, experience and skills. 
Swedbank follows up on the pay gap in all home markets on a monthly basis. 
This provides continuous control of any differences and supports work on equal 
pay. In collaboration with the trade unions, Swedbank conducts an annual salary 
equity mapping process that covers all employees in Sweden. The purpose is to 
identify and manage any unfair pay differences. Preparations for the upcoming 
Pay Transparency Directive also began during the year. The directive enters into 
force in June 2026 and entails new procedures for transparency, salary mapping, 
reporting and dialogue with trade unions. Overall, this is expected to contribute to 
a structured management of remuneration issues, with a focus on fairness and 
transparency. It is also expected to ­support workforce continuity through reduced 
staff turnover. Related KPIs are presented in section S1-16 Remuneration metrics 
on page 131.
New skills development programmes
Swedbank continues its work to promote a culture that values learning. During 
2025, several initiatives were launched that enable both managers and other 
employees to develop in their current roles or prepare for future roles. Six skills 
development areas have been identified, implemented and integrated into the 
annual performance and career development review. Follow-up is also carried out 
via the quarterly Performance Development reviews. There was also a focus on 
leadership development during the year. Development of potential leaders, AI, 
data analysis and digital leadership are areas where training programmes have 
been launched for all employees. Swedbank has also continued to invest in train-
ing, especially in ESG-related issues. Follow-up on performance and career devel-
opment as well as training takes place continuously. Related KPIs are presented 
in section S1-13 Training and skills development metrics on page 130.

Swedbank has adopted two Group-wide strategic targets in the areas of both 
employee engagement and equity and diversity. The targets cover the areas of 
working conditions, equal treatment and equal opportunities in own operations. 
Employee engagement is measured and followed up through regular surveys 
to follow up on the positive impact on employee well-being. This provides insight 
into how employees feel and how they perceive Swedbank as an employer and 
a workplace. Within the framework of this work, specific interim targets for 
employees have been developed. 
To contribute to an inclusive and equal workplace, Swedbank is also working 
actively to achieve an even gender balance. Equity and diversity targets have 
been set, while KPIs are used to follow up on pay gaps and the gender balance 
between managers at different levels.

Targets for employees are set by the respective process owners in Group HR & 
Facility Management based on prioritised areas, and are based on, among other

responsible for continuously evaluating the relevance and appropriateness of the 
targets. To enable follow-up over time, the aim is to maintain continuity in both 
targets and follow-up. No changes were made during the year in respect of met-
rics, methods, assumptions, baseline year, limitations, data collection or sources. 
The proposed targets are discussed in the Group HR & Facility Management 
management team to ensure that they support Swedbank’s employee strategy. 
The final decision is made by the CEO. Employee representatives are members
