Calculation methodology
Employees and forms of employment
The number of employees is reported as the number of people and refers to the 
total number of employees in the Group at the end of the reporting period. Swed-
bank uses internal information to count all employees broken down by gender, 
employment type and country. 
Data used for calculations is retrieved from Swedbank’s HR systems: HRMS, 
POL and HCM. If system data is not available for a legal entity, the entity’s repre-
sentative provides the data. 
To ensure data quality, Swedbank checks that the data is complete (that all 
employment types and countries are included in the data) and consistent (that 
the data is consistent with previous annual and monthly reports). 
Collective agreements and social dialogue
In Sweden, all employees are covered by collective agreements, except the CEO 
and the Group Executive Committee, as well as employees of Stabelo, the com-
pany acquired during the autumn. Employees in Denmark are also covered by 
­collective agreements. Employees in Entercard and Swedbank's Norwegian 
branches, as well as PayEx employees in Finland, are also covered by collective 
agreements. Other employees are not covered by collective agreements. 
In order to report the degree of collective bargaining coverage in Norway and 
Finland, a calculation was performed of what proportion of the employees in 
Norway and Finland are covered by collective agreements compared to the total 
number of employees. 
The table showing collective bargaining coverage and social dialogue only 
includes countries with a significant number of employees. A significant number 
of employees is defined as at least 50 employees (head count), which constitutes 
at least 10 per cent of Swedbank’s total number of employees. No assumptions 
were made. 
Diversity
Calculations and information on gender and age are based on the employee’s 
personal identity number and legal gender (female/male). They are not based on 
self-identifying data. Gender distribution in actual and percentage terms at the 
top management level refers to the number of employees per gender at the close 
of the reporting period. 
The top management level is deemed to be the CEO and the Group Executive 
Committee. 
The distribution of employees by age group is the number of employees 
broken down by age group (Under 30, 30–50 and over 50) at the close of the 
reporting period. 
Data used for calculations is retrieved from Swedbank’s HR systems: HRMS, 
POL and HCM. If system data is not available for a legal entity, the entity’s repre-
sentative provides the data. To ensure data quality, Swedbank checks that the 
data is complete (that all employment types and countries are included in the 
data) and consistent (that the data is consistent with previous annual and 
monthly reports). 
Skills development
The proportion of employees who participated in regular development reviews 
is broken down by gender. To report the average number of training hours, Swed-
bank uses the following calculation: total number of training hours completed 
by employees per gender category divided by the total number of employees per 
gender category. Figures reported in disclosure requirement S1-6 are used for 
total employment and employment by gender. 
Data used for calculations is retrieved from the HR system: SABA. If data 
about a specific legal entity is missing from the systems, a representative of 
the legal entity is asked to provide this information. 
To ensure data quality, Swedbank checks that the data is complete (that all 
employment types and countries are included in the data) and consistent (that 
the data is consistent with previous annual and monthly reports). 
Assumptions
If data is not available for a legal entity, the result is assumed to be consistent 
with the average or percentage for other legal entities. 
Health and safety
In the Group, work-related injuries such as work-related accidents and ill health 
are reported to the respective government agencies in each country in accor-
dance with current legislation. Work-related accidents, illnesses and ill health are 
also reported internally as incidents in Swedbank’s incident reporting system by 
the respective employee or non-employee or their manager, in consultation with 
the health and safety officer. 
Some companies within the Group do not have access to the incident reporting 
system. Information on health and safety-related incidents for these companies 
has been provided by representatives of the business.
The Health and safety indicators table presents internally reported occupa-
tional accidents in the form of work-related injuries and illnesses that have also 
been reported to government agencies. These occupational injuries have 
occurred at the workplace or due to work. Accidents that occur in connection 
with travel to or from work, so-called travel accidents, are not included. 
All employees in the Group’s own workforce are covered by Swedbank’s health 
and safety system. Swedbank’s health and safety system entails the Group apply-
ing local health and safety legislation in all countries and conducting systematic 
internal health and safety work in each country. With regard to non-employees, 
Swedbank, as the purchaser, has joint health and safety responsibility together 
with the employer of the non-employee workforce. 
Swedbank’s health and safety system is subject to external review. For exam-
ple, type: it can be mentioned that in Sweden, the Swedish Work Environment 
Authority conducts annual reviews of how Swedbank structures and manages 
its systematic health and safety and the results of the health and safety work, 
against the background of EU and Swedish health and safety legislation. 
­Swedbank also conducts annual internal reviews of health and safety work.
Work-life balance metrics
Number of employees taking parental leave or carer’s leave, per gender. Percent-
age was calculated by dividing total number of all employees who have taken 
family-related leave or carer’s leave during 2025 by total number of employees 
(headcount) as of 2025-12-31. 
Data is taken from the internal HR systems (POL and HRMS) and input from 
the legal entity representatives. 
Remuneration
Gender pay gaps are calculated as the difference between the gross hourly pay of 
all men and the gross hourly pay of all women, as a ratio of the gross hourly pay 
of men. The scope of application is all employees within the Group. A positive 
ratio means that men's remuneration is higher than women's, and vice versa. 
The total remuneration ratio for the CEO compared to employees is calculated 
as the annual total remuneration of the highest paid individual (CEO) in the Group 
in relation to the median of the annual total remuneration of all employees 
(excluding the highest paid individual). The scope of application is all employees 
within the Group. 
Differences in equal pay (Equal Pay Gap) are calculated as a comparison 
between average salary indices for men and women per job level and market. The 
scope of application is Swedbank’s home markets. A positive percentage means 
that men have higher remuneration than women for equal work, and vice versa. 
Data used for calculations is retrieved from Swedbank’s HR and finance sys-
tems. If system data is not available for a legal entity, the entity’s representative 
provides the data. 
To ensure data quality, Swedbank checks that the data is complete (that all 
employment types and countries are included in the data) and consistent (that 
the data is consistent with previous annual and monthly reports). 
Assumptions
If certain legal entities do not provide information at employee level, the average 
salary per gender for all employees in the legal entity is used for the total com-
pensation ratio.
If legal entity does not provide data by country for gender pay gap calculation, 
an assumption is made that average hourly pay in all countries is equal to legal 
entity’s average. 
Incidents and reports
Data on the total number of complaints is based on cases received in Swedbank’s 
whistleblower function during 2025 that have been forwarded to and investigated 
by Group HR & FM in Sweden. Data on cases of discrimination, including harass-
ment, also includes cases that have been received through other channels 
through which employees and managers can raise concerns and that have been 
investigated by Group HR & FM in Swedbank’s home markets. Swedbank has a 
working method in which the manager, with the support of Group HR & FM, is the 
person who initially handles matters relating to behaviour in the workplace. 
These cases can then be escalated to Group HR & FM for further investigation. 
Data on detected cases of serious incidents relating to human rights, such as 
forced labour, human trafficking or child labour involving Swedbank’s employees, 
has been provided by representatives of the operation.

Data protection
A significant volume of personal data is processed in Swedbank’s operations. 
The protection of customer information is a top priority, and correct handling is 
crucial to maintaining the trust of stakeholders. To ensure that processing takes 
place in a way that respects the rights of the individual, carefully structured 
­procedures and actions are applied.
Strategy and business model
	 S4 SBM-3    Strategy and business model
Swedbank offers a wide range of financial services that entail significant respon-
sibility for handling sensitive customer data. For Swedbank as a financial actor, 
this is fundamental to the Group’s strategy and activities, as it requires that all 
handling takes place in a correct and secure manner that prevents harm to cus-
tomers, employees and other stakeholders concerned. Inadequate handling can 
lead to a breach of personal privacy, loss of trust, distrust and anxiety among 
­customers, which can constitute a financial risk for Swedbank. 
Swedbank has processes to identify and manage risks in connection with the 
processing of personal data. This work is based on policies and guidelines in 
accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)1. This means 
that products and services are designed to comply with regulations and protect 
both customers and employees. Handling must be in line with the Group’s 
­strategy and internal governance. 
Different groups may be affected by Swedbank’s handling of personal data, for 
example existing and prospective customers, employees including consultants, 
and visitors to Swedbank’s branches. It is important for Swedbank to communi-
cate in a way that enables customers to understand how their data is being 
­processed and how they can exercise their rights, ask questions or lodge 
­complaints. This also includes vulnerable groups. 
Policies
	 S4-1    Policies related to consumers and end-users 
Swedbank has adopted a number of governance documents that constitute 
important guidelines and rules for the Group’s work to manage material impacts 
and risks related to the area of data protection. These documents consist of 
Swedbank’s Sustainability Policy, Swedbank’s Code of Conduct, Policy for 
­Conduct Risk and Customer Complaint Policy, which cover negative impacts 
and risks relating to data protection.

Protection of personal data in accordance with 
the GDPR
Swedbank complies with the GDPR, which entails a responsibility to protect the 
individual’s right to their personal data. This regulation is based on internationally 
recognised conventions and principles for the protection of human rights. These 
apply not only to Swedbank’s customers, but to everyone whose personal data is 
handled by Swedbank. 
Customers receive, among other things, information about the processing of 
personal data on Swedbank’s external websites and can also contact the Group’s 
Data Protection Officer. 
Swedbank’s risk management is based on the principle of three lines of 
defence. A structured chain of responsibility with independent controls ensures 
that non-compliance is followed up, managed and reported. This not only 
reduces risks and improves operational efficiency in Swedbank, but also builds 
trust among customers, employees and other stakeholders. Furthermore, this 
creates a culture of transparency and accountability that protects individuals’ 
right to privacy. Swedbank does not currently measure the number of reported 
cases concerning failure to respect international principles and guidelines 
­involving consumers and/or end-users in the downstream value chain. 
Remediation in the event of a personal data breach, in the form of compensa-
tion, is handled in accordance with current legislation. 
 
Procedures for customer contact
	 S4-2    Processes for engaging with consumers and end-users  
about impacts
 Swedbank provides information on how and why the Group collects and pro-
cesses customers’ personal data, and provides guidance on how customers can 
exercise their rights. This creates the conditions for customers to maintain their 
rights regarding the processing of personal data. The information is available on 
Swedbank’s external websites and applications, and via customer meetings. 
There are also other ways to get in touch with Swedbank, for example via the 
internet bank, the Customer Centre, by letter, by email or by visiting a physical 
branch. This information is made available in a clear and easily understandable 
way to all customer groups. 
If the customer has comments on the handling of data, there is an opportunity 
to lodge a complaint. Complaints are registered in the Group’s internal system for 
managing customer complaints and are an important source for Swedbank to 
identify and develop necessary changes based on customer requests. This pro-
cess enables the customer perspective to be integrated into Swedbank’s deci-
sions on actions. 
The customer complaint process includes follow-up, evaluation and imple-
mentation of improvement measures. Swedbank addresses complaints on 
a quarterly basis in order to identify and implement solutions.

Incident management
	 S4-3    Procedures for remediation
In addition to Swedbank’s policies, instructions and directives regarding compli-
ance with the GDPR, there are Data Breach Guidelines that describe how the 
Group should act in the event of personal data breaches and how the adequacy 
of actions is evaluated. In accordance with the applicable regulatory framework, 
Swedbank investigates whether any remediation should be made to the affected 
individual if Swedbank has contributed to a negative impact through inadequate 
data protection. 
If a review of a personal data case has taken place and the customer is not sat-
isfied with the final decision of Swedbank’s customer ombudsman, the customer 
can contact the Swedish National Board of Complaints (ARN), the Swedish 
Authority for Privacy Protection (IMY), the home municipality’s consumer advisor 
or the Swedish Consumer Banking and Finance Agency. Information about this 
can be found on Swedbank’s website. Swedbank also has data processors, com-
panies that process registered personal data on behalf of Swedbank, and a three-
step due diligence process. This entails:
•	Assessment of potential data processors before a contract is drawn up, to 
ensure that appropriate technical, organisational and contractual complemen-
tary measures are in place, to ensure compliance with GDPR requirements and 
to fulfil contractual obligations.
•	Monitoring that established data processors maintain and continue to develop 
the security aspects of handling personal data.
•	An off-boarding phase to ensure that the data processor returns and erases all 
personal data in accordance with the established data processor contract. 
There is no follow-up and reporting on customers’ awareness of this work.
Actions 
	 S4-4    Taking action on material impacts on consumers and end-users, 
and approaches to managing material risks and the effectiveness of 
those actions
Swedbank’s data protection work concerns several areas such as regulatory 
compliance, risk identification and customer communication. The actions 
described below aim to contribute to long-term resilience in the areas of privacy 
and data protection. They shall prevent and limit material negative impacts on 
consumers in the form of breaches of personal privacy, unauthorised use of per-
sonal data and inadequate opportunities for individuals to exercise their rights 
regarding data protection.
Follow-up indicates that the Group’s data protection measures are essentially 
appropriate. 
Swedbank has not identified significant capital or operating expenditure for

planning. 
Updating of governance documents 
Swedbank continuously improves its internal regulations in respect of privacy in 
order to ensure compliance with the latest data protection rules and established 
practice. The Group adopts a proactive approach to regulatory changes and 
closely monitors new regulations and legislation, and has implemented relevant 
requirements in its governance structures. To support compliance and promote 
a culture of accountability, Swedbank regularly develops and updates custom-
ised training packages that address the specific needs of different employee 
functions. 
Compliance and preparations
In 2025, a programme was established with the aim of strengthening the gover-
nance of AI systems and compliance with the EU AI Act. In this programme, activ-
ities have been initiated to ensure compliance with the AI Act and enforce the 
responsible use of AI with the support of representatives from the operation. 
A process for identification, risk assessment and documentation of AI systems 
has been established and a training programme has been developed that is avail-
able to all employees. This applies to employees working within the EU. The AI 
Act will enter into force in August 2027, which means that the programme’s 
­operations will continue during 2026. Compliance with the programme is fol-
lowed up quarterly by Group Compliance, in the CIO Risk Report and Swedbank’s 
AI Acceleration & Governance Council. A check of all AI systems is conducted 
and reported based on the risk level in accordance with the AI Act. The number 
of employees who have completed the two training programmes in this area is 
also monitored.
Employee training
To build a resilient organisation, it is important that Swedbank’s employees have 
good knowledge in the area of data protection, so that risks, such as personal 
data breaches, can be prevented. All Swedbank employees undergo annual man-
datory training programmes and are also offered a voluntary in-depth course on 
GDPR-related personal data processing. The purpose is to increase awareness of 
data protection among employees, which indirectly can have a positive impact on 
customers and society by promoting informed decisions regarding personal 
data. The number of training programmes completed is followed up.

Development of data protection processes 
Swedbank has established processes in the form of impact assessments, bal-
ancing of interests and related documentation to ensure correct handling of per-
sonal data and risk management. This is part of the Group’s risk assessment pro-
cess. The assessment is conducted by such means as applying the principle of

Directors every six months on how effective Swedbank’s data protection work is 
in relation to external regulations, requirements and Swedbank’s risk appetite. 
Swedbank ensures that the processing of personal data takes place by balanc-
ing the individual’s right to protection of their personal data with the Group’s right 
to process data. Personal data is saved for as long as it is necessary for the pur-
poses of collection and in accordance with law or other legal basis. After the 
agreement expires, the data is retained for such purposes as accounting, anti-
money laundering measures, capital adequacy requirements and legal purposes. 
This means that Swedbank sometimes has to retain data for longer than the 
duration of the agreement. Swedbank reports personal data breaches where 
the GDPR prescribes that these must be reported to the Swedish Authority for 
­Privacy Protection. There were no reports of serious human rights issues or 
­incidents linked to Swedbank customers during the year. 
Swedbank monitors the operating environment in order to adapt data protec-
tion processes to new regulations, practice and guidelines from the Swedish and 
European data protection agencies, and works continuously to improve its data 
protection processes. Swedbank monitors that measures are implemented when 
new systems and processes are developed, to maintain data protection princi-
ples. If Swedbank causes harm to an individual as a consequence of inadequate 
data protection procedures, the individual is in certain cases entitled to appropri-
ate compensation in accordance with legislation and the Group’s internal proce-
dures. For further information on remediation, see S4-3 Procedures for remedia-
tion on page 135.

Information security
Information security constitutes an important basis for financial stability, as 
­deficiencies in this area can result in serious consequences that have a negative 
impact on society. It is also a prerequisite for ensuring that individuals and busi-
nesses, regardless of background and circumstances, have secure access to 
financial services. Swedbank’s work in this area aims to secure access to finan-
cial services, protect information and maintain confidence in the financial system. 
Strategy and business model
	 S4 SBM-3    Material impacts and risks, and their interaction with the 
strategy and business model
As a systemically important actor in the Swedish and Baltic banking system with 
a broad customer base consisting of both private individuals and companies, 
Swedbank has a responsibility to protect the financial infrastructure against 
cyber threats. The global threat scenario is characterised by growing cybercrime, 
with actors trying to steal information, commit fraud or disrupt operations. The 
events may be of a systematic nature, relate to individual incidents or in some 
cases be linked to specific business relationships. This threat scenario has been 
assessed to have the ability to cause a potentially serious negative impact on 
consumers, in which all of Swedbank’s customer groups may be included. Exam-
ples of negative impacts for consumers are the spreading of misinformation, 
fraud and interruptions to or reduced availability of key financial services. These 
analyses are based on thorough threat and fraud analyses, as well as analyses of 
risks. A serious attack on the Group or its partners can have far-reaching conse-
quences for economic stability, societally important functions and individuals’ 
access to financial services. 
Information security also constitutes a financial risk for Swedbank. Threats of 
data breaches, cyberattacks and unauthorised handling of information can result 
in significant financial consequences for the Group. Violations can result in direct 
costs for incident management, legal action, fines and penalties for non-compli-
ance with regulations. In addition to direct financial losses, information security 
incidents can affect customer confidence and thereby Swedbank’s brand and 
market position. 
Policies
	 S4-1    Policies related to consumers and end-users 
Swedbank has adopted a number of governance documents that constitute 
important guidelines and rules for the Group’s work to manage material impacts 
and risks related to information security. Swedbank also specifies security 
requirements for its third-party suppliers and partners. 
The area is supplemented by two sets of CEO instructions, Instruction on 
­operational risk and Instruction on information security. These detail additional 
governance and the actions taken for information security.
In addition to these, Swedbank’s Sustainability Policy acts as a governance doc-
ument covering human rights, and the Code of Conduct acts as Swedbank’s ethics 
policy. Read more about these policies in S4-1, Data protection. All of these gover-
nance documents cover negative impact and risk relating to information security.

Actions

Swedbank invests continuously to enhance its work on security, both through 
technical safeguards and through active work on security awareness and train-
ing. Information security is integrated into business processes, product develop-
ment and the management of third-party relationships to create a holistic 
approach to security. This work is not only aimed at complying with legal require-
ments and the expectations of regulatory authorities, it is also important for 
strengthening the Group’s long-term resilience in a changing digital environment. 
In 2025, Swedbank carried out several activities that covered the entire Group 
and all Business Areas and customer segments, with the exception of partner-
ships. These collaborations are, however, considered to have positive effects for 
the entire Group. There were no reports of serious human rights issues or inci-
dents linked to Swedbank customers during the year. 
Swedbank has not identified significant capital or operating expenditure for 
the measures in addition to the resources already integrated in routine financial 
planning.
Systems to strengthen information security 
Through a structured, risk-based approach, information security threats are iden-
tified and managed, ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements. Swed-
bank has established an information security management system (LIS) based 
on international standards such as ISO 27001. Information security is integrated 
into Swedbank’s framework, processes and procedures, which contributes to 
reducing the risk of incidents and ensuring that information is protected and 
available when needed. Systematic management of information security reduces 
the risk of breaches. This work is crucial for Swedbank and is prioritised over 
other business needs. 
Security tests and vulnerability analyses
Swedbank carried out a number of security initiatives to strengthen its resilience 
to cyber threats during the year. Regular phishing simulation exercises can 
increase security awareness among employees. Tests are used continuously to 
improve the Group’s protection and response capabilities. Swedbank also con-
ducts periodic evaluations of security measures related to APIs and IT services, 
in line with current threat scenarios. Swedbank’s security testing framework gov-
erns various testing activities, such as penetration tests and information security 
risk assessments, which contributes to a proactive approach in order to 
strengthen the Group’s cybersecurity. 
The incident management process
Swedbank has established processes and supporting tools to manage informa-
tion security incidents and to effectively detect, address and follow up on such 
events. The purpose is to limit the impact of the incidents, take actions to reduce 
the risk of future events, ensure correct reporting to the relevant authorities and 
provide a general overview. The main incident management process is overseen 
by Group Operational Risk (GOR) and covers operational incidents as well as 
mandatory reporting. Information security incidents are managed as operational 
incidents. Cybersecurity incidents, such as cyberattacks, are managed by a pro-
cess to mitigate threats and analyse the course of events. This process uses IT 
incident management to restore normal operation in the event of major or critical 
events. During an ongoing event and in the subsequent analysis, the negative 
impact on direct customers and partners is taken into consideration via commu-
nication in accordance with established methods. 
Security culture and training
In addition to technical solutions, Swedbank promotes a strong security culture. 
Regular training programmes for employees and customers and initiatives to raise 
awareness strengthen resilience to security threats and reduce the risk of human 
error. Swedbank’s employees working in the field of information security undertake 
a mandatory training programme every year, with follow-up on implementation.
Partnerships 
Collaboration and partnerships are an important part of information security 
work. Swedbank works in collaboration with both government agencies and busi-
nesses within and outside the financial sector. One example is the banking col-
laboration known as the Swedish National Cybersecurity Centre, where Swed-
bank participates in the information sharing group, with the aim of strengthening 
Sweden’s collective capacity to deal with cyber threats. Collaboration between 
banks is an important part of this. For further information, see G1 Economic 
Crime Prevention on page 145.
Conflicts of interest
To protect Swedbank, customers and other stakeholders, there are policies for 
managing conflicts of interest. The purpose is to prevent conflicts of interest 
from affecting the interests of customers or, if this is not possible, to clearly iden-
tify and report them. Any conflicts of interest identified must be documented, 
assessed and prevented or mitigated in accordance with processes established 
by Group Compliance and followed up as necessary.
Targets and metrics
	 S4-5    Targets related to managing material negative impacts and 
material risks
Swedbank works continuously to develop and improve methods to deal with an 
increasingly complex and escalating threat scenario, and has established pro-
cesses to identify, monitor and manage risks linked to information security inci-
dents. One aspect of this is to raise awareness among employees through training 
and skills development. The proportion of employees who have undergone infor-
mation security training during the year is presented as a metric for follow­-up. 
Established security metrics and key risk indicators are applied to follow up on 
information security work. This means that Swedbank does not report any pub-
licly measurable outcome-based targets in this area, nor does the bank report 
comparisons over time. To follow up on the appropriateness of policies and 
actions, Swedbank has established internal processes for annual follow-up. 
Swedbank has an independent compliance function, Group Compliance, which 
manages the Group’s compliance risks. This work includes proposing and defin-
ing minimum standards in areas such as information security, and monitoring the 
management of compliance within the Group. If established thresholds are 
exceeded or if there is a significant increase in information security incidents, 
an in-depth analysis and, if necessary, an internal investigation are conducted. 
This then forms the basis of future development and actions.

Financial health
With 7.3 million private customers, Swedbank has a responsibility to encourage 
financial health. Boosting the financial health of customers is part of Swedbank’s 
strategy and business model, based on a long tradition of conveying knowledge 
about private finances and savings. Through ongoing and individually tailored 
advice, Swedbank can contribute to increasing financial knowledge in society.
Strategy and business model
	 S4 SBM-3    Material impacts and their interaction with the strategy  
and business model
Swedbank’s work in the area of financial health is based on the UN’s definition: 
to feel safe in your private finances and to have control, resilience and financial 
freedom. Swedbank’s initiatives in the area of financial health involve customers 
having the ability to create stable, long-term and secure finances with scope to 
deal with unforeseen events. The purpose is to support customers in gaining 
a better understanding of their current and future financial situation, desired risk 
level and protection in the form of insurance. The Group’s range of products and 
services provides customers with opportunities to boost their financial health 
based on their individual needs. 
The Group’s comprehensive financial offering includes lending, savings, insur-
ance, pension and payments for private customers. Financial health is integrated 
as a consistent theme in the private business segment. This work includes the 
development of digital and proactive information and advice, which makes it pos-
sible to reach more customers and offer advice on a larger scale. The theme of 
financial health brings together the Group’s competences in the areas of training, 
analysis and research, which are shared with customers through advice, reports 
and other initiatives. 
Through surveys and dialogues, the Group monitors people’s financial capa­
bility and knowledge in the home markets, in order to gain a better understanding 
of their financial health. In addition to the integration within the Group’s product 
and service offering, Swedbank offers specific training programmes and lectures 
in private finance. A significant proportion of these initiatives is specifically tar-
geted at young people. This work enables Swedbank to contribute to increased 
financial knowledge and sense of security, as well as financial inclusion, which 
can in turn have a positive impact on both individuals and society as a whole.

Activities to support financial health 
The Financial Laboratory is an initiative within Swedbank’s Baltic operations in 
Latvia and Lithuania. It offers an interactive space for learning outside the tradi-
tional classroom, where students explore finances through games and practical 
exercises. A Centre for Financial Knowledge was established during the year at 
the head office in Estonia. Designed for school students, it offers interactive train-
ing sessions on topics such as budgeting, loans, investment and entrepreneur-
ship. The aim of these initiatives is to provide participants with practical experi-
ences that boost financial awareness and skills. 
Young Economy is an initiative from Swedbank and the Savings Banks that 
teaches children and young people about private finance in Sweden. The initiative 
has been under way for several years and entails Swedbank offering free lectures 
for school classes, associations and other places where children and young 
people are present. The ultimate aim is to inspire and prepare them to make con-
scious financial decisions and understand the importance of financial planning. 
Swedbank Investment School is a free-of-charge training platform launched 
at the end of 2025 within the Baltic operation. The aim is to enhance knowledge 
about investments in the region. The platform, available in local languages, offers 
interactive videos for people between the ages of 18 and 45 who are new to 
investing or want to expand their knowledge. A certificate is issued upon comple-
tion of training and a pass in the test. 
Swedbank Institutes of Finance have been operating since 2010 in Estonia, 
Latvia and Lithuania. The aim is to deepen the understanding of private finances 
and strengthen financial behaviour in society. Through these institutes, economic 
factors are analysed, while practical advice on financial health is produced and 
distributed. The initiatives also aim to increase knowledge on topics such as 
­private finances, budgeting and entrepreneurship. 2024 also saw the launch of 
the Institute for Financial Health in Sweden. This brings together Swedbank’s 
expertise in training, analysis, donations and research support. 
Economists at the Institute regularly measure the finances and financial 
health of the Swedish population by analysing how both personal life choices, 
changes in the economy and political decisions affect the private finances of 
individuals. The Institute also studies the conditions for businesses and entrepre-
neurs. A Group-wide Financial Health Index has been developed. The index mea-
sures the financial ability and knowledge of people annually in terms of everyday 
finances, savings, loans and financial security. These measurements help the 
Group and society to understand the level of financial health in their home 
­markets. Based on the results, Swedbank can convey knowledge and create 
awareness to empower people in their pursuit of better financial health. 
The activities are in line with Swedbank’s Sustainability Policy, which high-
lights the Group’s ambition to increase financial awareness and the understand-
ing of key financial concepts. Group targets have been set for the number of par-
ticipants, and this is followed up on an ongoing basis. Evaluations are conducted 
on an ongoing basis, but there is currently no systematic follow-up on whether 
the level of knowledge is increasing among participants. 
Swedbank has not identified significant capital or operating expenditure for 
the measures in addition to the resources already integrated in routine financial 
planning. 
In addition to the above, Swedbank has been a long-term partner of Junior 
Achievement since 1985, with engagement as a jury member, advisor and 
­supporter for entrepreneurs of the future. There is more information about work 
within Junior Achievement on page 8.

report on a monthly basis within their respective areas, while reporting in the 
Baltic countries takes place quarterly. This enables continuous follow-up on and 
quality assurance of the reach of the initiative.

year. The focus has shifted from counting participants over a single day to mea-
suring engagement over time, primarily via teacher conferences. Changes in the 
event format can make it difficult to compare metrics between years, as collec-

Management of deviations and violations 
Business conduct is a top priority for Swedbank. Employees are encouraged to 
be vigilant for events in their day-to-day work that deviate from the Group’s corpo-
rate culture and constitute a breach of the rules that Swedbank is required follow. 
Swedbank’s fraud prevention work and investigation of internal fraud include 
ethical violations and bribery and corruption. The internal governance documents 
require the Group to ensure a risk-based framework against violations in accor-
dance with applicable laws and regulations. They also state the requirement to 
establish controls to prevent, detect and report suspected incidents. Internal 
guidelines include requirements for a uniform process to promptly investigate 
suspected incidents that are classified as internal fraud, in which technical and 
manual control environments are implemented to detect deviations in particu-
larly high-risk processes. Employees who discover deviations can report to their 
line manager, who will document and forward the information for investigation. If 
the investigation shows that there have been serious violations of rules, this may 
result in actions under labour law. Decisions on actions under labour law must be 
made based on recommendations from the units involved in the investigation. 
Swedbank has also established processes for identifying and managing conflicts 
of interest, which aim to support employees and strengthen trust in Swedbank. It 
is the responsibility of each unit manager to manage identified conflicts of inter-
est, with annual reporting and assessment. More information relating to corrup-
tion and bribery is reported in G1-3 Prevention and detection of corruption and 
bribery as well as G1-4 Incidents of corruption and bribery on page 144.
Whistleblower function
The Group-wide whistleblower function is an important element of supporting 
business conduct and maintaining a good corporate culture. Swedbank has 
established confidential and secure reporting channels and ensured strong pro-
tection against retaliation for whistleblowers1. The process enables the early 
detection, investigation and management of violations, contributing to increased 
transparency and accountability within the Group. External parties can also use 
the whistleblower function to report irregularities and other misconduct. The pro-
cedures established by Swedbank to protect whistleblowers are in accordance 
with the EU Whistleblowing Directive and Swedish whistleblowing legislation. 
Information about the Group’s whistleblower process may be found in the Code 
of Conduct, in the Group’s internal channels and on the external website. Employ-
ees also undergo mandatory annual ethics training, which includes information 
about the Group’s whistleblower process.
If there is any suspicion of irregularities within the operation, this must be 
reported to the whistleblower unit within Group Compliance, which owns the 
­process, and to Group Internal Audit respectively. The whistleblower can submit 
reports openly or anonymously, and remain anonymous in the dialogue. Reports 
and messages are encrypted and treated as strictly confidential by the whis-
tleblower unit within Swedbank that investigates the matter. The authorised 
employees within each unit operate independently and autonomously, with a 
­specifically regulated mandate to manage reporting channels and procedures. 
On any conflict of ­interest, the incident is transferred to another investigating 
whistleblower unit. The Board of Directors is informed of the number of whis-
tleblower cases, with ­general information about the matter, in connection with 
the quarterly report. 
Actions in respect of corporate culture
Swedbank’s governing documents serve as a central tool for integrating the 
Group’s values into daily operations and shape both ongoing and planned initia-
tives to strengthen the corporate culture. The Group works actively to ensure that 
employees feel good at work, have a healthy workload, feel included and have 
a good work-life balance. Swedbank conducts annual employee surveys with 
questions relating to strategic direction, leadership and corporate culture. The 
surveys aim to encourage continuous dialogue and an open corporate culture, 
where employees’ opinions are taken into account. All managers have to review 
the results and follow up with their unit to identify areas for improvement. Lead-
ers at Swedbank are guided by the leadership principles: build trust, inspire, and 
show courage, which outline the expectations for how leaders across the Group 
should act. 
Every employee is expected to act in accordance with Swedbank’s values and 
must follow the Code of Conduct, internal rules, laws and regulations, and good 
practice within their area of responsibility. All new employees receive training in 
Swedbank’s values. The Code of Conduct states that employees must undergo 
mandatory training required for their position and role at Swedbank. Certain

In 2025, employees underwent internal training in the area of ethics. The Code

the aim of how the Group is expected to manage business and relationships 
in accordance with the Code of Conduct.
Supplier relationships
	 G1-2    Management of relationships with suppliers
It is important that Swedbank applies the highest ethical standards when select-
ing suppliers. Segmenting the supplier base and identifying risk areas, as well as 
implementing adapted controls and follow-up, ensure the efficient management 
of supplier relationship. This provides Swedbank with the conditions to achieve 
compliance, minimise risks and build long-term relationships. 
Purchasing process 
Swedbank’s purchasing process is largely digitalised and includes the identifica-
tion and management of risks and impacts. To ensure compliance, Swedbank 
conducts comprehensive evaluations in the area of data and information secu-
rity, as well as business continuity, in order to minimise risks associated with out-
sourcing and critical suppliers. The process also includes checking conflicts of 
interest between purchasers and potential suppliers, and examining the anti-­
corruption work of suppliers. In addition to this, duality is used in the approval 
process for contracts, while background checks on consultants minimise the risk 
of corruption. To facilitate compliance with the purchasing process, Swedbank 
offers training courses for employees in the purchasing organisation and other 
stakeholders, such as purchasers and contract owners.The Group has also 
­developed guidelines and manuals for purchasing and risk management. 
The purchasing process stipulates that suppliers must sign the Group’s sus-
tainability requirements and Supplier Code of Conduct, which contain special 
clauses on corruption and bribery. Suppliers are also asked to answer questions 
about corruption and bribery in order to identify potential high-risk areas. Sustain-
ability evaluations are based on geographical and sectoral risks, covering environ-
mental, social and business ethical aspects through questionnaires. If a supplier 
does not meet expectations, an action plan for improvement is created. In 2025, 
139 dialogues were conducted to follow up on suppliers’ responses and support 
the development of their sustainability work. Swedbank does not currently moni-
tor local or certified suppliers, as they are deemed to be low-risk suppliers. 
Supplier Code of Conduct
Swedbank’s Supplier Code of Conduct describes the Group’s requirements in the 
area of business ethics with regard to human rights, working conditions and the 
environment. Suppliers are expected to distribute the content of the Code of Con-
duct further along their value chain, and are recommended to establish their own 
whistleblower processes. The Code of Conduct must be signed by the supplier in 
connection with the signing of a contract, unless an assessment is made that the 
supplier is already applying equivalent policies. If the supplier does not sign the 
Code of Conduct, a dialogue is initiated to reach an agreement on signing or 
­possible exemptions, agreed by the purchasing unit’s sustainability committee. 
Violations of the Code are considered a breach of contract and may result in 
a collaboration being terminated.

Actions relating to supplier relationships
During the year, Swedbank developed a method of conducting different types of 
supplier inspections, including audits. The purpose is to ensure compliance with 
risk-related requirements, increase transparency and accountability, and promote 
long-term collaboration with suppliers that share Swedbank’s values. In 2025, an 
update of internal rules on continuity management was also initiated to improve 
the management of disruption and ensure uninterrupted operation in critical 
functions, which strengthens the organisation’s resilience and better meets 
­customer expectations. 
The work that began in 2025 to strengthen the central unit for follow-up on 
strategic supplier partnerships has made it possible to conduct wide-ranging 
assessments of the entire supplier base. At the same time, the Code of Conduct 
has been updated with requirements for ESG data and rules on gifts and whistle­
blowing. The actions aim to reinforce preventive work against risks and ­negative 
impacts in the Group’s relationships with first-line suppliers, in line with relevant 
governance documents. 
Anti-corruption and bribery
	 G1-3    Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery
Swedbank has zero tolerance of corruption and bribery. The Group works to pre-
vent corruption and bribery in its operations and business relationships. In order 
to evaluate these initiatives, Swedbank has established internal processes for 
follow-up on preventive work.
Actions to prevent corruption and bribery
The Board of Directors determines Swedbank’s low-risk appetite in work against 
corruption and bribery and has, by delegation, established internal processes to 
evaluate the work and ensure that risk appetite is complied with and followed up 
continuously. An enterprise-wide risk assessment is conducted to identify and 
understand the risks associated with corruption and bribery to which the Group 
is exposed. The Group’s Chief Compliance Officer (CCO) reports quarterly to the 
CEO and the Board of Directors on Swedbank’s management of business ethics 
matters, on the effectiveness of Swedbank’s work to prevent corruption and 
­bribery, based on external and internal regulations and requirements, as well 
as risk appetite.
The Group’s independent compliance function, Group Compliance, works to 
monitor and identify the Group’s compliance risks, and evaluate the effectiveness 
of Swedbank’s internal rules and measures to maintain good business ethics, 
prevent corruption and bribery and maintain whistleblower protection. To ensure 
alignment with the Board’s risk appetite regarding compliance risks, the unit also 
provides advice and support to operations. 
Training in corruption and bribery
Swedbank has taken preventive measures against corruption and bribery in 2025 
in the form of training programmes to create awareness in its own operations. 
Training in the Group’s Code of Conduct addresses what employees, including 
the Group Executive Committee, should be aware of in relation to third parties, 
such as suppliers and consultants. Swedbank’s annual ethics training is con-
ducted digitally, applies at Group level, and includes general information on regu-
latory requirements, the reporting process, risks of insider trading, and permitted, 
prohibited, and inappropriate benefits. The training programme includes a sec-
tion on corruption and bribery at a basic level that covers external and internal 
regulations, risk assessments and preventive information. All units in the Group, 
including the Group Executive Committee, are required to complete the ethics 
training programme. For the Board of Directors’ training in sustainability-related 
issues, see GOV-1 The role of the administrative, supervisory and management 
bodies on page 92. 
In addition to the annual ethics training programme, two new programmes 
were launched in 2025 to further develop Swedbank’s work to prevent corruption 
and bribery, which was a planned action described in the 2024 Annual Report. 
One of the programmes is aimed at all managers at Swedbank, including the 
Group Executive Committee, and relates to the corruption risks they may encoun-
ter in their managerial role. The second programme is aimed at customer-facing 
staff to increase awareness of corruption risks in their day-to-day work. The aim 
of the training programmes is to help employees to act in accordance with the 
Group’s Code of Conduct and ethical rules in both operations and business rela-
tionships, thereby reducing the risk of corruption and bribery not being detected. 
The programmes are in-depth and mandatory for all managers and all custom-
er-facing staff in the Group. The proportion of employees who have undergone 
the training programmes is followed up regularly. In 2025, work also progressed 
regarding in-depth mandatory training for contract owners with high-risk 
­contracts on what employees should be aware of in relation to third parties. 
Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery
In its work to prevent corruption and bribery, Swedbank conducts an enterprise­-
wide risk assessment to understand the risks to which the Group is exposed and 
where inadequate preventive measures against corruption and bribery may have 
a negative impact on society. Swedbank works actively to prevent this in both its 
operations and business relationships by regularly updating the risk assessment 
of corruption and bribery risks and implementing controls and processes to pre-
vent the risks that Swedbank faces. The risk assessment is conducted at least 
every two years or as required. The Group-wide risk assessment for 2024 was 
completed in 2025. The updated risk assessment includes an assessment of 
risks associated with, among other things, the countries in which Swedbank oper-
ates and changes in business operations that may increase the risk of corruption 
and bribery.
Swedbank continuously assesses where in the operation there is the greatest 
risk of corruption and bribery. The evaluation is based on the enterprise-wide risk 
assessment, investigations of employees suspected of violations of rules in 
2024 and events in the operating environment. The evaluation shows that the risk 
of corruption and bribery is higher for customer-facing employees and employ-
ees who deal with purchases, primarily for large contracts or contracts in coun-
tries where there is a high risk of corruption. Recruitment and the procurement of 
consultancy services are also deemed to be areas involving a risk of corruption 
and bribery. Furthermore, Swedbank works to identify vulnerable roles within the 
organisation rather than identifying vulnerable units, as employees with different 
roles and duties can be part of the same unit. 
Targets and metrics
	 G1-4    Incidents of corruption or bribery
Suspicions of corruption and bribery can be reported by internal and external 
stakeholders through Swedbank’s whistleblower function. The units that investi-
gate incidents of corruption and bribery are independent of the employees and 
departments being investigated. 
Swedbank does not report any publicly measurable outcome-oriented targets 
in the area of corruption and bribery, nor does the bank report comparisons over 
time. To follow up on the appropriateness of policies and actions, Swedbank has 
established internal processes for follow-up. Group Compliance monitors risk 
development on an ongoing basis, and tests whether Swedbank’s controls and 
processes are effective and of the quality expected to ensure that the Group’s risk 
exposure remains low.

Economic Crime Prevention
Swedbank takes its responsibility to prevent and combat financial crime very 
seriously. The Group has a regulatory, system-critical and moral responsibility 
towards ­customers, shareholders and society at large to protect systems, prod-
ucts and ­services from being misused for criminal purposes. 
Policies
	 MDR-P    Policies
Swedbank’s Group Policy on Financial Crime Risk and Policy on Enterprise Risk 
Management are cornerstones of the work to combat impact and risk related to 
financial crime. Swedbank’s governance documents for business conduct are 
reported in G1-1 Policies for business conduct and corporate culture on page 141. 
Actions to counteract financial crime
	 MDR-A    Actions
As a leading financial actor in the Nordic and Baltic countries, Swedbank has 
developed strategic initiatives and proactive measures to combat potential 
impact relating to financial crime, both in its own operations and downstream 
in the value chain. This enables the Group to comply with its commitments and 
effectively manage risks relating to money laundering, violations or circumven-
tions of financial sanctions, facilitation of tax evasion and fraud. Swedbank has 
not identified significant capital or operating expenditure for the measures in 
addition to the resources already integrated in routine financial planning. 
Money laundering, financial sanctions and facilitation  
of tax evasion
Swedbank works continuously to adapt and develop internal processes linked to 
the prevention of financial crime. Key elements in this work are customer risk 
classification, transaction monitoring, sanction screening and regulatory report-
ing of suspected money laundering and financing of terrorism, as well as viola-
tions of sanctions.
A key starting point for Swedbank is the identification and understanding of 
the risks to which the Group is exposed. Swedbank has therefore established an 
enterprise-wide risk assessment process that forms the basis of the actions 
taken. Swedbank conducts enterprise-wide risk assessments at least annually in 
respect of the risk of the Group’s products and services being used for financial 
crime. The assessment is data-driven and indicates risk exposure based on 
­customer, product, geographical area and distribution channels.
Another important aspect is training and compliance culture. Swedbank 
focuses on ensuring that all employees receive training and information, based 
on their role and duties at work. In addition to the basic training provided to all 
employees, there is also a tailored training programme designed based on identi-
fied risks and aimed at strengthening the areas where the need for enhanced 
knowledge is greatest. Training is the key to developing and maintaining a good 
compliance culture in the operation.
Swedbank works continuously to develop the Group’s ability to prevent finan-
cial crime in the value chain, by strengthening both awareness and overall risk 
management competence. The effectiveness of Swedbank’s preventive work 
also depends on collaboration with Swedish law enforcement agencies and other 
banks. Swedbank participates actively in SAMLIT Economic Crime Prevention, 
a collaborative body between the police and the five largest banks in Sweden. 
Swedbank has also participated in multiple information-sharing initiatives with 
law enforcement agencies. Together, these external activities and sharing initia-
tives provide increased understanding, knowledge and efficiency in the Group’s 
internal activities to prevent financial crime. 
Fraud
Swedbank’s work to prevent and investigate fraud is based on three strategic levels 
of action: prevent, detect and respond. These help to prevent fraud and are continu-
ously strengthened through improvements in the security of products and chan-
nels, development of transaction monitoring and the streamlining of processes.
Finance Sweden has worked together with Swedish banks to develop a joint 
package of measures to further strengthen customer protection against fraud, 
both in own operations and downstream in the value chain. These measures have 
been applied in full by Swedbank. In 2025, the package of measures was 
expanded with additional measures, primarily aimed at investment and romance 
fraud. These extended measures are to be implemented in the banks during 2026 
at the latest. 
Swedbank has long been working continuously to strengthen customer protec-
tion against fraud in various ways, through product development, monitoring of 
transactions and development of day-to-day operations to manage attempted 
fraud and investigate incidents. Swedbank works continuously to help affected 
customers by stopping ongoing fraud, and also by recovering funds and restoring 
affected customers’ accounts. A joint fraud collaboration has been established 
between the biggest Swedish banks with the aim of sharing information about 
fraud trends and new modus operandi. The collaboration with Finance Sweden 
and SAMLIT Economic Crime Prevention takes place within different areas of 
fraud and working groups, to share experiences and lessons learned from day- 
to-day operations, and to follow up and evaluate the effects of the measures the 
banks have introduced. 
As one of Sweden’s largest banks, fraud via Swedbank’s products and services 
reflects the general development of fraud in society. Despite the volume of fraud 
remaining high, a decrease was noted in the first half of 2025 compared to the 
previous year. This trend is confirmed in the Swedish Financial Supervisory 
Authority’s statistics on payment service fraud and the Swedish Police’s statis-
tics on proceeds of crime from fraud. Customer losses due to fraud in Swedbank 
also decreased during the year. The reduction can be assumed to be an effect of 
the Group’s work on enhanced security in products, controls and processes, as 
well as increased awareness of fraud in society. For fraud through social manipu-
lation via phone and text message, called vishing/smishing, the reduction is par-
ticularly noticeable. On the other hand, there has been an increase in investment 
fraud, where fraudsters trick customers into investing in false or misleading 
investment opportunities. The levels of other types of fraud remained largely 
unchanged during the year.
Targets and metrics 
	 MDR-T    Target 
Swedbank has a low risk appetite for financial crime. This low risk appetite is 
established in internal regulations and monitored continuously by Swedbank’s 
independent compliance function, Group Compliance, which works on the 
Group’s management of compliance risks. To follow up on the appropriateness 
of policies and actions, Swedbank has established internal processes for fol-
low-up. Swedbank continuously monitors risk development and assesses 
whether controls and processes are adequate and sufficient to ensure that Swed-
bank’s risk exposure remains low. Reporting takes place quarterly to the CEO and 
the Board of Directors. In accordance with the anti-money laundering regulations, 
Swedbank has also established the role of an appointed officer for controlling 
and reporting obligations. The appointed officer reports to the Board of Directors 
on a quarterly and annual basis on Swedbank’s work to prevent financial crime in 
relation to external regulations and Swedbank’s risk appetite. Swedbank does not 
report any publicly measurable outcome-oriented targets in this area, nor does 
the bank report comparisons over time. The Group’s assessment is that publica-
tion of specific targets and metrics would provide unjustified insight into Swed-
bank’s control systems.

1. Basis of accounting
The financial reports and the consolidated financial statements are prepared in 
accordance with the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS Account-
ing standards), as adopted by the EU, and interpretations of them. The standards 
are issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) and the inter-
pretations by the IFRS Interpretations Committee. The standards and interpreta-
tions become mandatory for Swedbank’s consolidated financial statements 
­concurrently with their approval by the EU. 
The consolidated financial statements are also prepared according to the 
Swedish Corporate Reporting Board’s recommendation RFR 1 Complementary 
accounting rules for Groups and pronouncements, certain complementary rules 
in the Annual Accounts Act for Credit Institutions and Securities Companies and 
the regulations and general advice of the Swedish Financial Supervisory 
­Authority, FFFS 2008:25. 
The financial statements are presented in Swedish kronor and all figures are 
rounded to millions of kronor (SEKm) unless otherwise indicated. Adjustments 
for rounding are not made, therefore summation differences may occur.
The accounting policies and presentation remain unchanged in comparison 
to the 2024 Annual and sustainability report, except for the changes described in 
section 2 – Changes in accounting policies and changed presentation.
1.1 Critical accounting judgements and estimates
The preparation of the Group’s financial statements requires executive manage-
ment to make judgements, assumptions and estimates that affect the applica-
tion of the Group’s accounting policies and the reported amounts and disclo-
sures. The executive management bases its judgements and estimates on 
previous experience and several other factors that are considered reasonable 
under the circumstances. Actual results may deviate from the judgements and 
estimates applied.
 The critical judgements and estimates which executive management has 
assessed to have the most significant effects are described in the sections 
below.
•	Consolidated financial statements 
•	Financial instruments – Measurement of fair value
•	Financial instruments – Credit impairments
•	Intangible assets – Goodwill
•	Provisions and contingent liabilities
•	Pensions

3. Material accounting policies and critical 
accounting judgements and estimates
3.1 Consolidated financial statements 
The consolidated financial statements comprise the Parent company and those 
entities over which the Parent company has control. The Parent company has 
control when it has power and is capable of managing the relevant activities of 
another entity, it is exposed to variable returns, and it is able to use its power to 
affect those returns. These entities are subsidiaries and are included in the con-
solidated financial statements in accordance with the acquisition method from 
the day control is obtained and are excluded from the day control ceases.
According to the acquisition method, an acquired entity’s identifiable assets, 
liabilities and contingent liabilities that satisfy the recognition criteria are rec-
ognised and measured at fair value upon acquisition. Any surplus between the 
cost of the business combination (purchase price) and the fair value of the 
acquired share of identifiable assets, liabilities and reported contingent liabilities 
is recognised as goodwill. If the cost of the business combination is less than the 
fair value of the acquired company’s net assets, the difference is recognised 
directly in the income statement. The cost of the business combination includes 
the fair value of transferred assets and liabilities. Acquisition-related costs are 
recognised when they arise. A subsidiary’s contribution to equity includes only 
the equity that arises between acquisition and disposal. All intragroup transac-
tions and intragroup gains are eliminated. 
Holdings in non-controlling interests, the minority, are the part of the Group’s 
net assets that are not directly or indirectly owned by Swedbank AB. The minority 
share of subsidiary profits are included in the Group’s income statement and its 
share of the net assets are recognised separately as non-controlling interests 
within equity in the balance sheet.
Critical accounting judgements and estimates  
– ­Consolidated financial statements
Entities in the Group have established investment funds for their customers’ sav-
ings needs. The Group manages the assets of these funds on behalf of custom-
ers with investment contracts in accordance with the predetermined fund obliga-
tions approved by the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority. The return 
generated by these assets, as well as the risk of a change in value, is borne by 
customers. Within the framework of the approved fund terms, the Group receives 
management fees as well as, in certain cases, application and withdrawal fees for 
the management duties it performs. The decisions regarding the management of 
an investment fund are governed by the fund’s predetermined obligations. 
Since the Group determines the terms of the funds and is acting within them, 
the Group has the power over the decision making of the relevant activities of the 
investment funds. The Group’s exposure to variable returns from its involvement 
in the funds is primarily related to the management fees charged. In certain 
cases, Group entities also invest in the investment funds to fulfil their obligations 
to customers and these holdings represent an additional variable exposure in the 
investment funds. The Group’s interests in total are seen as a principal activity for 
the Group’s own benefit where the variable exposure over a longer period of time 
exceeds 35 per cent in an investment fund or 22 per cent in an alternative invest-
ment fund, and, consequently, the investment fund would be controlled and con-
solidated. In all other cases investment funds are not consolidated, instead the 
Group is considered to act as agent on behalf of the investment funds’ investors. 
The Group considers that holdings in investment funds through unit-linked 
mutual insurance contracts do not result in a variable exposure and are therefore 
excluded from the assessment of control over such investment funds. Holdings 
in investment funds through unit-linked mutual insurance contracts of SEK 383bn 
(349) are recognised as Financial assets for which the customer bears the invest-
ment risk and the corresponding liabilities of SEK 383bn (349) are recognised as 
Financial liabilities for which the customer bears the investment risk. If the Group 
had considered such holdings to be a variable exposure and that it had control 
over such investment funds, additional financial assets and financial liabilities 
corresponding to SEK 182bn (203) respectively would have been recognised in 
the Group’s balance sheet.
3.2 Associates and joint ventures 
Associates are entities where the Group has significant influence. Joint ventures 
are entities where the Group and one or more parties have joint control of another 
entity. Investments in associates and joint ventures are accounted for according 
to the equity method. 
The equity method means that the participating interests in an entity are rec-
ognised at cost at the time of acquisition and are subsequently adjusted for the 
owned share of the change in the entity’s net assets. Goodwill attributable to an 
associate or joint venture is included in the carrying amount of the participating 
interest and is not amortised. The carrying amount of the participating interests 
is compared with the recoverable amount of the net investment in an associate 
or joint venture to determine whether an impairment need exists. This is per-
formed annually or when events occur that would indicate a decrease in value.
The owned share of an associate’s or a joint venture’s profit according to the 
entity’s income statement including tax and together with any impairment, is rec-
ognised on a separate line in the income statement, Share of profit or loss of 
associates and joint ventures. The associates’ and joint ventures’ reporting dates 
and accounting policies conform to the Group’s.
3.3 Assets and liabilities in foreign currencies
The consolidated financial statements are presented in SEK, which is also the 
Parent company’s functional currency and presentation currency. The functional 
currency of a separate business within the Group, which may be a Group entity or 
a branch, is defined as the currency in which the business primarily generates 
and expends cash, but also where the business acts as an extension of the 
reporting entity rather than acting with a significant degree of independence.
3.3.1 Transactions in a currency other than the functional 
currency
Transactions in a currency other than the functional currency, foreign currency, are 
initially recorded at the exchange rate prevailing at the transaction date. Monetary 
assets and liabilities in a foreign currency and non-monetary assets in a foreign 
currency measured at fair value are translated at the rates prevailing at the closing 
date. All gains and losses on the translation of monetary items and non-monetary 
items measured at fair value are recognised as changes in exchange rates in the 
income statement within Net gains and losses on financial items.
3.3.2 Translation of foreign operations to the Group’s 
­presentation currency
Assets and liabilities in subsidiaries and associates with a functional currency 
other than SEK are translated to the presentation currency at the closing date 
exchange rate. The income statement is translated at the exchange rate for each 
transaction. For practical purposes, the average rate for the period is generally 
used. Exchange rate differences that arise are recognised in other comprehen-
sive income.
Financial liabilities in a functional currency other than the presentation cur-
rency which hedge net investments in foreign operations are translated at the 
closing date exchange rate. When the requirements for hedge accounting are 
met, exchange rate differences attributable to hedges of net investments in for-
eign operations are recognised in other comprehensive income, net of deferred 
tax. Ineffectiveness in such hedges is recognised directly in the income state-
ment in Net gains and losses on financial items. When subsidiaries and associ-
ates are divested, cumulative translation differences and exchange rate differ-
ences are reclassified from other comprehensive income to the income 
statement.

3.4 Operating segments 
Segment reporting is presented based on the executive management’s view and 
relates to the parts of the Group that are defined as operating segments. Operat-
ing segments are identified based on internal reports to the Group’s chief operat-
ing decision maker, which is the Chief Executive Officer (CEO). The internal 
reports used by the CEO to oversee operations and make decisions on allocating 
resources serve as the basis for the information presented.
The accounting policies for operating segments consist of the Group’s 
accounting policies and policies that specifically refer to segment reporting, 
which are described in note G5 Operating segments. 
3.5 Financial instruments – General 
Financial instruments are classified on relevant lines of the balance sheet 
depending on the nature of the instrument and the counterparty. If a financial 
instrument does not have a specific counterparty or is listed on the market, the 
instrument is classified in the balance sheet as securities. Financial liabilities 
where the creditor has a lower priority than others are classified in the balance 
sheet as Subordinated liabilities. Senior non-preferred liabilities that fulfil the 
minimum requirements for own funds and eligible liabilities (MREL) are pre-
sented on a separate line in the balance sheet.
3.5.1 Recognition and derecognition 
Financial assets and liabilities are initially recognised in the balance sheet when 
the entity becomes part of the instruments contractual terms. Regular way pur-
chase or sale of financial instruments measured at fair value, are recognised on 
the trade date. The trade date is the date that an entity commits itself to purchase 
or sell an instrument. Financial assets are derecognised when the right to receive 
cash flows from a financial asset has expired or the Group has transferred sub-
stantially all the risks and rewards of ownership to another party. Financial liabili-
ties are derecognised when the obligation in an agreement has been discharged, 
cancelled or expired.
3.5.2 Derivatives
All derivatives are measured and reported at fair value in the balance sheet. Deriv-
atives with positive fair values, including accrued interest, are reported as assets 
within Derivatives with the corresponding principle applied to liabilities. Realised 
and unrealised results are recognised in the income statement within Net gains 
and losses on financial items. The accounting principles for hedge accounting 
are applied where a derivative is identified as a hedging instrument and are pre-
sented in section 3.9. 
3.5.3 Embedded derivatives
An embedded derivative is a component of a hybrid instrument that also includes 
a non-derivative host contract. The impact of an embedded derivative is such that 
some of the instrument’s cash flows vary in a manner similar to a standalone 
derivative. Embedded derivatives in liabilities, finance leases and other non-finan-
cial assets are recognised as separate derivatives when risks and characteristics 
are not closely related to those of the host contract. Derivatives are not separated 
if the host contract is measured at fair value through profit or loss. 
Financial assets in scope of IFRS 9 Financial Instruments are not assessed for 
the existence of embedded derivatives. Each contract is considered in its entirety, 
including any features that alter the contractual cash flows, when concluding 
whether the contractual cash flows only consist of principal amount and interest.
3.5.4 Repurchase transactions
A repurchase transaction is defined as a contract where the parties have agreed 
on the sale of securities and the subsequent repurchase of corresponding assets 
at a predetermined price. The payment received is recognised as a financial liabil-
ity on the balance sheet, based on the counterparty. In a repurchase transaction, 
the sold security remains on the balance sheet, since the Group is exposed to the 
risk that the security will fluctuate in value.
The securities sold are also disclosed as pledged assets. The proceeds paid for 
acquired securities, so-called reverse repos, are recognised on the balance sheet 
based on the counterparty. The difference between the spot and forward price is 
accrued as interest.
3.5.5 Securities loans
Securities that have been lent remain on the balance sheet, since the Group 
remains exposed to the risk that they will fluctuate in value. Securities that have 
been lent are recognised on the trade date as assets pledged, while borrowed 
securities are not reported as assets. Securities that are lent are measured in the 
same way as other security holdings of the same type. Where borrowed securi-
ties are sold, so-called short-selling, an amount corresponding to the fair value of 
the securities is recognised within Other liabilities on the balance sheet.
3.5.6 Loan commitments
Irrevocable loan commitments are recognised off balance and are subject to 
credit impairment testing. Associated credit impairment provisions are rec-
ognised as provisions within Other liabilities and provisions in the balance sheet. 
The accounting policies for credit impairment provisions are presented in  
section 3.8.
3.5.7 Offsetting
Financial assets and financial liabilities are offset and recognised net in the bal-
ance sheet where there is a legal right of set-off, both in the normal course of 
business and in the event of bankruptcy, and there is intent to settle the items 
with a net amount or to simultaneously realise the asset and settle the liability.
3.6 Financial instruments – Classification and 
­measurement
Financial assets are classified in one of the following valuation categories:
•	Amortised cost
•	Fair value through profit or loss – mandatorily
•	Held for trading
•	Other
The classification is based on the entity’s business model for managing the asset 
and the asset’s contractual terms. 
The business model reflects how the Group manages portfolios of financial 
assets. The factors considered in determining the business model for a portfolio 
of financial assets include how the financial assets’ performance is evaluated 
and reported to management, how risks are assessed and managed, compensa-
tion models as well as frequency, volume, reason and timing for sales.
The Group assesses the contractual terms of financial assets to identify 
whether the contractual cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest. 
In making this assessment, consideration is taken whether the contractual cash 
flows are consistent with a basic lending arrangement. Principal is defined as the 
fair value of the financial asset on initial recognition. Interest is defined as the 
compensation for the time value of money, credit risk, other basic lending risks 
and profit margin. Where the contractual terms introduce exposure to risk or vola-
tility that are inconsistent with a basic lending arrangement, the related financial 
asset is not compliant with the solely payments of principal and interest criterion 
and the asset is measured at fair value.
Financial liabilities are classified in one of the following valuation categories:
•	Amortised cost
•	Fair value through profit or loss
•	Held for trading
•	Designated at fair value through profit or loss, fair value option
Financial assets and financial liabilities are presented per balance sheet item and 
valuation category in note G45 Valuation categories of financial instruments.
